#5582. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

Want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

A sold comp tells us where a buyer said yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

One of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”

When I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

This is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”

Twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:

We’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

#5581. Sanctuary Wealth Secures $250 Million Commitment from Kennedy Lewis to Support Partner Firms at Every Stage of Their Growth and Evolution

New capital will fund continued investment in Sanctuary's platform, provide more affiliation and liquidity options for Partner Firms and expand financing of both organic and inorganic growth strategies

MIAMI, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Sanctuary Wealth ("Sanctuary"), a leading platform that provides elite financial advisors the freedom, flexibility, control and choice to thrive in an evolving industry, today announced that existing investor Kennedy Lewis Investment Management ("Kennedy Lewis") has committed $250 million in new growth capital to the firm.

The investment will allow Sanctuary to broaden the expertise its Partner Firms can draw on to serve clients more comprehensively, attract new business and pursue acquisitions. It will also give Sanctuary greater flexibility to provide capital when Partner Firm owners want to finance growth, monetize a portion of their equity or prepare for succession.

"Sanctuary's platform was built to help wirehouse advisors become independent, deepen relationships with their clients and build enterprise value in firms of their own. That heritage remains central to Sanctuary's identity and growth strategy," said Adam Malamed, Chief Executive Officer of Sanctuary Wealth. "As our Partner Firms continue to evolve, this new capital enhances our ability to invest in what they need as established businesses, giving them more ways to grow and their owners more options for realizing the value they have created."

The depth and breadth of the platform Sanctuary has developed over the past eight years has attracted increasing interest from advisors and independent wealth management firms across the industry. In response, the firm has added affiliation options to give the industry's most sophisticated advisors more choice and flexibility to pursue their vision and objectives.

"Our Partner Firms are our clients, and we have to earn their business every day," said Vince Fertitta and Robert Walter, Co-Presidents of Sanctuary Wealth. "After years of helping advisors build enterprise value in their firms, we want them to have more ways to put that value to work. Founders should be able to monetize their businesses on their own timeline by selling a minority or majority stake and keep leading the business on the same independent terms that made ownership so attractive to them in the first place."

Sanctuary's network now includes 125 Partner Firms, with $71 billion in assets on the platform or in transition. To date, Sanctuary has made 13 minority investments in its Partner Firms.

Building on a partnership established in 2022The $250 million commitment from Kennedy Lewis, a multi-strategy private credit manager with approximately $40 billion in assets under management, consists of $50 million in mandatory convertible debt and a $200 million delayed-draw term loan. Kennedy Lewis has also elected to convert its existing outstanding convertible debt investment in Sanctuary into equity.

"Our partnership with Sanctuary demonstrates what can be accomplished when a talented leadership team and a committed capital partner share a common vision," said David Chene, Co-Founder of Kennedy Lewis. "We have tremendous confidence in Adam and his team, who have overseen growth that includes doubling the number of Partner Firms and almost tripling the assets on the platform since our initial investment in 2022. We believe Sanctuary is uniquely positioned to help independent advisors build and grow valuable businesses and are excited to deepen our partnership to support this next chapter."

"Sanctuary carefully considered the best path forward for this new phase of our evolution and chose to expand our relationship with Kennedy Lewis," continued Malamed. "Kennedy Lewis understands our business and is completely aligned with our focus on helping our Partner Firms achieve their full potential. We look forward to continuing this constructive relationship and working together to capture Sanctuary's long-term opportunity."

The transaction follows a thorough evaluation and negotiation of financing proposals by a dedicated committee of Sanctuary's Board. The transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to customary closing conditions, including the expiration or termination of the applicable waiting period under the Hart Scott Rodino Act and FINRA approval.

Goldman Sachs served as exclusive financial advisor to Sanctuary in connection with the transaction, and Willkie Farr & Gallagher LLP served as legal advisor. Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld LLP served as legal advisor to Kennedy Lewis.

About Sanctuary WealthSanctuary is a leading hybrid RIA that provides comprehensive wealth management solutions and platform partnerships to sophisticated independent wealth management firms.

Through its Partnered Independence model, Sanctuary helps advisors seeking greater freedom, flexibility, control and choice transition from large financial institutions to build enduring businesses of their own.

Sanctuary Wealth was built to serve elite wirehouse breakaway advisors. Today, Sanctuary supports a growing community of Partner Firms across a range of business models with integrated technology, marketing, operations and a robust, open-architecture platform, enabling advisors to serve clients at the highest level while building long-term enterprise value.

#5580. Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont said in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

“Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an important step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

“I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s important to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

“A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”

#5579. New-home mortgage applications fall 13.6% in October

Mortgage applications for new-home purchases fell 13.6% year over year and 7% from September, according to MBA’s Builder Application Survey. Rising mortgage rates and affordability pressures contributed to the decline.  AI Summary

Mortgage applications for new-home purchases fell 13.6% year over year in October as rising mortgage rates and affordability pressures weighed on buyer demand, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association’s (MBA) Builder Application Survey.

Applications also declined 7% from September. The figures are not adjusted for seasonal patterns.

The 30-year fixed mortgage rate climbed about 60 basis points over the two months leading up to October, reaching 7.5% last month, said Joel Kan, MBA’s vice president and deputy chief economist.

“As a result, applications for the purchase of newly built homes declined year-over-year for the fourth consecutive month,” Kan said.

MBA’s estimate of new-home sales increased slightly in October, but the annualized sales pace for the past two months remained at its weakest level since July 2022. Affordability pressures and uncertainty surrounding mortgage rates have prompted prospective buyers to delay purchases, even as builders continue offering incentives, Kan said.

MBA estimated that new single-family home sales ran at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 592,000 units in October, up 1.4% from September’s pace of 584,000 units.

On an unadjusted basis, MBA estimated 44,000 new-home sales in October, down 6.4% from 47,000 in September.

Conventional loans accounted for 47.9% of new-home mortgage applications in October, while Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loans made up 36.9%. U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) loans accounted for 14.1%, and  U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) loans represented 1%.

The average loan size for new homes declined to $368,934 in October from $374,724 in September.

MBA’s Builder Application Survey tracks mortgage application volume from homebuilder-affiliated mortgage companies nationwide. The association uses the data, along with other market information and assumptions, to estimate new-home sales at the national, state and metropolitan levels.

The survey provides an early indication of new-home sales because mortgage applications typically coincide with contract signings, when the Census Bureau records new-home sales in its monthly report.

#5578. /C O R R E C T I O N - Relativity/

In the news release, Most Legal Professionals Say AI Has Not Yet Changed Hiring, According to a Relativity Study, issued 12-Nov-2026 by Relativity over PR Newswire, we are advised by the company that changes have been made. The complete, corrected release follows, with additional details at the end:

CHICAGO, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Relativity, a legal data intelligence company, today announced findings from AI in Legal: 2026 Research Data, with research and analysis by International Data Corporation (IDC), a new study examining how legal professionals are adopting and governing AI. The study combines primary research from IDC, a survey of state court judges conducted by Relativity and the National Association of Women Judges (NAWJ), and findings from the upcoming eighth annual edition of The General Counsel Report, produced by Relativity and FTI Consulting. Together, these perspectives offer a broad view of AI use across the legal landscape, along with the growing importance of trust, governance and accountability.

The study draws on research conducted from April to October 2026, incorporating feedback from 700 legal professionals across 20 nations, including an IDC study of 401 respondents. Participants included lawyers, paralegals, legal technologists and legal IT professionals. The countries represented are Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, China (Hong Kong), Colombia, France, Germany, India, Ireland, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Singapore, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom and the United States.

"In this 2026 follow-up to our 2024 study, the data show that AI use in the legal profession is now a fait accompli. The question is no longer 'Are legal teams using AI?' but 'How and why are lawyers and their colleagues using it?'" said David Horrigan, Discovery Counsel and Legal Education Director at Relativity. "Some of the data, such as more than 91.0% of chief legal officers and more than 80.0% of all legal professionals using AI, was not surprising at all. What did surprise us was that, for most respondents, AI has had no effect on hiring at this point, and more reported adding staff than cutting it."

AI has not yet upended hiring or billing in aggregate

The data suggest AI is not yet driving widespread staffing reductions. According to IDC, 57.9% of respondents said AI has had no impact on their hiring, and more reported increasing hiring (24.2%) than decreasing it (9.2%).

"Many have predicted that AI will end the billable hour on the theory that faster work will lead clients to demand task-based billing," said Horrigan. "The research indicates that has not happened broadly, at least not yet."

The billable hour remains the most common primary billing method among law firms (45.7%), ahead of hybrid billing (31.8%), task-based billing (17.2%), and contingency fees (5.3%).

The research also points to cost savings, with 82.8% of respondents saying AI has saved their organization money.

AI becomes the baseline, not the differentiator

The research indicates 80.5% of legal professionals and more than 91.0% of chief legal officers currently use AI in their legal work, and more than 99.0% of respondents either use it now or plan to within 12 months. The level of usage is also growing, with 93.0% of respondents saying they have increased their AI use, by an average of 65.0%, while just 0.9% have decreased it.

Outlook on and adoption of AI differ by role

According to data from The General Counsel Report, 86.8% of chief legal officers are very or somewhat optimistic about AI.

Judges, by contrast, are adopting AI at a slower pace. Data from the Relativity-NAWJ survey indicate 16.6% of respondents never use AI and another 33.3% use it only rarely. About one in five federal and state judges (20.4% and 20.0%, respectively) prohibit court staff from using AI, while 7.4% of federal judges and 14.2% of state judges permit and encourage it.

Their outlook is also more divided. In the Relativity-NAWJ survey, 47.1% of state court judges said they are very or somewhat optimistic, and 36.0% said they are very or somewhat concerned. Among federal judges surveyed by The Sedona Conference, 43.6% were optimistic, and 41.7% were concerned.

Accuracy beats speed, and trust beats cost

In the IDC research, trust consistently outweighed speed and cost. When forced to choose, respondents favored accuracy over speed by 92.3% to 7.7%, and higher trust over lower cost by 79.3% to 20.7%. Respondents also preferred keeping a human in the loop (64.1%) over complete automation (35.9%).

As AI agents enter legal workflows, the study indicates that oversight will determine whether trust keeps pace with adoption. For agentic AI, respondents said human approval (67.0%) and mandatory source citations (60.0%) are the most commonly required safeguards.

Security posture (59.9%), governance capabilities (59.4%) and clear AI principles (51.9%) are the top three qualities legal professionals look for in AI vendors.

"Buyers aren't shopping for features first," said O'Leary. "They're checking whether you're safe to let near their data."

Inside organizations, governance work is still underway: about 91.0% have an AI governance framework in place or in progress, yet only 23.0% have fully adopted one, and 9.0% have no plans at all, according to IDC's research.

Concerns about accuracy and data security remain the gatekeepers to deeper adoption. Hallucinations, which were not a leading concern in the 2024 study, are now respondents' top worry (52.0%), followed by data loss (46.0%) and data bias (41.0%). Yet hallucinations are also the risk legal professionals feel best equipped to handle: 44.7% say they are almost or fully prepared for them, and only 15.5% say they are not prepared at all.

To learn more about the findings in AI in Legal: 2026 Research Data, with research and analysis by IDC, download the full study here.

Relativity is a leading legal data intelligence company that builds technology to help users organize data, discover the truth, and act on it. Its AI platform, Relativity aiR, transforms complex data into actionable insights at massive scale for litigation, investigations, regulatory inquiries, data breach responses, and other legal use cases. The world's largest law firms and corporations, government agencies, and a robust network of channel partners rely on Relativity's legal AI to securely surface and manage the most relevant and impactful information in their matters. The company also expands access to technology by providing its platform at no cost to academic institutions through its Relativity Academic program and to organizations supporting pro bono legal work through its Justice for Change initiative.

#5575. Enterprise AI hits a wall of power and cooling, not GPU supply

Enterprises racing to build AI factories and push edge inference into the field are learning that buying graphics processing units is the easy part. Power, cooling and network throughput now decide whether those costly systems produce intelligence or sit idle.

Those physical limits shaped much of the high-performance computing and AI conversation at SC26, where commercial AI infrastructure increasingly shares the floor with scientific computing. Rack densities that once topped out at about 10 kilowatts are now on a path toward a megawatt, a step change that forces enterprises to look both above and below the traditional network, storage and compute layers, according to Jack Hogan (pictured), vice president of advanced growth technologies at SHI International Corp.

“When we look at the full stack, we recognize that customers are getting tripped up. They can go get the GPUs, but they can’t power them. They can’t cool them,” Hogan said. “These are not cheap systems either. Procuring the infrastructure is just the start.”

Hogan spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed edge inference and how power, networking, model choice and business outcomes are reshaping the way enterprises build and run AI infrastructure. (* Disclosure below.)

The economics of AI infrastructure are shifting along with the hardware. Enterprises once sized deployments by the rack unit or the rack, but entire data centers now operate as a single system with shared memory, and every GPU must be kept fed to justify its cost. That change has altered how SHI measures success, Hogan explained.

“Now we’re talking about row and now data center scale. … We’re measuring that now in megawatts,” Hogan said. “So the megawatt now starts to become a measurement that people start to grasp and understand. How many flops can you get through that megawatt? How fast can you process your tokens?”

SHI’s role spans the full life cycle of these systems. Drawing on 37 years in the industry, the company builds customized racks in its integration facilities around the globe and runs pre-site assessments so systems can be powered on as soon as they arrive. In a recent New Jersey project, SHI is hosting and operating the customer’s system in its own data center. Location matters at the edge, too, where workloads such as video input generate data that must be processed in place, Hogan noted.

“You can’t backhaul that. The networks are not necessarily the right way to move that,” Hogan said. “We’re creating the scenario of both the mega hyperscaler as well as the edge inference and be able to tie those two things together.”

Busy GPUs are not necessarily productive ones. SHI starts every engagement by asking customers what they are trying to achieve, then works backward to the right model, whether that means frontier intelligence or a small language model running on an edge device. Silicon follows the same logic, with GPUs, newer CPUs, inference-specific chips and neural processing units validated in the company’s AI and Cyber Lab.

“It’s not about the cost of the token or reducing the number of tokens or even finding cheaper tokens. It’s about optimizing and ensuring that those tokens are turning into business value,” Hogan said.

The Agency has released its 2027 Red Paper, examining the wealth dynamics, buyer preferences and design innovations shaping luxury real estate markets worldwide.

Affordability pressures are changing how Americans think about homeownership, with buyers prioritizing flexible living spaces, personal expression and long-term functionality, according to the 2027 Better Homes and Gardens Real Estate Trends Report.

The report identifies three trends: distinctive design, creative uses for existing space and longer-term homeownership.

Buyers are embracing color. More than half of respondents (55%) said distinctive color choices would make them more likely to purchase a home. Younger buyers were particularly receptive, with 79% of Gen Z respondents and 64% of millennials favoring distinctive colors, compared with 38% of baby boomers and older consumers.

Homeowners are maximizing existing space. With higher housing costs making moves and additions less practical, 53% said they had repurposed underused space within the past one to three years. Buyers are thinking longer term. Consumers are considering how homes can accommodate multiple life stages. Nearly one-third (31%) would accept an older home needing updates, while 30% would compromise on square footage.

#5572. What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in New York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He said he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”

His co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be said for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

“I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan said. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”

Jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

“Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he said. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

Daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she said, but it showed cold.

“By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova said. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”

For mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

“If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova said. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

She leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

He also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

“In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer said. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea says she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”

Marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

His Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

“Every week, I share new songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”

On setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she said.

As for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova said she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

So the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova said, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”

#5571. Etherscan Warns of Support System Access Attempts as Security Scares Hit Crypto and Banks

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Another day, another security scare. This time, Etherscan is warning users after detecting attempts to gain unauthorized access to its customer support system. But the timing could hardly be worse for an industry already dealing with a growing list of cyberattacks.

The warning comes just days after hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely, injecting malicious code into websites operated by 178 organizations. The affected names included HSBC, BBC, Ledger, IKEA, Salesforce, Zoom, and CNN.

Meanwhile, crypto platforms have faced separate attacks involving compromised API keys, protocol vulnerabilities, and stolen customer information. Traditional banking has not escaped either, with a French bank recently losing approximately €100 million to hackers.

So what kind of security era are we entering? The problem is no longer confined to crypto exchanges or experimental DeFi protocols. Banks, technology companies, payment providers and blockchain businesses are increasingly exposed to the same interconnected digital infrastructure.

Etherscan disclosed earlier today that attackers had attempted to gain unauthorized access to its Freshworks customer support and ticketing system. The company is investigating and has introduced precautionary measures. It has not confirmed that customer records were successfully accessed, but warned users about suspicious support communications, unexpected links, and requests for sensitive information.

Security Notice: Reminder Regarding Etherscan Support CommunicationsEarlier today, we detected attempts to gain unauthorized access to our customer support and ticketing system (Freshworks).We are currently investigating the situation and taking precautionary measures.In…

The concern is particularly relevant because support impersonation remains an effective way to steal users’ crypto and money. An attacker posing as an Etherscan representative could exploit a user’s existing support request to make a phishing message appear legitimate.

But Etherscan is hardly the only name facing security questions this week. Just two days ago, hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s Web Experimentation signup process. They injected malicious JavaScript into customer projects, allowing the code to run on websites using the affected software.

Optimizely confirmed the vulnerability and said it had removed the injected code and fixed the flaw. Its November 17 incident report said the unauthorized party exploited the signup process rather than stealing customer administrator passwords.

The financial damage remains unclear. It is reported that investigators could not establish how many visitors were affected or whether the attempted thefts succeeded.

The uncomfortable takeaway is that attackers did not need to breach 178 separate companies. They exploited one software provider whose code was embedded across hundreds of websites.

Crypto’s security problems extend beyond Etherscan and the Optimizely incident. DeFiLlama’s hack tracker recorded several attacks during the week, including a $10.39 million incident involving Lighter Perps on November 16. The attacker exploited a compromised trader API key, enabling unauthorized withdrawals.

Lighter said its protocol and smart contracts were not compromised. It temporarily suspended withdrawals and activated Guardian mode to prevent further unauthorized activity.

Another incident hit MORE Markets, where an attacker exploited a lending mechanism to drain approximately $308,000 in WFLOW. B18 TimeBank also suffered an exploit on November 17, losing $404,540 in USDC through its reward voucher redemption mechanism.

These incidents show different weaknesses across crypto infrastructure. Not every loss comes from a broken smart contract. Compromised credentials, vulnerable applications and flawed authorization mechanisms can be equally damaging.

Traditional finance faces its own problems. French lender Crédit Mutuel Arkéa disclosed a cyber heist earlier in November, with hackers stealing approximately €100 million through fraudulent transactions originating from the bank’s own accounts. The bank said customer assets were not affected, although some transactions were temporarily suspended.

Deutsche Bank also made headlines on November 17 after confidential internal documents surfaced through an international journalistic investigation. It was a document leak, not a confirmed breach of its current banking systems.

Deutsche Bank said security testing found no indication that its current IT environment, account information, login credentials, or payment data had been compromised. Still, the leak could have wider geopolitical repercussions.

Banking institutions are not immune to major security incidents simply because they operate under traditional financial regulations.

Crypto has suffered enormous losses. The October Binance incident alone involved $6.3 billion in stolen digital assets, making it one of the largest cryptocurrency heists on record. Yet, traditional finance also faces attacks involving payment infrastructure, third-party service providers, and internal transaction systems.

The Optimizely incident is particularly revealing. Both HSBC and Ledger appeared among the affected organizations. The vulnerability did not care whether visitors were interacting with a traditional financial institution or a crypto company.

Neither system offers complete protection. The real question is whether companies can secure the increasingly complex infrastructure connecting their services. A single compromised vendor can expose hundreds of organizations, while one stolen credential can bypass otherwise sophisticated security systems.

Crypto users have every reason to demand stronger protections. But traditional banking customers should not mistake regulation and familiar branding for immunity.

With Etherscan investigating attempted unauthorized access, the data provider is now joining the growing list of companies dealing with security incidents.

#5570. Trust, talent and accountability define final day of Africa Tech Festival 2026

Africa Tech Festival, the continent's longest-running and most influential technology gathering, concluded its 29th edition at the Cape Town International Convention Centre, welcoming more than 15,000 delegates over the three days

CAPE TOWN, South Africa, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AI is opening up opportunities for African businesses to improve performance, develop new revenue streams and equip young people for a changing workplace. This was a central theme as Africa Tech Festival (www.AfricaTechFestival.com) 2026 concluded in Cape Town yesterday, with industry leaders sharing how digitalisation is changing the way companies operate, create jobs and broaden access to digital services.

Providing an enterprise perspective, Frederik Zietsman, Group CEO of Takealot, opened the final day's headline programme in conversation with Tomiwa Aladekomo, CEO of Big Cabal Media. Their discussion explored the realities of building a profitable e-commerce business in South Africa, including the importance of customer trust and investment in the infrastructure needed to reach consumers. "It starts and ends with trust. Because if you don't have trust, then ultimately, you fail," said Zietsman. He described how Takealot has invested in its own delivery infrastructure and developed a network of approximately 20,000 personal shoppers to help consumers in underserved communities access online retail.

Turning to Africa's role in the AI economy, Hardy Pemhiwa, President and Group CEO of Cassava Technologies, discussed how to make innovation more accessible and help local ideas reach wider markets. "I really would love to see an Africa where innovation is not limited by traditional education," he said, noting that AI could help overcome language barriers that have historically prevented promising ideas from being commercialised. Martin Manniche, CEO of AXON Networks, considered the role of automation and cloud-native technologies in modernising telecommunications infrastructure to support sophisticated digital services.

As technology changes how businesses operate, it is also changing the skills employers need and the opportunities available to young people. Charles Murito, Regional Director, Government Affairs and Public Policy, Sub-Saharan Africa at Google; Tiara Pathon, AI Skills Director at Microsoft; and Ziyad Cassim, Group CEO of UVU Africa, examined the implications for Africa's workforce. Murito asked how young people can move from being job seekers to value creators, advocating entrepreneurship and new sources of employment. Pathon challenged conventional approaches to training, saying that "organisations like ours need to stop treating learners as beneficiaries of learning, and see them as participants and creators." Cassim warned that "the biggest risk we're seeing right now is young people losing that first opportunity to work," calling on employers to give young talent opportunities to gain practical experience.

However, the growing use of AI also raises questions about accountability when technology fails. Lawrence Matemba, Chief Policy Analyst and Deputy Director-General in the South African Presidency, and Geoff Okao, Chief Digital Officer and Deputy Director, Digital Impact at UNICEF, examined who should be held accountable when automated decisions cause harm. Matemba argued that organisations providing services must accept responsibility for failures, emphasising that citizens must remain central to the design and delivery of those services. Okao cautioned that "a risk register does not by default protect the person who's harmed", calling for safeguards that consider the people affected, not just the risks facing organisations.

Access to finance was another area of discussion, with SME funding among dozens of topics explored across the festival's nine content stages. On the fintech stage, executives from Makko Brothers Credit Limited, Nomba, Edge Growth and Absa Corporate and Investment Bank examined alternative lending models, transaction-based credit assessments and ways to improve access to working capital.

Africa Tech Festival, the continent's longest-running and most influential technology gathering, concluded its 29th edition at the Cape Town International Convention Centre, welcoming more than 15,000 delegates over the three days.

"This week we've heard from government leaders, technology companies, investors and entrepreneurs on issues ranging from digital sovereignty and infrastructure investment to AI governance, business growth and skills development. Africa Tech Festival provides a platform for these different perspectives to come together, forging connections and partnerships that will help drive the industry forward," said David Monaghan, Vice President, Africa Tech Festival.

Africa Tech Festival returns to Cape Town from 16â18 November 2027 for its landmark 30th edition, celebrating three decades at the heart of Africa's technology industry.

#5569. House bill takes on judicial foreclosure requirements for FHA loans in non-judicial states

Reps. Young Kim and Nikema Williams introduced the Housing Process Parity Act, a bipartisan bill to clarify FHA partial claim lien treatment in nonjudicial foreclosures and move foreclosed homes back to market faster.   AI Summary

Representatives Young Kim (R-California) and Nikema Williams (D-Georgia) introduced this week the bipartisan Housing Process Parity Act, a bill that would streamline how certain foreclosed Federal Housing Administration (FHA) properties return to the market and direct a federal study of zero-down-payment FHA loans.

Under current law, differing federal requirements around partial claim liens can force servicers to pursue judicial foreclosures on some FHA loans even in nonjudicial foreclosure states, lengthening timelines and increasing legal costs before a vacant home can be resold.The bill, H.R. 11082, seeks to clarify how partial claim liens are treated following nonjudicial foreclosures for FHA-insured mortgages, bringing FHA authorities closer to those Congress granted the Department of Veterans Affairs’ (V.A.) home loan program last year.

“I’ve been proud to champion bipartisan legislation to alleviate the housing crisis and put the American Dream back within reach,” Rep. Kim said in a statement. “My Housing Process Parity Act will build on these efforts by getting homes back on the market faster and exploring new pathways to homeownership for everyday Americans.”Williams said the limited stock of affordable homes is undermining families’ ability to build wealth. “The bipartisan Housing Process Parity Act cuts unnecessary barriers to get homes back on the market faster and expand housing supply,” she said. “Every family, no matter their ZIP code or bank account, deserves a fair shot at building wealth for the next generation.”

The Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) endorsed the bill, saying it “advances FHA program improvements, provides parity across government-insured mortgage programs, and supports broader efforts to expand access to sustainable homeownership,” according to a statement from MBA President and CEO Bob Broeksmit, CMB.

“Clarifying partial claim lien treatment following non-judicial foreclosures would provide greater certainty for servicers and lower costs for borrowers,” Broeksmit said. “While foreclosure is never the desired outcome, a non-judicial process reduces legal costs, shortens timelines, and limits the financial impact on homeowners.”

Beyond foreclosure process changes, the bill would require the Government Accountability Office (GAO) to study the feasibility of a new FHA-insured mortgage product with no down payment.

The study would examine potential benefits to low- and moderate-income and first-time buyers, as well as risks to taxpayers and the FHA Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund, and identify safeguards needed to keep such loans sustainable.

An Urban Institute analysis – authored by Alexei Alexandrov, Laurie Goodman, Ted Tozer and Sam Valverde – from earlier this year showed that moving from a loan-to-value (LTV) ratio range of 96% to 99% to a range of 100% to 104% LTVs raises the default probability by just 12 basis points — a difference the authors describe as statistically insignificant.“Allowing zero-down payment mortgages would level the playing field for potential homeowners without family wealth,” the researchers wrote in the report. “Moreover, FHA zero-down payment loans would also replace the inconsistent patchwork of down payment assistance programs.”

#5568. NAR’s latest data, must-have AI tools, Compass’ 15 new lawsuits

Congratulations, you’ve made it to Friday again this week. But before you head out for the weekend, we’re bringing you a quick catch-up on the biggest headlines and the most helpful how-tos for your business. So, Take 5 and peruse our top editor picks for this week and why they matter to your business.

P.S. Don’t miss The Download, our weekly column that breaks down one of the week’s top stories and equips you with what you’ll need to meet next Monday head-on.

Homeownership is slipping further out of reach for young Americans, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

Why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

EXTRA: The buyer who can’t close for a year is your best asset in 2026

AI has been the topic of conversation for the past couple of years. And there’s a lot of talk. So how do you suss through the noise and find what works for your business? Jimmy Burgess has created a no-nonsense list of seven AI tools that are actually worth your time.

Why it matters: Burgess shares not only his top tools but also how to use them. These tools will help you turn prompts into better questions, find the questions your future clients are asking, remember the details that matter, evaluate your AI search visibility, turn one video into multiple pieces of content, make video editing easier and use AI as a strategist rather than a writing assistant. Don’t feel overwhelmed. You don’t have to use all of them at once.

Krystopher Benyamein recently sold a property in San Pedro where his team hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. They found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and they had to start again.

They eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when they shared the case study on Instagram, they didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing they’d done. They opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”

That opening puts the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, they explained how they responded, got the property back in front of buyers and ultimately closed.

Why it matters: In today’s market, there are many stories of buyers backing out of deals. This approach allows you to create content that keeps you top of mind, show sellers exactly how you work and reach a wider audience. Benyamein shows you how to do it and shares a FREE Canva template to help get the job done.

VA loans often get passed over for conventional loans. Inman’s Nick Pipitone spoke with Fathom Realty’s Lindsey Schmidt, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, about why VA financing still carries a stigma among sellers and listing agents, how she gets around it and why VA assumptions remain one of the most misunderstood tools in the market.

Why it matters: Military members often have to move. Understanding and busting myths about VA loans can help you get ahead of objections before making an offer, which will help you get more deals across the finish line and get more service members into homes.

Compass has been busy, creating and formalizing policy around employees in association leadership positions and how Compass brokerage agents cooperate on private listings.

The company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

Why it matters: Compass International Holdings is currently in litigation with 16 total MLSs across 18 federal lawsuits. Not only is this big news that’s making waves throughout the industry, but its ripple effects could impact your MLS’s rules, if they haven’t already.

#5566. America builds cool things, except houses

Matt Winter argues U.S. homebuilding has faced limited pressure to improve cost, quality, and design. He outlines five root cause pitfalls, including zoning constraints and prescriptive rules that restrict experimentation.  AI Summary

If housing were an importable product, most American homebuilders would be out of business. Because it isn’t, our industry has never faced the competitive pressure that drives innovation. Decades of rising home prices have made matters worse. When buyers tolerate every cost increase, nothing pushes us to cut costs.

We no longer know how to build a quality product at an affordable price, and we’re approaching a crisis that may finally force change.

When the American auto industry fell behind, higher-quality imports pressured Detroit to innovate. Detroit may have lost market share, but Americans could still get quality cars. If the American homebuilding industry can no longer supply affordable housing, it raises questions about whether homes fit the model of the type of product the USA excels at building.

America’s reign of manufacturing dominance took place during an era when most of the everyday objects we’d now call “products” weren’t manufactured in the modern sense – they were made at home or by local artisans. We excelled at mass-producing novel and exciting products like cars or firearms. By contrast, China’s contemporary manufacturing dominance built a world where almost every household object that exists is industrially manufactured.

American manufacturing is still the second largest globally, but our dominance applies to sophisticated products like monoclonal antibodies, jet engines, and advanced industrial machines. If a proposed product has near-magical requirements and a large enough R&D budget, we’re the right country to produce it, but we’ve never held anything like China’s role as the dominant mass producer of cheap, quotidian consumer goods.

The products the US manufactures competitively are typically regulated very differently from new homes. The FAA doesn’t require Boeing to use quarter-inch titanium rivets spaced one and a half inches apart. Instead, it lets manufacturers compete to engineer solutions that meet performance standards set cooperatively by a group of industry stakeholders. Many nations use performance-based standards in their housing codes, and stricter standards don’t have to mean less affordable housing. Japan is often cited as a success story for maintaining housing affordability despite having some of the world’s most demanding seismic standards.

Another major regulatory barrier limits where housing gets built. After World War II, federally subsidized highways and mortgages made the car-oriented suburb the default, and cities rewrote their zoning codes to reflect that model. Minimum lot sizes, deep setbacks, density caps, and parking requirements effectively banned the “missing middle” housing that once met demand in the most desirable areas. Instead of letting neighborhoods grow through small, continuous infill, zoning froze them in place and pushed new growth outward.

Under these rules, housing development is now effectively squeezed into just two viable business models: the large-scale suburban single-family homebuilder, and the institutional apartment developer. Both models require large swathes of vacant land where they can run the repeatable processes of a century-old mass manufacturing model.

Manufacturing has moved on. The art of producing boring things at hyperscale is a uniquely Chinese invention built around a state-orchestrated model of supply chain networks featuring industrial clustering and dynamic capacity pooling. Widespread adoption of the right technology could coordinate labor resources and supply chains to maximize network resource efficiency. Before any of that matters, we have to admit that the housing we’ve been building isn’t good enough.

Nobody will drive by a contemporary master planned community in a hundred years to admire its architecture. Almost every American production homebuilder returning from a European vacation has had the same unsettling feeling that not a single home we spent our careers building will still be standing a hundred years after we die. Builders have so little unique brand identity that a customer driving through a new development has to rely entirely on marketing signage to know when they’ve left one builder’s tract and entered another’s.

Customers are opting out of choosing between buying in a dull, exurban neighborhood and renting an overpriced “luxury” 5-over-1 apartment building in a more desirable area. They want it cheap and they want it good. When the available housing presents insufficient value, they double up with roommates or family.

Unique designs carry a level of risk that’s largely incompatible with the scale of the predominant business models. Even in Hollywood, a few low-budget originals have begun outperforming franchise blockbusters. If buyers are opting out of what we’ve been building, maybe it’s time we built something more congruent with what we’re good at building: products with nearly magical requirements. A home that’s affordable, durable, and worth admiring a hundred years from now is exactly that kind of product.

People with the means and knowledge to build their own quirky homes have captivated social media onlookers with Earthships, Quonset huts, geodesic domes, and structures made from compressed earth bricks, straw bales, and all manner of materials that are wildly unsuited to production homebuilding. None of those methods is likely to scale, but each of those wacky homes is a testament to the creativity we’re capable of. Our business models leave that creativity nowhere to go.

What might housing look like if we took more risks? Emerging technologies are enabling the rapid iteration of new designs and accelerating the administrative processes behind bidding out new product. Builders could take more chances on small projects built differently. A small bet that fails costs little, and one that succeeds can prove out a profitable model worth repeating.

As a nation, we’ve never done our best work on bland things. We’re at our best when we’re solving a nearly impossible problem or designing something enduringly lovable. It’s time we treated the attainable American home as one of those problems.

#5564. NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO says

License under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license.

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents said.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint said he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”

White also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton said it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or plan.”

Pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also said the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

“NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears said the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

“John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” said David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”

“Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”

#5563. Anthropic goes public, but is it too late to save the AI trade?

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof

Anthropic came through with its initial public offering Thursday, but did it just signal a top in the AI trade?

The artificial intelligence model maker’s IPO went almost picture-perfectly, really, producing a 17% pop that wasn’t so high that it left an excessive amount of money on the table but high enough to call it a success. But it seemed to take some of the air out of AI stocks. Continued worries over AI spending and prospects, as well as factors such as a likely interest-rate hike, dragged down the entire market, including other AI names from Google, Microsoft and Meta to AMD, Broadcom and Nvidia. Asian stocks too.

No doubt Anthropic stock will be at least as volatile as other AI stocks, but it can live with that alongside the more than $90 billion now in its bank account. Now all eyes turn to OpenAI, which finds itself chasing after Anthropic in more ways than one, with plans to go public sometime in next year.

Nvidia posted its usual better-than-expected earnings this week, which didn’t help its stock much but indicates, along with interim CEO Colette Kress’ bullish comments during the earnings call, that it’s going to be fine for some time to come in disgraced former CEO Jensen Huang’s absence.

Meantime, Huang said he’s open to returning — but that’s not only appallingly premature, the board appears adamant it’s not going to happen. The supposed friends clamoring for his return are just reinforcing their selfish, clueless nature, the attitude that has plunged tech into such low esteem that auto salespeople and journalists have more company now. Maybe those guys (always guys) approve of behavior like this.

What’s with all the outages all over the place? That’s what everyone’s asking, and we looked into what’s behind them all. It doesn’t seem to be the obvious thing — cybersecurity attacks — or really any single cause. Perhaps it’s a lot of 20th century technologies that just aren’t ready for the AI-driven speed of the 21st century, making everything less reliable. Or: All those AI-driven fixes to vulnerabilities are getting done so fast they’re breaking things along the way. Still, is it only a coincidence that the U.S. cyber director just got canned this week?

Palo Alto Networks remains one of the most acquisitive cybersecurity companies out there, once again laying out a tidy sum this week, buying AI startup Applied Compute this week $4.5 billion. It’s a sure bet consolidation will accelerate as AI enables more and much faster attacks.

Next week’s significant earnings reports include Dell, HP, Nutanix, Workday and Zoom. And then we can all take a brief respite for Thanksgiving before gearing up for AWS re:Invent the following week in Las Vegas, with its blizzard of news. SiliconANGLE, theCUBE and theCUBE Research will be onsite with news, analysis and interviews.

Here’s all of this week’s enterprise and emerging tech news, analysis and commentary from SiliconANGLE and beyond:

#5562. Does your brokerage need a mortgage servicing arm to keep past clients engaged?

Mortgage servicing became a key ancillary service in 2026, but many regional brokerages cannot own a servicer. To maintain mindshare, firms used practical homeowner value adds such as automated valuation tools, seasonal maintenance reminders, home transition handbooks, and education first content.  AI Summary

In 2026, mortgage servicing became one of the real estate brokerage industry’s must have ancillary services.

For Peter Voss, the broker-owner of 3% Listing Co.,  Rocket Companies’ acquisitions of Redfin and Mr.Cooper in mid-2025 was a real wake up call as to what true vertical integration looks like.

“That was like the blinders coming off for everyone,” Voss said. “It was like ‘Holy cow! That is real vertical integration.’ It was just so different from what everyone else had been thinking about.”

This move by Rocket was followed in 2026 by eXp Realty’s mortgage joint venture with Newrez, Revenos Mortgage, which includes a servicing component, and HomeServices of America adding in-house mortgage servicing through its wholly owned lender, Prosperity Home Mortgage, LLC.

At the time of the launch, Chris Kelly, the CEO of the RealTrends Verified HomeServices of America, told HousingWire that the company decided to venture into servicing because they were “increasingly seeing that loans end up with a servicer and those servicers are moving further upstream.”

“It used to be that a broker started a mortgage company, but now mortgage companies are starting real estate companies and the whole point of it is to use that servicing to try and siphon off that business and acquire home buyer and seller clients before they even start browsing for homes on a search portal,” Kelly told HousingWire in late summer.

But for smaller, regional brokerages owning a mortgage servicer is not an option. However, this doesn’t mean that they have given up in their efforts to stay top of mind with past clients.

Instead of venturing into mortgage servicing, Voss said 3% Listing Co. has employed a variety of strategies to ensure his company is the one past clients turn to when it is time to move, from a home value tool that allows homeowners to see the estimated value of their property without having to talk to an agent to reminders about seasonal home maintenance.

“We just sent out an email ahead of the winter season reminding people to unhook their outdoor hoses,” Voss said. “It’s really small things like that, trying to be real and making sure what we are doing is beneficial to past clients.”

Voss said his firm is also exploring a partnership with an HVAC filter company that sends homeowners new filters every three months when it’s time to swap out filters.

“We’re looking at the possibility of setting it up as a closing gift for clients where every three months they get a filter in the mail that is branded to us,” he said. “We want to think outside of the box because just because everyone else is doing things one way doesn’t mean we have to.”

Home Handoff is a proptech company focused on helping agents and their clients manage their home transition, provides home sellers with a structured space to provide information regarding property utilities, renovations and service providers that can then be shared with buyers or prospective buyers. The firm is all about finding different ways for agents to keep their name in front of past clients. The company is working with agents, teams and brokerages, to put their own branding on the “home handbook” the company provides clients with. In addition to information regarding the property, agents can also provide links to vetted service professionals such as contractors, landscapers and pet sitters.

“The whole platform is built to keep the agent as the hero. Every time the seller or buyer logs into the platform they see it is provided by their agent or their brokerage,” Cody Bartkoski, the CEO of Home Handoff, said.

In New York City, Brown Harris Stevens (BHS), a RealTrends Verified brokerage, is also employing different means of maintaining relationships with clients. The firm, which does not own any ancillary services operations, instead operates an advertising arm that works with trusted mortgage and title professionals to create content from podcasts, to blog posts to short video series.

According to Matt Leone, BHS’s chief marketing officer, the primary goal of this marketing and advertising program is to educate viewers and listeners and that they are not creating content just for the sake of “generating clicks.” He added that they don’t necessarily view these efforts as a lead generation tool, but as a way to get their “name out there as a thought leader.”

“You don’t want it to be a traditional ad message,” Leone said. “You want it to be through your thought leadership, your insights and being seen as an expert that you earn these opportunities.”

Leone added that consumers encounter so many different advertisements each day that many just tune out that type of content.

“We want to educate them, both consumers and agents, with the individuals in those spaces that are the most knowledgeable,” Leone said. “We work with our agents to find the providers that are the best at their craft and we see if they’d be interested in collaborating with us.”

While regional firms like 3% Listing Co. and BHS may not have mortgage servicers or even a stable of ancillary services within their company, they are still finding meaningful ways to engage with and keep their names in front of consumers.

“It isn’t just about handing out branded T-shirts to people, but about how you connect with them and give the T-shirt value so that people are going to reuse it,” Voss said. “I think that is where a lot of brokerages are struggling. They’re trying to find that additional income stream and where that additional lead source is, but without a whole lot of added cost.”
