#5535. Nvidia stock is heading for its longest losing streak since 2008

The stock was under pressure even before Jensen Huang's ouster as investors question whether demand for the company's AI chips can be sustained

Nvidia $NVDA stock is poised to finish its seventh consecutive week in the red. That would mark its longest slide since 2008.

The stock changed hands at about $147 on Thursday, a 2.6% drop for the day. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF, whose largest positions include Nvidia, lost 2.3% that day.

The decline has continued despite third-quarter revenue that rose 103% from a year earlier. The slide worsened once Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO on Nov. 12, with CFO Colette Kress taking over as interim chief executive that day. The stock was under pressure before then as investors questioned whether demand for artificial intelligence can be sustained.

Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion on Tuesday, in its first earnings report since Huang resigned. Data Center revenue reached $107.6 billion, up 110% from a year earlier. For the fourth quarter, the company expects revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, with the outlook excluding any Data Center compute revenue from China. Nvidia stock climbed by up to 4% in after-hours trading following the report.

Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer. U.S. intelligence officials suspect she is an agent of Beijing's spy agencies. The board has retained law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz for an independent probe into whether Huang shared corporate or national security secrets.

Nvidia has also hired Heidrick & Struggles to lead the search for a permanent CEO. Board Chair Harvey Jones said on Tuesday's earnings call that directors will weigh insiders and outsiders. Jones also said the board "does not intend to reinstate" Huang.

Huang said Tuesday that he would be open to returning if directors asked him to. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pushed the board over the weekend to hire someone from outside the company. "They need a dramatic shakeup," Bessent said.

#5533. Jimmie Johnson's Legacy Motor Club is valued at $450 million after new fundraise

Knighthead Capital Management led the $85 million round, which will fund growth and a new headquarters expected to open in 2028

Legacy Motor Club, the NASCAR team that Jimmie Johnson, a seven-time Cup Series champion, owns, wrapped up an $85 million fundraising round headed by Knighthead Capital Management, according to Bloomberg.

The round puts Legacy's worth at $450 million, according to Bloomberg, which attributed the figure to a source with knowledge of the deal who lacked permission to discuss it in public.

Legacy will put the money toward growing its operation and building a new headquarters in Mooresville, North Carolina, according to Bloomberg. The headquarters is expected to open in 2028.

In July, Legacy revealed an earlier capital raise backed by investors such as Philadelphia Phillies player Bryce Harper, tennis champion Andy Roddick, musician Darius Rucker and chef Guy Fieri, according to Bloomberg. Johnson told Bloomberg that Legacy returned to investors for additional capital so it could keep expanding.

Johnson said the investment positions Legacy to reach its goal of being "a tier one racing operation in the Nascar series," according to Bloomberg.

Legacy operates three NASCAR teams with charters, and each of them runs the Toyota $TM Camry XSE. Josh Berry, Erik Jones and Riley Herbst will drive for the team in the coming season, according to Bloomberg.

Knighthead's leader is co-founder Tom Wagner, who launched the investment company back in 2008. Wagner is also a part owner of both the Las Vegas Raiders and Birmingham City Football Club, according to Bloomberg.

Bloomberg noted that Knighthead bought into Legacy in January 2025, taking a minority stake by purchasing a large portion of the shares airline entrepreneur Maury Gallagher held. That transaction made Johnson the team's majority owner.

Kyle Kneisly, a Knighthead partner and Legacy board member, told Bloomberg that deploying growth capital was part of the plan from the start.

The new round follows NASCAR's settlement of a federal antitrust lawsuit with Michael Jordan's 23XI Racing and Front Row Motorsports. The settlement made charters permanent for NASCAR teams, a change that could raise the worth of clubs, according to Bloomberg.

#5532. Connected Nation podcast spotlights two urgent issues shaping America's digital future

Bonus episodes recorded at the Broadband Nation Expo examine the threat to E-Rate and how Google is helping set the first quality standard for data centers

NEW ORLEANS, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A federal program that connects more than 100,000 schools and libraries is in jeopardy. The data centers that power the internet are changing faster than the rules can keep up.

Two new bonus episodes of the Connected Nation podcast take on both issues. Connected Nation (CN), a national nonprofit, interviewed leadership at SHLB and Google during the Broadband Nation Expo taking place in New Orleans Nov. 18-20.

Ep. 57: The program that keeps schools and libraries online is in danger

The federal E-Rate helps connect more than 100,000 K-12 schools and libraries across the U.S. Now its future is uncertain.

Joseph Wender, Executive Director of the Schools, Health & Libraries Broadband (SHLB) Coalition, explained the Fifth Circuit ruling that puts the $8 billion-a-year program at risk. The court found that USAC, which runs the Universal Service Fund, was improperly set up.

Wender also covered the FCC's proposal asking whether E-Rate should end, and what schools and libraries are telling him.

"They're saying E-Rate cannot go away. It just cannot," Wender said of the schools and libraries SHLB represents. "That if it goes away, it will blow a hole in the budgets of schools and libraries."

Gino Tozzi, who leads data center quality and commissioning at Google, explained DCE 9000, the first quality standard for data center infrastructure. Google and the Telecommunications Industry Association (TIA) are building it with more than 90 companies, and it's expected in early 2027 (Q1).

Tozzi also explained why some suppliers face as many as 50 audits a year, and what really goes into building a data center.

"We need to go at hyper speed because we need it fast," Tozzi said of developing the standard. "We couldn't afford to wait three or five years."

"These conversations get at what it takes to get and keep America connected," said Jessica Denson, Communications Director, CN, and host of the podcast. "One episode is about protecting the program that keeps students online. The other is focused on the infrastructure behind almost everything we do on the internet. President Donald Trump outside the White House. (Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images)

President Donald Trump said on Friday that American technology firms would be hit with "a tremendous tax" for constructing AI data centers overseas.

Trump described the penalty as either a ban on building data centers abroad or a tax, according to CNBC. He gave no details on how the policy would work, according to The Associated Press.

Trump told Americans they should accept data center projects where they live and push developers for concessions, according to the AP. "You ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don't shut them off," he said.

Trump urged data center companies in October to pay local communities a "dividend" to win support for new facilities. In a Truth Social post, he said projects that were unpopular in an area became popular once a financial deal was struck.

#5530. Seattle tech vet and Sounders FC minority owner Chee Chew joins front office to lead AI push

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:02 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:02 am

Chee Chew helped build the Windows 95 Start menu, started Google Hangouts and ran consumer engagement at Amazon. Now the Seattle tech veteran is taking on a new job with the Sounders and Reign FC, where he’ll lead how the soccer clubs use technology, data and AI.

Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club announced Tuesday.

“His knowledge of and passion for the Sounders and Reign allow him to hit the ground running,” Hanauer said in a statement. “His experience leading teams through major shifts in technology gives us a unique opportunity to strengthen both the soccer and business sides of our organization.”

Chew most recently was chief product and technology officer at Zapier, where he helped steer the workflow automation company toward AI. Before that he was chief product officer at mParticle and at Twilio, where he oversaw the communications company’s $3.2 billion acquisition of Segment.

He spent four years at Amazon, nearly eight years as a vice president of engineering at Google, where he also led the company’s Seattle and Kirkland offices, and 14 years at Microsoft working on Internet Explorer, Windows Mobile and Xbox Live.

Chew said his direct team will stay small, but its work will reach every corner of the business, including HR, ticket sales, customer service, match-day planning, corporate partnerships, legal, and player recruiting and scouting. He also wants every department to have its own “builders,” staffers who can create AI tools and automations for their own teams.

“In order to do a change like this, it’s more than technology,” Chew told GeekWire. “Technology is in many ways the easiest part. Driving change, getting deep, building side by side with folks, I think is what it takes.”

Chew didn’t grow up playing soccer. “My family was a very traditional Chinese family of study and play piano,” he said. “It was a stereotype, but it was true for my family.” He caught the bug in college, where he played a ton of intramurals, and later from his wife, Christine, who played through college, and their two kids.

The couple joined the Sounders ownership group in 2019 as one of 11 Seattle-rooted families, many with deep ties to the region’s tech industry. Former Microsoft executive Terry Myerson pulled the group together, and it included Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, CFO Amy Hood, and others.

A group of owners has met every other Friday since 2019, and “leveraging technology has always been part of the strategy” for the club, Chew said.

The job grew out of a demo Chew built for Hanauer about two and a half years ago: an AI agent that could handle complicated fan requests, such as a season ticket holder with four seats who wants to buy a block of eight. The club later brought in consultants to train staff on AI, but the effort never quite gained momentum, he said.

Talks about a bigger role started early this year and came together by midyear. “Adrian and I talked about it, and we agreed for me to come on board and take an operational role and hack on some code,” Chew said.

“I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years. It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.”

Chew describes Hanauer as a visionary on “the art of the possible” who comes in daily asking, “Could you do this?” Recently, as Chew was boarding a flight home to Seattle, Hanauer called from a meeting where staff doubted they could scale up one effort tenfold without hiring more people. Could AI help?

On the flight, while using the plane’s Wi-Fi, he built a prototype with Anthropic’s Claude. “By the time I landed, I sent it to them and said, ‘OK, give this a try,’” he said. The club used it in an experiment to scale up performance marketing before a match.

It’s the kind of hands-on building Chew says he’s been doing a lot of lately.

“I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years,” he said. “It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.”

He recently ran an AI analysis of one player’s game, based on stats such as touches, expected goals and distance run. It pointed out strengths and areas to improve. The player was “very hungry for it,” Chew said, and asked if they could do it every game.

The club’s performance analytics group, led by data analyst Tyler Cox, was already ahead of much of the organization, and Chew said he’s helping speed up that work with AI.

The bigger challenge is getting people to change how they work, Chew said. At Zapier, he saw many companies struggle to get results from AI, with some spending “massive token budgets” without a big win. He said the answer is blending AI with traditional automation and fitting it into how people already work.

“It has to be approachable for folks,” he said. “You can’t go in and just throw everything up and start from scratch.”

The Sounders host Real Salt Lake in the wild-card round of the MLS Cup Playoffs on Thursday at Lumen Field. Asked whether AI could help figure out a win, Chew passed.

“I don’t want to get involved and interfere with our coaching staff,” he said.

The KBW Bank Index is down as much as 7.7% this week as cyberattack worries and an AI selloff weigh on the sector

The KBW Bank Index, a 24-member gauge of big U.S. banks, has lost as much as 7.7% since Monday, putting it on course for its steepest weekly drop since April 2025, according to Bloomberg.

Shares of Morgan Stanley $MS and Goldman Sachs $GS each fell more than 10% this week, placing them among the index's worst performers, according to Bloomberg. Both banks hold top roles on Anthropic's IPO.

Bank stocks fell on Friday, when heavy selling of artificial-intelligence shares unsettled markets worldwide.

Financial stocks slid on Thursday after JPMorgan $JPM Chase, Visa $V and Mastercard $MA disclosed that an attack targeting one of their vendors had exposed certain customers' details, according to Bloomberg. That followed earlier disruptions this week, including an outage at the National Security Agency's internal communications network and a "technical issue" at JPMorgan, according to Bloomberg.

"Bank stocks are getting hit by a confluence of macro concerns rather than anything fundamentally new with the banks themselves," Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Herman Chan said, according to Bloomberg. "The broader risk-off move in technology hasn't helped either, particularly for capital-markets-oriented banks."

Chan also pointed to inflation and the Federal Reserve. "Persistent inflation has put higher-for-longer rates back at the forefront, with Fed officials raising the possibility of a 50-basis-point hike in December," he said, according to Bloomberg. "Renewed geopolitical tensions around Iran are adding another layer of uncertainty and could complicate the inflation outlook through energy prices."

The KBW index formed a "death cross" on Thursday, a bearish technical signal that may point to more short-term weakness, according to Bloomberg. Bank stocks have given back all of the advance they had built up since January.

The sector was already under pressure before this week. In October, the index was headed for a sixth straight weekly loss and had fallen 13% from its August record, putting it in correction territory. Worries about how artificial intelligence will disrupt financial services were weighing on the stocks then.

The wider market has also dropped. Through Thursday's close, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 6.2% for the week, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq $NDAQ had each lost 5% as technology stocks sold off.

#5527. Seattle police unleash dog-like robot whose best trick is bomb dispoal

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:43 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:43 am

Seattle police already have a dog that sniffs out tech. Now they’ve got a piece of tech that looks like a dog.

It’s a big upgrade for the squad, which has handled more than 600 calls so far this year. SPD’s main bomb robot is nearly 20 years old, weighs more than 100 pounds and rolls on tracks, and it can only be hauled around in the squad’s mobile workshop. Spot weighs under 100 pounds, climbs stairs and rides in a pickup truck that bomb techs drive daily.

The robot will only be used for explosive threats in the city and at the port, and it won’t carry a weapon. SPD said a weapon would go against Boston Dynamics’ rules for its robots. Spot’s 360-degree camera sends an encrypted live feed to the operator but doesn’t record or use facial recognition.

The only thing the robot does on its own is open a door, after an operator lines it up. As one bomb technician put it in SPD’s post, Spot will “be as dumb in 10 years as it is today.”

It’s not the first time SPD has turned to a four-legged partner for tech-related work.

Nala, an electronic storage detection K9 — profiled by GeekWire in 2024 — is trained to smell a chemical compound used in making electronics. The Labrador retriever helps SPD’s Internet Crimes Against Children task force find hidden phones, hard drives and micro SD cards during warrant searches. Her handler, Det. Daljit Gill, told GeekWire at the time that Nala turns up a device human searchers missed about 30% of the time.

Boston Dynamics, maker of backflipping Atlas humanoids and other viral-video robots, first unveiled the robodog in 2015. A smaller, all-electric version followed a year later.

The machines have long stirred dystopian unease. A 2017 “Black Mirror” episode featured killer robot dogs inspired by the company’s designs. Still, Spot has turned up in friendlier settings: then-Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos walked one at the company’s MARS conference in 2018 — a scene described by GeekWire’s Alan Boyle as featuring the “anxiety-inducing” robot.

Police departments have embraced the robots, too. More than 60 bomb squads and SWAT teams in the U.S. and Canada use Spot, Bloomberg reported last year, including a regional bomb unit in Portland. New York police returned one in 2021 after public backlash, then brought the robots back two years later.

Back in Seattle, SPD’s bomb technicians see more potential uses down the road, according to the department’s post, including communicating and observing from a distance as part of de-escalation. For now, Spot’s job is limited to explosives.

And the robot won’t be getting a new name, SPD said, “because it is not a toy, or a dog, even though it kind of looks like both.”

#5525. Senate Budget chair's Social Security fix might add trillions to U.S. debt

Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget estimates the Stop Scaring Seniors Act would add $190 trillion over 75 years

Senate Budget Committee Chairman Ron Johnson, a Wisconsin Republican, proposed a bill on Wednesday that would prevent Social Security benefits from being reduced when the program's trust fund is depleted. Johnson calls it the Stop Scaring Seniors Act and asked on X $TWTR who would cosponsor it.

The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a nonpartisan deficit-hawk group, estimates that over 75 years the bill would increase the national debt by $190 trillion after adjusting for inflation, equal to 165% of GDP, according to Fortune. The measure would allow the Treasury secretary to shift general-fund dollars into the retirement program's trust fund once its reserves are exhausted.

The retirement trust fund has under six years of reserves left, according to Fortune. Depletion would set off an automatic reduction of roughly 22% in benefits, a loss the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget estimates at around $500 monthly for the typical recipient.

Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, criticized the proposal. "We usually say that inaction is the worst option when it comes to Social Security, but now we found something even worse," she said, according to Fortune. She called the bill "a cynical pander that ducks all the real decisions we need to confront."

MacGuineas also warned of market effects. "Even simply passing the legislation could spook the bond market enough to spark financial turmoil," she said, according to Fortune.

In an analysis published last November, the group calculated that paying for Social Security out of general revenue would lift interest rates roughly 2.6 percentage points above where they would stand if the trust fund stayed whole, according to Fortune. Under that scenario, the 10-year Treasury yield would climb from 4% to 6.6%, while mortgage rates on 30-year loans would go from 6.3% to 8.9%.

Johnson contends lawmakers ought to tackle the entire deficit rather than treat Social Security separately, according to Fortune. MacGuineas called that "a reasonable position," but said a law "that fails to fix Social Security while ballooning the debt" was not the way to do it. She suggested lawmakers consider a bipartisan commission.

A Senate Budget Committee report Johnson released Wednesday, titled "Social Security: The Reality… a Legal Ponzi Scheme," forecasts a gap of roughly $511 billion in the program's finances by 2032, according to Fortune.

The bill follows other recent remarks by Johnson. On Wednesday he called Social Security a "scam" that should be "shut down" during a Fox Business segment. A day earlier, he previewed a Senate Budget Committee hearing on the program in an X post that described it as a "legal Ponzi scheme."

#5524. Bitcoin Price, Gold and Oil Fall: Should the US Repeat Its $2.2T 2020 Rescue?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin price is getting hammered in the aftermath of the FOMC minutes. Gold isn’t doing much better; oil and stocks have joined the sell-off. The markets are already nervous about the Federal Reserve’s next decision, and yesterday’s FOMC minutes gave us another reason to worry: policymakers are still talking about raising interest rates.

Almost all officials saw further hikes as appropriate under their baseline outlook. Two even floated the possibility of a bigger increase if inflation refuses to cool.

This is a nasty combination for markets. Bitcoin fell around 3.2% over 24 hours, gold futures dropped more than 3%, and WTI crude lost around 3%. The dollar climbed to a 19-month high. Wall Street was mixed, though, with the Nasdaq finishing higher while the Dow and S&P 500 slipped.

Here’s the comparison. In March 2020, the Fed was slashing rates, buying bonds and throwing emergency liquidity at a financial system under immense pressure. Congress approved a $2.2 trillion rescue package to keep households and businesses afloat.

Today, we are watching markets fall while the Fed is possibly making money more expensive.

October’s FOMC minutes weren’t exactly what markets wanted to hear. The Fed held rates at 3.75%–4% during its October meeting, but almost all participants believed further increases would likely be appropriate. Two officials also said a hike larger than the usual 25 basis points could be considered if inflation data came in hotter than expected.

And there was more in those minutes than just interest rates. Officials raised concerns about hedge fund leverage and the growing debt tied to artificial intelligence investments. Some financing arrangements could become a problem if investors start questioning enormous AI spending, and whether it will generate the returns companies expect.

The risk is forced selling. Leveraged funds facing losses or investor withdrawals may have to dump assets quickly, potentially pushing prices down further.

Gold has its own problem. A stronger dollar and higher interest rates make it less attractive to investors who can earn a return elsewhere. Bitcoin price, meanwhile, remains vulnerable when traders cut exposure to speculative assets.

The Fed hasn’t declared a financial emergency. Its minutes actually describe the banking system as resilient. But officials are clearly paying attention to risks that could amplify a market shock.

March 2020 was brutal. COVID-19 lockdowns brought businesses to a standstill. Investors rushed for cash, stocks collapsed, and Bitcoin briefly slipped below $4,000 after sitting near $10,000 just weeks earlier.

The Federal Reserve didn’t wait around. It cut rates by 50 basis points on March 3, then delivered another 100-basis-point cut on March 15. The federal funds target range dropped to 0%–0.25%.

On March 23, the Fed announced unlimited purchases of Treasury securities and mortgage-backed securities, promising to buy whatever amounts were necessary to support market functioning. It also introduced emergency lending programmes to keep credit flowing.

President Donald Trump signed the $2.2 trillion CARES Act on March 27. The package included direct payments to eligible Americans, expanded unemployment benefits, and assistance for businesses struggling to survive lockdowns. The Paycheck Protection Program gave small businesses access to loans designed to help them keep employees on payroll.

The response was enormous, but the economy was facing an extraordinary shutdown. Millions of Americans had lost their jobs, businesses were closing, and normal economic activity had practically disappeared.

Markets eventually bounced back. The S&P 500 recovered its pre-pandemic record by August 2020. Bitcoin climbed above $12,000 during the same month.

The current US economy isn’t in the same position as it was during the pandemic. Inflation remains above the Fed’s 2% target, and policymakers are discussing rate increases rather than cuts.

Slashing rates to zero and flooding markets with liquidity might help asset prices. It could also make inflation worse. Another multitrillion-dollar spending package would face an entirely different argument in Congress, especially without a pandemic-style economic shutdown.

The Fed doesn’t have to choose between doing nothing and repeating the 2020 rescue. If banks struggle to fund themselves or credit markets start freezing, it can step in with emergency lending and liquidity operations. That’s a much narrower response than another round of unlimited bond purchases.

The Fed’s concerns about leveraged hedge funds and AI financing could become more relevant if investors start selling indiscriminately. A market correction is one thing. Forced selling spreading through the financial system is another.

At the moment, there’s no evidence that we’re facing another March 2020. The banking system remains resilient, and falling Bitcoin prices alone won’t trigger a government bailout.

But the Fed has a problem that didn’t exist in quite the same way during the pandemic. It may need to protect financial stability without giving up its fight against inflation. In 2020, Washington opened the taps. This time, we wait and see, and Bitcoin price will survive.

#5523. Microsoft jabs at OpenAI and Anthropic, touting cheaper, customizable AI models of its own

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:57 amNovember 17, 2026 at 12:33 pm

Microsoft is a partner and investor in both OpenAI and Anthropic, and it sells their AI models to its own customers. But another role was on full display during the company’s Ignite keynote Tuesday: competitor.

“Simply stated, anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot and for less,” said Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft’s commercial business, during the opening keynote at the company’s annual conference for IT professionals and business customers in San Francisco.

Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, went further. “We’ve all seen Anthropic and OpenAI embrace documents, slides, and spreadsheets, but their simplified viewers and editors force compromise on power and collaboration,” he said.

The full versions of Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot are included in the subscription. “That means that Copilot is the only way to draft a PowerPoint presentation without spinning a meter,” Andreou said.

Microsoft’s cost comparison: Andreou backed up the pitch with a chart of estimated monthly costs per business user, including subscription and usage fees. It put Copilot at $30 for an “everyday” AI user, compared with $81 for ChatGPT and $205 for Claude.

For “advanced” users of each company’s agent tools, it showed $96 for Copilot, $149 for ChatGPT and $299 for Claude. Most of the Claude figure is estimated usage charges on top of Anthropic’s $20 enterprise seat.

The numbers come from research Microsoft commissioned and paid for from GigaOm, based on testing Microsoft ran in October on modeled workloads. They reflect enterprise pricing, which adds usage charges to a per-seat fee, not the flat monthly subscriptions that individuals pay for ChatGPT and Claude.

Partners and rivals: The pitch comes as Anthropic expands into Microsoft’s core business. Last week it introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards that compete more directly with Office. The company is expected to make its IPO this week, putting new scrutiny on its financials and long-term growth prospects.

The companies’ products are also intertwined. Anthropic’s Claude for Microsoft 365, for example, lets people use Claude inside Office apps for tasks such as sorting email and creating slide decks.

The product has less than a tenth as many weekly users as the paid version of Copilot in Office, The Information reported Monday, citing internal Microsoft data. Andreou is one of the executives who see that as a sign Microsoft can keep customers from switching, the report said.

New MAI models: Microsoft AI also released a new batch of its own MAI models, built to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic for a fraction of the price. It’s a notable stance, given that Microsoft still sells their models, too. On the same stage, CEO Satya Nadella announced that OpenAI’s GPT-6.2, released Tuesday morning, is now available in Microsoft Foundry.

The lineup includes MAI Code 2, available in GitHub Copilot starting Tuesday. Microsoft says it delivers 96% of the coding performance of Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the price, on benchmarks Microsoft chose.

Microsoft also introduced MAI Cyber 2 Flash, a security model it says matches OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on one benchmark at less than 2% of the cost per task. Other new models cover image editing, live speech and transcription.

The other new business: MAI Licensed Weights. Companies can take a Microsoft AI model, customize it with their own data and run it in their own Azure environment, with help from Microsoft’s Frontier Company consulting arm. AT&T used an earlier version of the program, Custom Models, to build a MAI model for 5G network analytics.

It’s the latest step in Microsoft’s push for what Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has called “long term self-sufficiency,” which started with seven homegrown models at Build in June.

Keeping costs in check: The cost theme ran through the keynote. In a demo, Althoff showed Copilot building a keynote outline, a slide deck and a customer tracker for a retail conference, plus an agent he named Amelia to keep the work going.

The cost of his two-hour Sunday session: about 10,000 credits, or roughly $100. Althoff presented that as a bargain compared with the staff time it would have taken: “my team hits the ground running for NRF without me bothering them,” he said.

Microsoft is also selling tools to keep that bill in check. A new Agent 365 Business Analytics feature shows business leaders what’s driving their AI spending and what they’re getting for it, and a companion Cost Management tool lets IT set spending policies and get alerts. Microsoft cited a McKinsey survey in which 93% of respondents reported exceeding their AI budgets.

In another notable announcement, Microsoft and Salesforce unveiled “Copilotforce,” bringing Salesforce customer data and actions into Copilot, Teams and Fabric. The Copilot plugin is available in preview.

Earlier, Nadella opened the keynote by addressing last week’s global Outlook outage.

#5522. Dental Expert Dr. Theresa Trapp, DDS Guides Patients Through Expectations For Clear Aligner Treatment

Dr. Theresa Trapp explains how dental health, alignment needs, and consistent daily wear influence clear aligner treatment and long-term results.

EASLEY, S.C., Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ --

Are clear aligners the right choice for straightening your teeth?

Dr. Theresa Trapp, DDS, Dental Expert of Advanced Family Dentistry in Easley, SC, explains what determines treatment eligibility in a HelloNation article. Understanding dental health requirements, treatment expectations, and daily responsibilities helps patients evaluate their options.

Clear aligners are custom-made, removable trays that gradually reposition teeth through controlled pressure. Patients switch between sets according to their dentist's instructions.

Unlike traditional braces, the trays have no metal brackets or wires. They can also be removed for meals, brushing, and flossing, offering greater convenience during treatment.

Who Is a Good Candidate for Clear Aligners?

A good candidate for clear aligners generally has alignment concerns that can be addressed predictably with removable trays.

The article explains that crowded teeth, gaps, and certain bite problems may respond well. However, more complex cases may require braces or another form of orthodontic treatment.

A dental evaluation helps determine whether clear aligner treatment is appropriate. Dentists examine tooth positioning, bite alignment, gum health, and existing dental conditions before recommending treatment.

Dr. Theresa Trapp, DDS, Dental Expert of Easley, SC, emphasizes the importance of following the prescribed wear schedule.

Patients typically wear aligners for 20 to 22 hours daily. Removing them too frequently can delay progress and interfere with planned tooth movement.

Treatment duration varies from several months to a year or longer. Regular appointments help dentists monitor progress and determine whether additional adjustments or refinements are necessary.

What Happens After Orthodontic Treatment?

Completing orthodontic treatment does not guarantee teeth will remain in their new positions without maintenance.

Retainers after clear aligners help prevent gradual shifting. Consistent retainer use is important for preserving results.

The article also notes that treatment costs and insurance benefits vary based on individual circumstances.

Are Clear Aligners Right for You? features insights from Dr. Theresa Trapp, DDS, Dental Expert of Easley, SC, in HelloNation.

Can Clear Aligners Correct Every Alignment Problem?

According to Dr. Theresa Trapp, DDS, Dental Expert of Easley, SC, some complex alignment problems require traditional braces or alternative approaches.

How Many Hours Should Aligners Be Worn Daily?

Patients are generally instructed to wear their trays for approximately 20 to 22 hours daily, removing them for meals and oral hygiene.

Can Patients With Gum Disease Get Aligners?

Dr. Theresa Trapp, DDS, Dental Expert of Easley, SC, explains that untreated gum disease or cavities may need treatment before tooth movement begins.

Treatment may last several months or longer than a year, depending on alignment complexity and patient compliance.

Yes. Retainers help maintain corrected tooth positions and reduce shifting. Patients should follow their dentist's recommended retention schedule.

#5521. 6 post-earthquake checks every Californian can finish before the next quake

Six checks for Californians after this week's quakes, from emergency kits and phone alerts to insurance, and why a quick version is not enough.

When the shaking stops, most Californians feel relief first. Then they start to wonder whether they would be ready for a worse quake. The quake centered in Mendocino County, Calif., this week was a magnitude 5.6, according to Bay City News, and it brought that question back for households across Northern California. For the many households that came through it unhurt, the days after a scare are a rare stretch when preparing feels urgent and the next quake has not yet come. The risk behind the scare comes with living in California, where the danger of earthquakes is greater than in any other state except Alaska, according to CNBC Select. This week's quake is part of the ordinary, lasting risk of life in the state, not a rare event.

Most advice after a quake sounds like a quick errand: switch on a phone setting, buy batteries, glance at an insurance policy. A household can tick those boxes in five minutes without becoming any safer than it was before. The task this week is to test the basics against a real scare, not to collect new tips.

Nacionale set out to lay out the preparedness steps residents should take after the recent California quakes, from insurance coverage to the bookshelves in a bedroom and the settings on a phone. Each one is easy to start and just as easy to leave half-done. Every step costs less and causes less stress to settle now, while the house is still standing, than in the hours after a bigger quake.

Most households tick off the emergency kit without opening it, because buying it once feels like finishing it. A kit needs refilling, and a fresh scare is the closest thing to a refill date most households will get. Supplies such as water and lights should be replenished while the quake is still on people’s minds, according to Nacionale. A real check means opening the box and replacing what is used up or expired.

The refill covers the most basic needs: water to drink, and flashlights and batteries to see by. The CDC’s checklist covers natural disasters in general, so fitting it to a quake is up to each household.

Decide how many people the kit must cover and for how long, then stock it to that, rather than stopping at a closet with a flashlight in it.

After a quake, the useful walk through the house looks for what could have landed on a person, not for what broke. The hazard is ordinary furniture that already stands in most living rooms and bedrooms. Nacionale advises residents in areas near active fault zones, such as the San Andreas Fault, to secure their bookshelves and wall art. Nearly every home has these pieces, and that makes the step easy to overlook. A person sitting on a couch or sleeping in a bed beside an unanchored bookcase is at greater risk than the books on its shelves.

A shelf that stayed upright this week has passed no test, because the shaking may not be over. The CDC warns that aftershocks, not only the main quake, can shift household objects, knock them down or smash them. Seeing nothing fall feels like a pass, but it shows luck, not readiness. The days of aftershocks are when securing these items does the most good, and the job should not wait for a quieter week.

Brackets and anchors are only half of the fix, and placement is the other half. Bulky and heavy items belong on the bottom shelves, according to the CDC, so the top row of every bookcase is the first thing to rearrange. Start in the rooms where people sleep and sit. Heavy art hung over a bed or couch hangs directly over a person and should come down first.

The check is finished when nothing heavy remains high up or overhead where people rest, however tidy the room looks.

A phone alert matters most when everyone in the house is asleep. Nacionale advises making sure alerts are enabled ahead of early-morning quakes, such as one at 3:30 a.m. This week’s quake struck at 8:10 a.m. Wednesday, after most households were already up, according to Bay City News. The test that counts is whether an alert would wake the household.

Switching alerts on is not a single step, because warnings are sent through several separate channels. Bay City News reports that iOS, Android, FEMA's wireless alerts and the MyShake app each carry warnings, and that different phone operating systems send alerts at different thresholds. Two neighbors with different phones who both turned alerts on may not get the same warning from the same quake. Whether a warning gets through depends on the phone's setup, not only on the switch. "A lot of it has to do with what you have on your phone, how you have it set up,” said Robert de Groot, a scientist at the U.S. Geological Survey's Earthquake Science Center in Pasadena, Calif. MyShake is free, so cost is no reason to rely on one channel.

An alert by itself does not mean the danger is close. Well over 1 million people in Northern California received ShakeAlert notifications this week, including residents of Oakland, Berkeley and Concord, according to Bay City News. The first alert is issued from about one second of data, yet de Groot says people very near the source will likely notice the shaking before any warning comes. At 3:30 a.m., an alert by the bed is a cue for people to protect themselves where they lie, not a promise of time to spare.

The check worth doing tonight is whether everyone in the house would wake to a phone alert, and whether they would know what to do in the seconds after.

The most urgent danger in a house can begin after the shaking stops, in pipes behind walls and under floors where nobody can see it. Nacionale advises that residents locate the main valves beforehand so they can act quickly if a bigger aftershock arrives. The need does not depend on a second quake. Leaking gas and water pipes are among the dangers that can remain once an earthquake is over, according to the CDC, so the shut-off is a response to damage that may already exist.

Most households stop once they have found the valves. Acting quickly at a leaking line also takes knowing how to close each one. The calm days after a moderate scare, with nothing leaking, are the right time for every adult in the house to learn the steps for each main valve.

If a line breaks, the minutes that matter are better spent turning a valve than working out how to.

A family communication plan covers the hours after a strong quake when relatives can’t simply call one another. Loved ones need an agreed place to gather in case phone service fails, so each person knows where to go without calling anyone. Picking the spot takes a short conversation, and it’s easy to treat that as the whole job.

A single meeting place assumes every family member can physically get there, and after a strong quake that may not be possible. A family therefore has to plan for two separate problems: losing phone service and losing access to the meeting place. The CDC recommends choosing an out-of-area relative whom family members can reach if they can't get to their reunion location, and it puts that relative at least 100 miles away. Someone that far from the quake is outside the local disruption. That person can take word from each family member and pass it along, and nobody has to search a damaged neighborhood for anyone else. A household with only a meetup spot has solved the first problem and left the second one open.

The plan has to work for people who can't use their phones. A plan saved only on a phone is lost when the phone dies or goes missing, and writing the meeting spot and the relative's number on paper keeps both within reach. Every member of the household, including children, should know both answers ahead of time. Nobody can explain the plan to a family member they can't reach.

With a place to meet and a person to call, a family has a plan that still works when the first answer fails.

A policy review looks like the easiest check on this list, because it involves reading a document rather than installing anything. Nacionale urges households to review their quake coverage now, ahead of any large disaster. That timing matters because the protection a household assumes it has may not exist. Standard homeowners and renters insurance both exclude earthquake damage, according to CNBC Select. A real review means confirming whether the household holds a separate earthquake policy.

Fixing that gap is a budget decision, and high home values in California make it a heavy one. Coverage is priced on the value of a home, and the median California home costs just over $900,000, CNBC Select reports, which means a typical owner has a great deal of house to insure. By its rough estimate, a policy for a median-priced home could cost $4,500 to $9,000 a year. A household has to weigh that expense against the risk of paying for quake repairs on its own. Even with a policy, an owner pays a large amount before any claim pays out. Quake deductibles are typically set at 10% to 25% of dwelling coverage, a share of the home's insured value rather than a flat fee. A homeowner can't skip the review, but buying a policy remains a judgment call, and the goal is to make that choice deliberately rather than by default.

Households that already carry quake coverage need to check what their policy leaves out. Fires, landslides, flooding and tsunamis caused by an earthquake are typically excluded from earthquake policies, according to CNBC Select, so an owner can be covered for the shaking and still be uninsured for the damage that comes after it.

A review is finished only when the household knows plainly what is covered and what is not, and that is the difference between holding a policy and being ready.

#5520. Seattle startup Aarden raises $8M to help landowners navigate the AI and energy building boom

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 1:36 pmNovember 17, 2026 at 2:36 pm

Seattle startup Aarden AI on Tuesday announced $8 million in new funding to grow its team and accelerate its work helping landowners evaluate potential uses for their properties and navigate deals with developers building data centers, clean energy projects, housing and other developments.

Founded last year, the company says its clients collectively own or manage approximately 14 million acres worldwide — nearly the land area of West Virginia. Aarden’s team said it has evaluated more than $500 million worth of land deals.

“But land markets remain opaque and manual with far too much friction. Finding the right site, and building trust with the right partners quickly, is more important than ever for our economy and our environment,” founder and CEO Danan Margason said in a statement.

The company combines data on hundreds of land attributes with historical market data and proprietary models to assess development suitability, valuation trends, ownership and community sentiment. Its tools and services also help developers identify sites and connect with landowners.

Aarden generates revenue through subscriptions to its technology, which includes AI-native data, models and investment tools, and through fees for services tied to specific deals or analyses.

The new round brings Aarden’s total funding to $12 million. Overture Ventures led the round, with participation from Madrona and Propeller Ventures. The startup previously raised $4 million in a round led by Planeteer in June 2025. The company has 13 employees and plans to nearly double in size over the next 12 months.

Margason said he launched the business on the premise that while there have long been tools to support developers, landowners have been largely on their own to evaluate and optimize deals so they’re not taken advantage of or end up partnering with untrustworthy organizations.

One customer, timberland investment manager Resource Management Service, uses Aarden to evaluate whether tracts are best suited for continued timber production, conservation, solar development or other uses.

“Diligence that used to take months now produces investment-grade answers we can act on, and that is shaping how we manage value across our portfolio,” said Alex Hinson, president and CEO of Resource Management Service.

Other companies offering property research and analysis tools include Acres, which provides land data, valuations and due diligence tools, and Land id, which offers property insights and mapping tools.

Ben Eidelson, a partner at Stepchange Ventures, which participated in the startup’s first funding round, said the company is already having an impact.

“We now have the capability to make smarter decisions about land, optimizing for the outcomes that matter from conservation to the local economy,” Eidelson said on LinkedIn.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5519. Bessent said U.S. AI chip policy toward China is unchanged after Trump-Xi talks

The Treasury secretary said Nvidia's H200 is the threshold chip allowed for sale to China, and Jensen Huang was not discussed

Maxim Shemetov / POOL / AFP via Getty Images

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC on Friday that Washington's stance permitting Nvidia $NVDA to sell its H200 processors in China has not shifted since the most recent round of discussions with Beijing.

"We've already agreed that the H200s are the threshold level of chips that could be sold to the Chinese, and, you know, that continues as planned," Bessent said on "Squawk Box." Asked about Nvidia's statement that it has stopped selling H200s to China, he said, "I wouldn't anticipate any change in the policy."

Bessent also said former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang did not come up in the talks. He answered "No" without elaborating when asked.

The interview came after President Donald Trump returned from an Asia trip that, according to CNBC, featured a meeting in Shenzhen, China, with Xi Jinping, China's president, and Vladimir Putin, Russia's president. Bessent said Trump and Xi had a "robust discussion" on trade policy and AI. He said the two leaders settled on keeping a person in the loop whenever AI is used to make military choices, and on barring AI from operating independently in significant armed operations.

Asked whether he and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are at odds on the forcefulness of the push to restrict exports to China, Bessent said, "I think we're all committed to following President Trump's instructions." He added that "the proper chip restrictions" will be in place and "the remote access has been curtailed." Commerce has moved to shut off one avenue Chinese buyers use to obtain AI processors, according to CNBC.

Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO last week after acknowledging an affair with a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. U.S. intelligence officials suspect the executive of spying for China. Megaspeed is suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China in breach of U.S. export controls. Nvidia's board named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO.

Bessent said in a CNBC appearance last week that Commerce "has the pen" on adding Megaspeed to the export blacklist. He said the Treasury, State and Defense departments and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative supported the move. As of last week, Commerce had declined to list the company.

In that Nov. 13  interview with CNBC, Bessent also said Trump had made clear China should not receive Nvidia chips above H100s, and he called any leakage of chips "very frustrating."

#5518. ‘Do not search Amazon’: Meta’s Muse now shops elsewhere by default

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 2:36 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 9:45 am

Two months after Amazon slammed the door on Muse, the AI agent has stopped knocking.

The shopping skill that guides Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent, now tells it to “leave out Amazon unless the user asks for it,” according to the instructions Muse provides when asked. The instructions include a template brief for Muse’s browser that says, “Do not search Amazon.”

The change was spotted last week by Juozas Kaziukenas, founder of the e-commerce research firm Marketplace Pulse, who asked Muse for the text of its shopping skill and compared it with the version from the day before. He posted the before-and-after on Friday. GeekWire asked Muse for its shopping skill and got the same language.

“Amazon blocked Muse, so now Muse blocked Amazon,” Kaziukenas wrote on X.

Muse is also told not to name Amazon as a site to search in that browser brief, “even as an example,” unless the user asked for Amazon. The skill steers the agent to Walmart and Target for general goods, Best Buy for electronics, and Home Depot or Lowe’s for home improvement.

For Muse users, not much changes in practice. Amazon began blocking Muse in September, less than two weeks after Meta launched the agent, showing anyone who tried to shop through it a message saying continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use. Kaziukenas said any Amazon search would fail anyway because of the block.

What’s new is that Meta appears to be going along with what Amazon asked for. When it began blocking Muse, Amazon said it had asked Meta to “remove Amazon from the experience.” Meta hadn’t said publicly how it would respond.

Meta didn’t respond to an inquiry about the change. An Amazon spokesperson said the company had nothing to share.

Amazon objected that Muse didn’t identify itself when it browsed the site and appeared to capture and store customer credentials. Meta has said Muse has no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods. The standoff set off a broader debate over who owns the customer relationship when an AI agent does the buying.

Since then, both sides have kept moving. More than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada signed up for Muse in its first six weeks, Forbes reported, and Walmart, Best Buy, Sephora and Wayfair are among the retailers working with Meta on it.

The business stakes are high for Amazon. It generated more than $68 billion in advertising revenue last year, including sponsored products that appear as people browse its pages — ads a shopper might never see if an outside agent does the searching. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said Muse will take a small cut of the transactions it handles.

Amazon has fought this battle before, suing Perplexity last November over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. It’s now pressing that case in part on the same Conditions of Use it cited in blocking Muse.

On Amazon’s earnings call last month, CEO Andy Jassy said outside shopping agents aren’t making a meaningful dent in Amazon’s advertising business. “Few customers are doing much shopping this way yet,” he said, adding that the experience still isn’t great or more convenient than going straight to a retailer.

Jassy said Amazon expects to work with “horizontal agents,” general-purpose assistants like Muse, but believes its own Alexa for Shopping will be the main agent people use to shop Amazon. Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May, combining its Rufus shopping chatbot with the Alexa+ assistant.

It has since started letting some customers text Alexa to shop, much as people do with Muse.

#5517. The robots are shopping now

A version of this article originally appeared in Quartz’s members-only Weekend Brief newsletter. Quartz members get access to exclusive newsletters and more. Sign up here.

Somewhere in Silicon Valley, some of the most powerful tech leaders in the world decided the best use of a superintelligence was buying toilet paper.

Meta $META launched its , and 10 million people in the U.S. downloaded it within 40 days. Buying was the most popular task, and the .

Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz.

OpenAI followed with Dots a few weeks later, its own always-on agent. Both promised a tireless assistant that never got distracted and could comb a hundred sites for the cheapest flight while its owner slept.

It was an easy pitch to love. The trouble was that the internet had been built for people, and the people had just sent robots.

Agentic web traffic roughly tripled from August to September, and most of it headed to e-commerce sites. Retailers had to quickly decide what to do.

Walmart $WMT didn’t seem to share the worry. It announced a system that would give each agent its own profile, with shoppers able to require approval for every purchase or set a spending limit. The idea was to give agents access just to the information they needed without handing them the shopper's entire account history.

Banks drew a harder line. JPMorgan $JPM said it would not let outside agents into customer accounts, and several large banks reported customers handing over credentials in ways that broke their terms of service.

Even friendly sites found surprises. The RealReal, a luxury resale site, holds any item in a shopper’s cart for 20 minutes. A reporter told Muse to keep re-adding a brand’s newest pieces and keep grabbing them each time the clock ran out, and the agent obliged for hours, shutting every human out of those items. Within days, the company said it had updated its anti-bot filters, and agents could browse listings but had a far harder time logging in or buying.

For shoppers, the upside was real. Agents were good at the chores people hated, like chasing refunds, tracking fares and escaping subscriptions designed to be forgotten. Some of that value came from the same inattention that businesses had long relied on.

The downside landed on everyone else. As sites tried to tell agents from people, they stacked up bot checks, and the people got caught in them too. Shoppers who sent nothing but themselves found more puzzles between them and a pair of shoes.

But getting through checkout was only part of the problem. The bigger issue was whether the agent was really working for the shopper. Someone who once compared two tabs now had to trust a system built by a company with its own commercial deals. Meta had partnerships with Walmart, Sephora and others, and its chief executive said the company would take a commission on purchases.

There was no evidence here that Muse favored those partners. But shoppers had little way to know whether its recommendations were impartial. If an agent said it found the best price, how would anyone know?

In a recent preprint, researchers at Carnegie Mellon and Cisco $CSCO gave AI agents the inboxes of made-up users and asked each for help on different purchases. The agents weren't given bank balances. Instead, they inferred financial circumstances from emails about tax filings, stock vesting and other clues, then recommended pricier options to wealthier users.

The most practical fix may be an old one. Financial advisers are subject to fiduciary duties in certain circumstances, requiring them to put their clients' interests first. Lindsay Owens, an economist and author of the new book Gouged, has argued that a similar standard should apply to AI shopping agents. If a product calls itself your personal agent, her argument goes, it should be legally bound to work for you, not for whoever pays to be shown first.

Until the law said whose side a personal agent had to be on, shoppers had only the word of the agent and the company that profited from it.

#5516. Jeff Bezos has some advice for Nvidia’s board on its CEO search

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 5:05 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 9:50 am

Jeff Bezos says Nvidia should look inside the company for its next CEO, and he doesn’t give an outsider much chance of success. The Amazon founder, now co-CEO of AI engineering startup Prometheus, made the comments Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event.

“If you don’t bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider. Nvidia is too complicated,” Bezos said. Outside CEOs at complex companies, he added, “have a vanishingly small chance of succeeding,” and he would consider hiring one “a last resort.”

Nvidia’s board says it has no plans to bring Huang back. Harvey Jones, the longtime director named the company’s first board chair last week, opened Nvidia’s earnings call Tuesday afternoon by saying the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

Jones said the search will include internal and external candidates, and that the board wants a permanent CEO in place quickly but won’t rush the pick.

Huang, the Nvidia co-founder and CEO for 33 years, had posted a statement on X that morning offering to return. He said he had “made serious mistakes” in his personal life and would cooperate with the board’s independent investigation.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation last Thursday, a day after the New York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman who U.S. officials believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence, according to the Wall Street Journal.

CFO Colette Kress, who spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career, is interim CEO.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to leave open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives wrote in a note Sunday that talk of a Huang comeback is “ridiculous.”

The Amazon precedent (not really): Bezos has been through a founder handoff of his own. He turned over the Amazon CEO job in 2021 to Andy Jassy, a longtime insider who built AWS. When Semafor raised the comparison, Bezos called it a poor one, saying there has never been a more carefully planned transition.

He said he didn’t know enough about what happened in Nvidia’s board meetings to say whether Huang should return. But he called Huang a remarkable founder who deserves “admiration and respect no matter what.”

Huang himself said in a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14 that he hoped his successor was already inside the company.

The Nvidia comments came in a wide-ranging interview. Bezos also said Blue Origin is using Prometheus tools on two projects, called President Trump by far the most communicative of the presidents he has worked with, and said Robert Pattinson was the clear choice to play the next James Bond after screen tests of five finalists.

Business as usual, officially: Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, including $107.6 billion from its data center business. On the call, it raised its forecast for next fiscal year’s revenue growth to about 75%, from 70%.

Kress didn’t mention Huang by name on the call. Asked about the leadership transition, she said customers, suppliers and employees remain behind the company, calling it “business as usual.” She ended the call with a short pep talk that finished, “We’ve got this.”

In case the board was wondering about one outsider in particular, Bezos is spoken for. During the Semafor interview, he described running Prometheus as “Nirvana.”

#5515. Europeans are asking AI for the best price. They may not be getting it

AI now picks the products and prices many European shoppers weigh. Those buyers can still miss a better offer unless they search the stores themselves

Armin Weigel / picture alliance via Getty Images

The European Commission proposed a new law earlier this moth, the Digital Fairness Act, and promised that people in the E.U. "will have clear rights when using an AI agent to buy products on their behalf." The announcement didn't list any of the new rights.

Europeans need to know, because more than half of them have already used AI to help them shop, according to a survey by the consulting firm Deloitte. It took just 18 months for half of European shoppers to start using AI, compared with about five years for online shopping. Of the Europeans already shopping with AI, more now compare products by asking it than by browsing marketplaces, retailers' websites, or store shelves. Few let AI pay, though. For every person in the survey who would let AI complete a purchase, three to four would let it compare products and find prices. Most Europeans still take the short list an AI gives them, pick from it, and then go to a store or a retailer's website to buy.

The price on that short list isn't always the lowest one available. In August, the research firm Productrise compared Google $GOOGL's AI Mode with an ordinary Google search across more than two million product listings in the U.S. and the U.K. For about one in four products found by both AI Mode and an ordinary Google search, AI showed a higher price for the identical item that day, according to a summary of the study by the pricing-data company TGN Data. The study covered only the U.S. and the U.K., and none of the E.U.'s three main consumer laws in force, as the Commission describes them, requires a seller or its software to act in shoppers' interest. Whether Europeans see the cheapest offer depends on whether the AI works for them or for the company that built it.

Most products never reach the short list at all. Only about one in 80 items that ranked in an ordinary Google search also turned up in AI Mode when Productrise ran the identical query. AI Mode never showed its users the other 79, however little they cost. Google hasn't verified the study, and the company says people can click through its shopping results to compare sellers. Deloitte warns retailers that an AI tool will leave their goods off the lists it gives people if it can't read the product information.

Paul F. Accornero, a senior executive at the appliance maker De'Longhi Group, spent about three months watching AI agents choose among items in many categories and wrote in California Management Review in February that they favor products with claims they can check. In one example, an agent compared two brands of noise-cancelling headphones. The first brand listed its specifications in detail, including 30 hours of battery life and a certified rating for how much outside noise the headphones block. The second brand opened its listing with a slogan and lifestyle photos, the product of $2 million spent on photography and influencer deals, and gave few numbers. The agent picked the first brand. Accornero wrote that he couldn't tell whether the first brand's headphones were actually better. The agent picked them because it could verify what their maker said about them.

Most brands haven't adjusted. Across the brands Accornero has studied, 60% to 80% of the basic product details an agent reads are usually missing, or they differ from one site to the next. Over six months, he interviewed 30 executives, and more than half were still planning mainly for human shoppers. If agents keep favoring products they can check, the sellers on AI short lists will be the ones that fixed their product details, whether or not they charge the least.

The companies building AI shopping agents plan to make money from what people buy off these short lists. Meta $META launched its agent, Muse, in the U.S. and Canada in September, and more than 10 million people there had set it up by Oct. 21, CEO Mark Zuckerberg told investors. Shopping is what they use it for most. More than one in four people who open Muse in a given week buy something through it, Meta said on the call, and the average order tops $200.

Meta plans to keep Muse free for most people and make its money by taking a fee on the purchases the agent helps them make. Zuckerberg told investors that Meta would start earning money from Muse sooner than it usually does with a new product, in part because "such a large part of what people are doing is commerce." Once the fee is in place, Meta will earn more each time someone buys an item Muse found.

Mark Bartholomew, a University at Buffalo law professor who studies AI and the law, said in October that people won't be able to tell whether their agent is recommending the best deal. "If, behind the scenes, an AI platform prioritized products that it made itself or that it received a commission from retailers for, that would drain this new technology of its promise," he said. Bartholomew was describing a risk, not a case he had found.

Doubts about Meta haven't kept people off its apps before. Trust in Meta remains low, Kate Winick, a principal analyst at the research firm Forrester, told Business Insider, yet "consumers almost expect to have their data mismanaged in exchange for a high level of connectivity and utility, and have shown that they're willing to keep showing up as long as the product experience delivers."

None of the rights the Commission promised protect anyone yet. The Digital Fairness Act is still a proposal, and the Commission said the European Parliament and the Council, where the member states' governments sit, will now debate it. The Commission set no date for a vote or for the rules to take effect.Until the proposal becomes law, Europeans rely on the E.U.’s three main consumer laws: the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive, the Consumer Rights Directive, and the Unfair Contract Terms Directive. The Commission's own 2024 review found gaps in how the three laws handle the tricks sellers use online.

Bartholomew wants a law to protect AI shoppers. In a paper in the William and Mary Law Review, Bartholomew and Samuel I. Becher, a law professor at the City University of Hong Kong, recommend that trusted outside auditors check shopping agents and certify whether they serve the people using them. "It's too hard for someone to figure out on their own whether an AI recommendation is truly trustworthy or not," Bartholomew said. The two professors also want every agent to come with a simple way to switch it off, so people can go back to researching products themselves whenever they choose.

Until the European Parliament and the Council pass the proposal and say what the rights they promised actually mean, Europeans have to trust that the price AI shows them is the best one. To find a cheaper offer, they would have to search the stores on their own and do the chore they had hoped to hand off.

#5514. Data centers went from about 3% of Oregon’s electricity use to about 23% in a decade — and account for 96% of its power-sales growth since 2020

It takes a lot of electricity to power the sprawling computing campuses undergirding the artificial intelligence boom: a lot for servers, a lot for cooling the chips, a lot for networking, and a bit for keeping the actual lights on. Yet translating “a lot” to real numbers pinned to individual facilities requires usage data, something that data-center operators are loath to disclose.

A Harvard-led study published this week in Nature Sustainability gets us closer to these numbers. Researchers extracted locations and building footprints for as many U.S. hyperscale data centers as possible, ultimately cataloguing 403 of the warehouse-sized facilities across the country. Translating power capacity to theoretical electricity usage, the authors estimated these facilities gobble up roughly 82 terawatt-hours of electricity annually, the equivalent of nearly 8 million homes. They suggest this electricity is associated with about 26 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions.

The 82-TWh estimate corresponds to about 2 percent of U.S. electricity. Though noteworthy in its own right, that figure shrouds high state-to-state variability, with many states boasting data-center electricity shares in the double digits. When viewed as a fraction of the retail electricity sales reported to the Energy Information Administration (EIA) in 2024, Oregon’s studied data centers used the equivalent of 18.6 percent of the electricity sold in the state. In Virginia and Iowa, data centers consumed 15.5 and 13.1 percent, respectively.

While data-center electricity consumption remains a national issue, electricity prices and utility planning look very different from state to state. And the speed of hyperscale buildouts mean these figures can change quickly.

In Oregon, for example, the state’s data-center share of electricity use grew from about 3 percent in 2015 to about 23 percent in 2025, according to analyses presented to the state by energy economics firm ECOnorthwest and the University of Virginia. The group estimated that data centers were associated with approximately 96 percent of the state’s electricity sales growth between 2020 and 2025.

Hyperscalers can “no longer be understood as a marginal component” of Oregon’s electricity demand, the authors wrote — and in the Wild West of hyperscaling, it’s a component poorly matched to current regulatory structures. In its most recent biennial energy report, the Oregon Department of Energy noted that the state “currently lacks a policy mechanism to address emissions from data center load growth.”

Many states are grappling with the ramifications of recent data-center buildouts. Because the Harvard study was limited to hyperscale facilities the authors could verify, its electricity-use estimates are likely undercounts. In Virginia, for example, the study’s 142 included facilities account for about 15 percent of the state’s electricity sales — itself a staggering sum. But Dominion Energy, the largest seller of electricity in the state, has estimated that data centers purchased 28 percent of the electricity its Virginia subsidiary sold last year.

Currently, there is no federal apparatus to track or check these figures, as surveys of utilities’ sales tend to label customer segments as merely residential, commercial, industrial, or transportation-related. In March, Senators Elizabeth Warren and Josh Hawley wrote to the EIA, arguing: “Without this data, policymakers, utility companies, and local communities are operating in the dark.” The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, the infrastructure permitting bill currently under consideration in the Senate, would direct the agency to explicitly measure data-center electricity usage.

Hyperscale electricity can also be understood in terms of the plant-warming gases emitted during its generation. Together, the facilities catalogued by the Harvard researchers emit more annually than the carbon-dioxide equivalent of countries like Jordan, Kenya, and Guatemala.

State context matters here, too, since emissions estimates depend on a given state’s grid, which vary by energy mix. The Nature Sustainability study’s authors used federal power-plant data to estimate the average per kilowatt-hour emissions for each confirmed data center. The resulting rates range from Washington’s hydropower-heavy 10 grams of carbon dioxide per kilowatt-hour to Virginia’s fossil-fuel-backed 325.

Yet even grid averages fail to capture the growing phenomenon of on-site power plants. Frequently gas-fired, these generators are built at or near hyperscale campuses to generate electricity directly for the data centers themselves. Electricity usage from on-site power can be harder to measure, given it is often “behind the meter” — that is, the electrons might never touch a public grid. As of June, about 2 GW of gas generators powered four data centers around the country, including Elon Musk’s xAI sites in Memphis, Tennessee. There are 143 GW of gas plants currently proposed to power data centers around the United States, according to the Environmental Integrity Project (EIP), a watchdog group.

Most of this proposed on-site power could push the hyperscale buildout outside the Harvard study’s map. West Virginia, for example, hosts exactly zero of the data-center campuses confirmed by the Nature Sustainability study. Yet the state is second only to Texas in proposed on-site gas capacity, with more than 15 GW tagged by EIP.

If built, these projects could reshape the geography of U.S. data centers — and make their electricity use less visible in utility-sales and grid-demand data. Behind-the-meter power doesn’t show up as utility purchases.

It’s possible many of these proposed plants will never actually break ground; only about two dozen of the 74 proposed plants tagged by EIP are currently permitted for construction under the Clean Air Act. Yet if the recent supercharged data center build-out offers any indication, applications for new on-site facilities will continue to roll in.

“What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” said Gianluca Guidi, lead author of the Nature Sustainability study, in a statement. Forget 2 percent: The electricity and emissions estimates offered by his team “could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”

This article originally appeared in Grist at https://grist.org/energy/data-centers-use-2-of-us-electricity-in-some-states-the-share-is-far-higher/.

Grist is a nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to reporting on climate change.
