#5513. ‘You said spicy, right?’ Panel takes on Washington’s economic blind spots — and what needs to change

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:15 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 11:49 am

Washington’s biggest economic threat may be the conviction that it’s already doing everything right.

That was the pointed warning from a Technology Alliance panel Tuesday, where a conversation about talent and economic growth became a challenge to the state’s self-image as an innovation leader.

“You said spicy, right?” Rob Ogburn asked, taking up the invitation to speak bluntly.

“The economy is very strong. The economy is not competitive at all,” said Ogburn, executive director of Business and Community Services at Central Washington University.

While tech giants such as Microsoft and Amazon and sectors including aerospace and biotech are powering today’s economy, that doesn’t mean Washington is positioned to win tomorrow’s investment, develop its workforce or spread opportunity beyond its major employment centers.

Amelia Ransom, former vice president at Smartsheet and past Nordstrom leader, questioned the definition of success, arguing that future growth also depends on investing in people and businesses outside the corporate spotlight.

“Who do we mean when we say winning? Who is it? Who are we talking about, and who are we leaving out?” Ransom said, later adding, “We have to close the daylight between who we say we are and who we actually are.”

The panel was held in downtown Seattle and moderated by Jolenta Coleman-Bush, director of Microsoft Philanthropies. It also included Rachel Smith, president of Washington Roundtable.

Rather than simply calling for more talent and innovation, panelists examined how Washington develops the people already here, whose perspectives inform its decisions and how effectively its institutions and stakeholders work together.

Unification is essential. U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., led the passage of the CHIPS and Science Act in 2022 to bolster semiconductor manufacturing and innovation in AI and energy. But her home state has received just 0.3% of the funding awarded so far, Ogburn said.

He argued that other states and regions were more effective at uniting to make their case for investment, showing their collective resources and the problems they could solve.

“We showed up and said, ‘We’re competing with our neighbor, and we’re better than them.’ No investor is going to look at that and say you’re going to make the best use of my money,” Ogburn said.

Cultivate talent, don’t just recruit it. Ransom compared workforce development to a restaurant, a grocery store and a garden: recruiting ready-made workers, developing the talent already here and growing the long-term pipeline.

“The middle is where we probably need to spend more time, which is at the grocery store, which means you’ve got to learn to cook,” she said. Her point: Invest in Washington’s existing employees, students, and businesses.

Smith wants employers to identify the high-wage, high-skill jobs they need filled so educators and businesses can coordinate strategies to prepare workers for those roles.

Fill essential information gaps. Panelists called for a clearer picture of community skills and barriers to opportunity, more voices to challenge prevailing assumptions, and closer examination of how regulations affect businesses.

“We’ve gotten in this war of the rankings where everybody’s like, “No, we’re the best. No, we’re the worst.” And we we’ve got to stop doing that,” Smith said.

The region needs data-backed insights into the reasons behind the rankings, she said. Smith pointed to the recently formed Economic Development Council and its planned statewide strategy as a step toward a more coordinated approach.

Whether these efforts succeed, Ogburn said, should be judged by the communities themselves.

“And then, if you want to measure success, go back to those communities and ask them if they feel successful,” he said. “Do they have agency and self-determination?”

#5512. I Never Saw My Team’s Daily Work as Content. It Turned Out to Be a Powerful Marketing Tool.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The everyday work you take for granted could be the most compelling story your business has to tell.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For years, I thought I knew what separated my moving company from others. I’m a fourth-generation mover and have worked in this industry professionally since I was 18. My father always said moving was in my blood — hence our name, Can’t Quit Moving. I built my business on lessons passed down through my family: Work hard, treat people and their belongings with respect and do the job the right way. After hearing countless moving horror stories from customers, I knew we operated differently.

And I thought that was enough: doing honest work and making sure people had a good moving experience. I certainly didn’t see our everyday work as content, as something other people would want to know more about or as something that could help grow the company. That changed when someone from outside the industry spent a day with us.

During the pandemic, a good friend of mine who worked as a cameraman was out of work, so he joined our crew for a day. At the end of it, he climbed into the truck looking rattled. “That was a crazy day,” he told me. My response: “That was a Tuesday.”

Every day, we dealt with closing delays, low bridges, furniture that wouldn’t fit, last-minute additions and customers navigating one of the most stressful days of their lives. To me, that was second nature. To him, it was a story, and he told me we needed to film it.

That eventually became an unscripted docuseries about our company, but it also changed how I thought about growing a business. Until then, we had relied solely on word of mouth. What I hadn’t realized was that showing people what sets us apart from the competition could become a growth strategy.

When you spend every day doing the same thing, you lose sight of what makes it interesting. I didn’t think twice about the problems we encountered on a move, because solving them was my job. But to an outsider, the process was wild. Parking and loading our truck, for example, fascinated our cameraman. It made me realize that the work my team and I do takes real skill.

That’s something business owners in any industry can overlook. You don’t need a glamorous product or a business built for social media to have a story worth telling. A contractor solving a job site issue, a restaurant prepping for a Saturday night or a bookseller opening their store all have something customers rarely get to see.

Simply put, your best content could already be happening. You just have to recognize and document it.

When we started filming, I had to unlearn some of my business owner instincts. After our second day, my wife paused a piece of footage and asked what I had been thinking in that moment. The truth was, I had been thinking plenty. I just wasn’t saying it.

I was trained to stay calm even when things went off the rails. My wife told me to talk to the camera like I was talking to my best friend. I had to rewire my thinking: Explain the problem. Share what you’re thinking. Admit when you’re frustrated. Just be real.

That taught me the difference between advertising and real storytelling. Business owners spend a lot of time telling customers who they are: We’re trustworthy. We care. We go above and beyond. And so on.

Documenting our work allowed us to show those things instead. Our motto is “We take the stress out of your move,” and now people could see that firsthand: how our crew wraps belongings to protect them from torrential rain, how we responded when a move didn’t go as planned because of an insurance headache and how we treated customers even when we were close to pulling our hair out under high-pressure deadlines. The messy moments showed more about the company than the camera-ready ones.

Other entrepreneurs can learn from this. What do you claim about your business that you could demonstrate instead?

After we finished filming the show, a former customer who worked in the film industry encouraged us to start sharing our story on social media. Creating content consistently has sometimes felt like starting another business, but it also changed how I think about marketing. Traditional advertising usually tries to reach someone around the time they’re ready to buy. Telling a story and building an audience can create a relationship long before that.

That’s especially important in a business like moving. People don’t need movers every month. Someone might discover one of our videos today and not move for another year. But if they keep following the company and seeing our crew at work, we don’t have to introduce ourselves when they’re finally ready for a quote. The audience comes first. The customer can come later.

And we’re starting to see that play out. When we ask new customers how they found us, more and more of them mention our videos. One man contacted us about moving his lemon trees because he’d seen us move palm trees on Instagram. During another move, a customer’s 6-year-old recognized us from our YouTube Shorts. To me, that was proof: People weren’t just remembering our moving company. They were remembering us. They felt like they’d gotten to know the people behind the business, and more importantly, they already trusted us.

Don’t get me wrong: You don’t need to create a docuseries to apply this strategy. I’d start with three questions:

The goal isn’t to capture someone’s attention for the sole purpose of selling something. That’s empty, and it doesn’t build trust. The point is to give viewers, your potential customers, a reason to keep paying attention.

Your competitors can offer similar services. They can lower their prices and make the same claims about why they’re better. What they can’t replicate is your people, your experiences, your perspective and how you do your work.

For years, I thought I knew what separated my moving company from others. I’m a fourth-generation mover and have worked in this industry professionally since I was 18. My father always said moving was in my blood — hence our name, Can’t Quit Moving. I built my business on lessons passed down through my family: Work hard, treat people and their belongings with respect and do the job the right way. After hearing countless moving horror stories from customers, I knew we operated differently.

And I thought that was enough: doing honest work and making sure people had a good moving experience. I certainly didn’t see our everyday work as content, as something other people would want to know more about or as something that could help grow the company. That changed when someone from outside the industry spent a day with us.

During the pandemic, a good friend of mine who worked as a cameraman was out of work, so he joined our crew for a day. At the end of it, he climbed into the truck looking rattled. “That was a crazy day,” he told me. My response: “That was a Tuesday.”

#5511. Holiday shoppers let AI agents find gifts — but don't trust them with their credit cards

Walmart, Shopify and Meta have built ways for AI agents to pay. By default, those tools still need the shopper's okay on each order before money moves

Amando Komoda runs a Minneapolis company that sells supplies for dry-aging meat, and he uses an AI agent called Instinct to set up alerts for hard-to-find parts, such as a particular Raspberry Pi chip, so he doesn't have to search for them himself. Often he still buys the part himself. When he does let Instinct pay, he approves the purchase first and gives the agent a credit card number that works only once, so it can't charge anything he hasn't agreed to. "I wouldn't give it access to my best credit card," he told Business Insider. "I've watched enough sci-fi movies that I can't trust it completely."

Komoda's caution is the opposite of what Meta $META and OpenAI promised when they launched their agents this fall. Meta and OpenAI pitched agents that would shop day and night and find the cheapest option without their owners having to check. Millions of people signed up. Meta said on Oct. 21 that more than 10 million people had set up Muse, the agent it launched in September.

Far fewer have let their agents pay. Just 12% of U.S. shoppers, about one in eight, say they've let their own AI agent buy something for them, according to a holiday survey that Salesforce $CRM, the business software company, published Nov. 12. Shoppers don't trust AI agents to spend their money yet, and Meta can't earn much from Muse until people let it complete their purchases.

Loni Stark, Adobe $ADBE's vice president of strategy and product, has built two AI agents herself and expects tools like them to take over the part of shopping people dread. "We don't like the anxiety of wondering whether we got the best price or not," she told Business Insider. "We're going to offload that to agents." She still decides when her agents spend her money. Museli, the agent she built on Muse, handled an entire purchase of ballet shoes from Nordstrom $JWN's website, but it got her permission before it paid. Her other agent, Molty, researches products she's thinking about buying, and she has never connected it to a way to pay.

People can approve every payment themselves and still end up paying with the wrong card. Katie Notopoulos, a senior correspondent at Business Insider, asked Muse to order her a salad while she was reviewing three agents. Muse offered her a debit card or a Mastercard $MA from the accounts she had already linked. She picked the Mastercard because she didn't recognize its last four digits and assumed it was the new credit card that had just come in the mail. When she checked her wallet, she found she had chosen her health savings account card, which works only for medical expenses. She was so busy sorting out the mix-up that she never told Muse to place the order, and Muse never sent it. "This turned out to be a real fiasco," she wrote, "and I learned my lesson: it would have been infinitely easier for me to just do it myself.

Like Notopoulos, most U.S. holiday shoppers still want to handle their own payments, even when AI does the searching. About two in five U.S. shoppers now rely mainly on generative AI for at least one holiday task, the consulting firm Deloitte's annual holiday survey found, yet fewer than half of them would trust the tool to complete a purchase, even with their permission. Nearly twice as many people would trust an AI agent to pick gifts for friends and family as would let it pay with their card, even if they could check its work first, a September survey by the customer-service software company Talkdesk found. Shoppers are ready to let an agent find the gift but not to let it spend their money.

Muse users do buy things. More than a quarter of Muse's weekly users shop with it, Meta told analysts on its Oct. 21 earnings call. In Muse's first week, people bought so much more than anyone expected that Meta had to work with the payments company Stripe to raise credit limits.

Across the web, though, agents mostly browse. HUMAN Security, which sells software that spots and blocks bots, found that AI agent traffic on the sites it protects grew about eightfold from August to October, and most of it landed on shopping sites. Nearly all of the agent visits were for browsing. Most went to product and search pages, and fewer than one in 50 reached a checkout or payment page. HUMAN counts where a request lands, not whether anyone bought anything, so even a visit to a checkout page doesn't prove a sale.

Many of the sites HUMAN protects keep Muse out entirely. Blocked agent requests hit a record in September, and HUMAN said Muse was the main reason. The company's fraud software blocks Muse unless a site chooses to allow it, and because the agent is so new, many sites still haven't. Susan J. Li, a Meta executive, told analysts on the earnings call that some businesses are "understandably focused on protecting customer relationships." On sites that block Muse, the agent can't buy anything, and its users have to shop for themselves.

Even where agents get in, the puzzles and texted login codes that stores use to confirm a person is buying can stop them before they pay. Komoda, the Minneapolis business owner, often finishes purchases himself because Instinct can't always solve the Captcha puzzles some checkouts require. When Business Insider reporter Notopoulos had OpenAI's agent, Dot, get her lunch, Dot kept getting stuck on the six-digit login code sent to her phone, and she had to request the code three times before the order went through.

Walmart $WMT and Shopify $SHOP have built checkouts for agents, and both keep a person in charge of every purchase. Walmart announced on Oct. 21 that each AI agent would get a profile of its own inside a customer's account, under a system the company calls Agent Profiles. By default, the agent has to ask for approval before it buys anything. People can instead let it buy on its own up to a limit they set, such as $50, and the agent never sees their card number.

Shopify asks people to approve every payment an agent makes at its merchants' stores. Shopify's checkout inside Meta's AI services, Muse among them, is switched on by default for eligible stores, and it covers buyers in 11 countries, including the U.S. In every purchase Shopify describes, people review the order and approve the payment before it goes through.

Meta's plan to make money from Muse depends on how often people approve a purchase. On the earnings call, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Meta would start making money from Muse sooner than it usually does with a new product, under a model in which it collects "a percent of the value that we are helping to create for people." But Meta collects its percentage only on the sales people let Muse finish. Li, the Meta executive, told analysts that the company expects many Muse experiences to "remain AI assisted rather than fully autonomous" in the near term.

Once Meta collects a share of each sale, people have one more reason to check the price and the seller before they say yes. Shoppers already worry about AI pushing them toward the wrong purchase. Nearly three in four people in Talkdesk's survey want stronger rules on how retailers use AI, and 40% worry they could be misled into buying something that isn't right for them.

This Cyber Monday, many shoppers will send agents to find gifts but still read the price, check who's selling, and type in their own card numbers. The agents save them the search. Checking out is still a job people do themselves.

#5510. I Used to Counteroffer My Best Employees With More Money. Now I Rely on These 3 Strategies.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Raises and equity can delay a top performer’s exit, but smarter compensation structures can keep them for the long haul.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Like all business leaders, I have had some of my top performers tell me they were leaving. There is no way to sugarcoat the feeling. It’s like a kick in the belly — and in the wallet.

According to statistics reported by HR Morning, replacing an employee costs upwards of 200% of what they were making. And that is probably a conservative figure, given that losing a valuable team member can cause a ripple of lowered productivity and tabled projects as people scramble to pick up the ex-employee’s work.

Given these facts, I used to follow the standard pattern of attempting to keep talented team members by offering them higher compensation, bonuses or company equity. It was a tactic that almost always worked, but it didn’t create loyalty. Instead, it made those people price-sensitive, and they eventually found organizations willing to pay more, so they left anyway.

I am not suggesting that it is wrong to counteroffer someone’s resignation with money. However, it’s reactive and arbitrary. Unless you have put a cap on how high you are willing to go, your negotiations will begin to feel like a moving target that’s out of your control. Again, you may end up delaying someone’s departure, but you won’t keep them forever unless you put more proactive measures in place.

Some positions in your company drive enterprise value and some don’t. McKinsey and Company suggested in an older article that these will probably make up about 5% of your workforce — and contribute 800% more than others across your organization.

Over the years, I’ve found that I could typically name fewer than 10 roles that would materially impact my business if they remained vacant for an extended period. My recommendation is to name those roles and then create retention plans for each of them.

What are some focused plan ideas? Deferred compensation structures allow team members to grow their money tax-free as long as they stay with your organization. That way, you won’t inflate your overall payroll and can concentrate your resources where they matter most. This type of long-term incentive can be tangibly meaningful because it’s tied to tenure and not merely performance. Since it’s only applicable to a small group of high-value employees, you aren’t raising your compensation across your organization, either.

I once considered using equity as a major retention lever. Why not? It felt right and seemed to be a no-brainer way to get people to stick around and contribute to our company’s growth. Yet when I mapped out the risks and rewards, I realized that giving away equity has massive long-term costs.

Here’s the issue: equity permanently dilutes your ability to use equity in other ways later. For example, you can’t bargain with equity with potential investors if a chunk of it has been given to your employees. Going the equity route also complicates your organizational governance, which can make your financial picture blurry.

Rather than offering equity to someone who wants to leave, explore non-equity alternatives. Treat equity as a last resort that you’ll only consider if you think it will bring out an employee’s long-term ownership behavior. And be open to talking about this with a professional who has helped other businesses design executive benefit and compensation structures that retain key people while protecting tax exposure and equity. Looking for a resource to get your feet wet? Colin Steinberg, a partner at Institutional Architects, frequently shares advice on executive planning and related topics.

There are many business-friendlier alternatives to simply handing an employee who’s about to leave more money or equity. As mentioned before, you might provide deferred compensation, a way to delay income that benefits both you and the team member.

You might also look into supplemental executive retirement plans. Chances are strong that you already offer retirement benefits. Could you offer additional ones directly tied to both tenure and performance? Supplemental executive retirement plans help C-suite employees see meaningful future value in putting down roots, which SmartAsset explains can help trim churn among your highest-paid performers.

When structured appropriately, these types of retention strategies avoid immediate financial strain on your balance sheet. They also allow you to turn retention tools into ways to improve your tax efficiency, reduce volatile compensation models and retain control over your equity.

I firmly believe that founders who lose their most valuable people (but are otherwise building solid, fair companies) don’t have a problem with their retention. They have a problem with the way they’ve structured their long-term compensation packages for their most impactful roles. If you want to get real leverage as an employer, you need to develop smarter systems that incentivize your key players without losing your ground.

Like all business leaders, I have had some of my top performers tell me they were leaving. There is no way to sugarcoat the feeling. It’s like a kick in the belly — and in the wallet.

According to statistics reported by HR Morning, replacing an employee costs upwards of 200% of what they were making. And that is probably a conservative figure, given that losing a valuable team member can cause a ripple of lowered productivity and tabled projects as people scramble to pick up the ex-employee’s work.

Given these facts, I used to follow the standard pattern of attempting to keep talented team members by offering them higher compensation, bonuses or company equity. It was a tactic that almost always worked, but it didn’t create loyalty. Instead, it made those people price-sensitive, and they eventually found organizations willing to pay more, so they left anyway.

#5509. Trump, Putin and Xi signed onto a 1985 Reagan-Gorbachev nuclear line in 90 minutes of talks — Ukraine didn’t even come up by name

It was touted as a history-making summit of the year. Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping sat down on Nov. 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China, on the sideline of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, for the first such trilateral meeting of the three leaders.

Going into the talks, the trio had much to dicuss: the ongoing war in Ukraine, Middle East conflict and the march of artificial intelligence technology chief among them.

But what did 90 minutes of conversation deliver?

As an expert on U.S.-China relations at Harvard Kennedy School, I saw a lot of style, but less substance.

The first thing to pay attention to is the symbolism of the occasion. And so much of what was presented in Shenzhen was about the body language of the three men, their interactions and what that may indicate in regards to how they view themselves in a potentially new global order.

And this was on show even before the leaders sat down. At the beginning of the trip, when Trump landed in Shenzhen, he was met by Xi. Meeting a foreign leader at the airport is seen as a special honor bestowed by the Chinese president.

And then came a hug – that really was unprecedented. I haven’t seen the general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party hug anyone before – certainly not his Politburo comrades.

It was all choreographed, of course. But it continued into the summit itself. The picture of a big table with Trump, Putin and Xi there is also symbolic. And look who was in the middle: Xi. Here we have China presenting as the “Middle Kingdom,” steadying the world. Whether that is an accurate depiction of China’s global presence is beside the point – it is how Xi would like Beijing to be seen.

In terms of policy, however, not much was actually done, but we did get a glimpse of what was on the three leaders’ minds.

So we had talk of reforming the U.N. – something all three agree needs to be done. In particular, China wants more power in the organization, while Trump has become increasingly disillusioned with the international body.

And there was also a lot of discussion on nuclear weapons controls. In fact, all three signed off on a document that made statements and aspirations – with fewer commitments – to tamping down nuclear threats. Interestingly, this was all based around a phrase that U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev first aired in 1985: “Nuclear war cannot be won, must never be fought.”

All three leaders signed onto the phrase, although there was not an awful lot of substance on how nuclear controls would be implemented. The main treaties on the matter expired a while ago, and Beijing, which lags behind Washington and Moscow in regards to capacity, may have different thoughts on the matter.

The big thing not discussed in any substantive way was the wars raging in the domains of two of the three nations.

For Trump, that means Iran. Washington has not been able to bring the conflict in Iran to a conclusion some nine months after it began. The thinking going into the summit may have been that if China – or even Russia – were able to help pressure Iran and bring an end to the conflict, that would be encouraged.

But the spectacle of the U.S. not being able to end the war in Iran is not, I suspect, something that the Russians and Chinese are in a rush to bring to an end. In any case, neither appeared willing to give up a key card – assistance to Washington in the matter – in this meeting.

At the other end of that Eurasian spectrum is Ukraine. It was not mentioned by name at the summit. Besides the fact that the three leaders are not on the same side of the conflict, there is also the fact that Ukraine’s European allies were not in the room – and it would have been far too much for Europe for Trump to make news on Ukraine in the company of Putin and Xi.

Beyond those conflicts, AI regulation and critical mineral supply chains were not discussed by the three leaders. But that isn’t to say that those issues – crucial ones in the U.S.-China economic rivalry – were not brought up in the bilateral conversations that took place in Shenzhen. It may be that they were heard in these more discreet, private settings.

There were some immediate similarities with the Yalta Conference – the February 1945 summit at which the U.K.’s Winston Churchill, Joseph Stalin of the Soviet Union and U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt planned out the end of World War II and began discussing postwar Europe. But these were largely about the imagery of the three men around the table.

Of course, the big three then included Britain; there was no China. That alone tells you how much geopolitics has changed over 80 years.

Also, Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill were all on the same side in 1945. It was a case of comrades in arms that would soon be drifting apart as the Cold War developed.

Here it may well be the other way around. China and Russia are partners, but the U.S. is seen as their adversary.

What Trump may want is detente rather than a new Cold War. Does this mean an emerging policy of Russia, China and the U.S. coming together in a new order? I imagine the Europeans may have something to say about that.

Rana Mitter, Professor of U.S.-Asia Relations, Harvard Kennedy School

#5508. If an AI agent pays for the wrong thing, there are few ways to get a refund

Shoppers have started to approve each charge on an AI agent's own card. Every sign-off leaves a record that may be their best proof in a refund fight

Minh Connors / Bloomberg via Getty Images

J.P. Morgan Private Bank, the part of JPMorgan $JPM Chase that serves wealthy clients, told its clients on Nov. 11 not to give their login details to an AI agent. The warning came from a bank that doesn't currently let any outside agent into a client's account at all. Two days later, OpenAI began rolling out ChatGPT Wallet, which lets its AI agent pay without a shopper's login. The card network issues a one-time substitute number for each purchase and charges the shopper's real card behind it. Shoppers approve each purchase with Face ID or a fingerprint, and the agent never sees the real card number.

Shoppers have already shown they will let an agent spend their money. Within 40 days of Meta $META launching its Muse agent in early September, 10 million people in the U.S. had downloaded it. They used it for shopping more than for anything else, and their purchases averaged more than $200. Muse pays through Link, Stripe's wallet for agents, and the shopper okays each total in the Muse chat window before any money moves. Stripe says the card or bank account behind the purchase remains hidden from Muse.

ChatGPT Wallet's one-time numbers and Stripe's Link give shoppers a way to let an agent spend without handing over the bank login that banks are telling them to keep to themselves. Keeping the login safe doesn't settle everything, though. A store still decides for itself whether to let agents shop. And when an agent gets an order wrong, neither Visa $V nor Mastercard $MA has a dispute code written for an agent's mistake, which makes the shopper's record of each approval the strongest proof they have in a refund fight.

Every order agents put together sits on a screen in ChatGPT Wallet until it's approved. People can check what the agent picked, which store is selling it, what it all costs, which card will be charged, and any shipping fees or repeat billing. They can also turn the whole order down if anything looks wrong. When the wallet does pay, it uses a stand-in number, so the store never gets the real card either. For now, OpenAI limits the wallet to U.S. adults with ChatGPT Pro and an eligible American Express $AXP, Chase, Mastercard, or Visa credit card. Debit cards won't work.

Other companies let shoppers cap what an agent spends. Robinhood allows customers with its Gold Card give an outside AI agent its own virtual card, then either approve each purchase or set a monthly spending limit, according to Finovate, a fintech news site. OnePay, which announced a product called Agentic Banking in October, has eligible customers put money into a separate account for their agents, with a cap on each purchase and on each month. The agent never touches the customer's main account.

Those controls match what many shoppers say they want before an agent spends for them. A third of Americans surveyed by Global Payments, a payment technology company, want to approve every purchase before the money goes out. OpenAI's wallet makes that step mandatory, and Robinhood offers it as a choice. "Making purchases with a spending limit, in an approved category, and with a requirement to confirm the purchase are very different from giving an agent open-ended authority," Global Payments Chief Product Officer Cindy Turner explained.

A bank login hands an agent open-ended authority over the whole account, with no spending limit and no step to confirm a purchase. Madison Mills, a senior AI reporter at Axios, told CBS News that in many cases, customers had shared their bank logins with agents the bank hadn't verified. Agents holding those logins don't always ask first. In one case Axios found, an agent phoned a bank to lodge a complaint and never asked the account holder beforehand.

Customers could also end up paying for an agent's mistakes when they share a login. Regulation E, the federal rule that limits what a bank customer owes for a debit card charge or transfer they never approved, makes an exception for someone who hands over an "access device," the legal term for a card or credentials. The Consumer Bankers Association, the trade group for retail banks, warns that a login shared with an agent may count. If the agent then spends beyond what the customer allowed, the customer, not the bank, could be left covering the whole loss. An agent paying with a card number made just for it never holds the login, so that exception never comes into play.

Stores can still turn an agent away, however it pays. Within two weeks of Muse's launch, Amazon $AMZN began stopping its purchases with a popup that warned that "continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon's Conditions of Use." Amazon didn't block Muse over how it paid. The company said Muse doesn't tell stores it's an agent, keeps copies of customers' Amazon logins, and pulls data out of their accounts. A stand-in card number fixes none of those problems.

The RealReal, a luxury resale site, now makes it much harder for any AI agent, not only Muse, to sign in, fill a cart, or pay, according to Luke Friang, the company's chief technology officer. The company tightened its defenses after The Verge tested whether someone could use an agent to hold items indefinitely so that no one else could buy them. On The RealReal, an item goes on hold for 20 minutes once it lands in a cart, and nobody else can buy it during that time. The Verge's reporters told Muse to put the same listings back in its cart when the timer ran out, and for hours, no other shopper could buy those designer pieces. Friang said agents can still find listings and link to the product pages, but people have to buy the items themselves.

Walmart $WMT plans to let agents in, but only on its own terms. Under the rules Walmart announced on Oct. 21, an agent shops inside the customer's Walmart account and never sees the customer's card details, and it has no power to put a new way to pay on the account or swap out an existing one. With Walmart's planned Agent Profiles, the agent asks for approval on every purchase by default, and the customer can instead let it buy on its own up to a limit the customer sets. Walmart says it will block any agent that breaks its terms.

When an AI agent buys the wrong thing, whether people get their money back depends mostly on how the agent paid, according to Security Boulevard, a cybersecurity news site. A credit card gives them the most protection. Under Regulation Z, the federal rule for credit cards, cardholders can dispute a charge for goods that didn't arrive as agreed, as long as they write to the card issuer within 60 days of the first statement that shows it. When the issuer credits the account, the store usually ends up taking the loss. Visa and Mastercard sort these disputes into their existing "not as described" categories, and neither network's published list has a category for an agent's mistake. A debit card or bank transfer protects people far less, because a login handed to an agent can count as permission to spend under Regulation E. For the newest ways agents pay, the Consumer Bankers Association, the banks' trade group, says it's "at best, unclear" whether the old protections apply at all.

With the rules that unclear, a fight over an agent's purchase often comes down to what people can prove they told it to buy. Each ChatGPT Wallet approval leaves a record of exactly that. Visa CEO Ryan McInerney told investors on the company's Oct. 27 earnings call that Visa's payment product for agents records each customer's instructions and ties them to a biometric check, such as a fingerprint, so the agent buys only what it was asked to, and that Visa's usual dispute rules apply if something goes wrong. Security Boulevard says records like these can decide disputes in either direction. Some customers may change their minds about a purchase and tell their bank, "My AI bought that, not me," a false claim the payments company Worldpay already counts as fraud. If the store can show a confirmed approval for that purchase, it wins. The record protects customers, too, when they need to show their bank exactly what they told the agent to buy.

OpenAI plans to stop asking people to approve every purchase. Over time, the company says, people will be able to give an agent standing rules, such as a spending limit, a type of purchase, or a time period, and approve its buying ahead of time with a biometric check that records the rules they set.

People would no longer have to scan a fingerprint at every checkout. The record would change, too. Instead of listing every item people picked, it would hold only the rules they set, such as a $300 limit. If the agent then spent $900, the fight would turn on whether the customers could prove the limit they gave it and whether the store could show what the agent was allowed to spend. Without that record, it's their word against a log they can't see.

#5507. Bezos and Bond: Amazon founder played a big role in casting new 007

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:36 pmNovember 17, 2026 at 6:36 pm

Jeff Bezos has a space company, a newspaper, an AI startup that’s raised $14.5 billion and, apparently, a seat in the room when Amazon decides who gets a license to kill.

Speaking Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, the Amazon founder said he was “heavily involved” in the casting of Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond, a pick Amazon MGM Studios announced Monday.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond franchise when it acquired MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, then took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

Bezos said a large initial pool of would-be Bonds was narrowed to five finalists, who then did “real old-fashioned screen tests”: three scenes apiece, in full costume on real sets with other actors.

The other finalists were Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner, according to The New York Times, which reported that the tests took place in London in late October.

Bezos said the decision-makers got together Friday and spent a couple of hours reviewing the screen tests before settling on Pattinson.

“By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing,” Bezos said. “But there was something special about Rob Pattinson and his performances.” He said the group, including director Denis Villeneuve, reached a quick consensus. It was “kind of immediately undebated.”

Bezos admitted that the group was initially “slightly biased” against Pattinson because he’s already so famous.

“We sort of thought, you know, maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown,” he said. “But in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.”

#5506. She Left Bank of America to Sell Empanadas From Her Back Porch. Now Customers Drive From Out of State to Try Her Food.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Maria Leon Rodriguez’s La Colombiana went from back-porch side hustle in 2020 to full-time food truck six years later.

Maria Leon Rodriguez traded deposit slips for empanadas. The former Bank of America employee now runs La Colombiana Hamburger, a food truck business in Fitchburg, Massachusetts, that draws customers from as far as Boston and New Hampshire, according to Edible Boston.

Rodriguez got her start serving empanadas, arepas and hot dogs with tangy sauces and melted cheese from her back porch. Word spread faster than the cheese could melt. She enrolled in the Worcester Regional Food Hub’s Launching New Food Entrepreneurs program, a free eight-week course covering permits, food safety, wholesale ordering and marketing. In August 2024 she opened a stall at the Fitchburg Public Market, a shared kitchen and food hall for small vendors.

Her bestseller is a Colombian burger topped with onions caramelized in brown sugar and butter. “I think my food gives people the comfort of home,” she says.

In July 2026 she bought a trailer and took La Colombiana on the road full-time. She still uses the market as her commissary kitchen. “Now people come from Springfield, from Boston, from New Hampshire to try my food,” she says.

#5505. SNL’s viral ‘Sister’ sketch asks why pay for elder care when a daughter does it free — a home health aide runs about $6,688 a month

A “Saturday Night Live” sketch that introduced a fictional elder care service simply called “Sister” has gone viral. The premise was simple: Why pay for professional care for an aging parent when a daughter can do it for free?

The clip, which first aired on Nov. 15, 2026, struck a nerve because this kind of arrangement is familiar and burdensome for millions of American families.

According to a 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, 63 million Americans provide ongoing care to a family member or friend, an increase of nearly 50% over the past decade. About 61% of these caregivers are women.

As researchers who study aging, long-term care and financial security, we’ve found that those who become caregivers initially have better health and financial status than noncaregivers. But they then experience relatively worse health and financial decline over time compared with their noncaregiving counterparts.

While societal gender expectations help explain why daughters often assume the bulk of caregiving responsibilities, government policies have also determined how much care families must provide.

One of the most consequential features of America’s long-term care system is that Medicare, the federal health insurance program covering most adults 65 and older, generally does not pay for ongoing care and assistance with everyday activities.

Medicare covers hospitalizations, physician visits and certain home health services. However, those who need help with daily tasks such as bathing, dressing, preparing meals or getting to the bathroom generally cannot rely on Medicare to pay for that assistance. Under Medicare’s home health benefit, limited personal care may be covered only when a patient also qualifies for skilled nursing or therapy services following surgery or a medical emergency and meets Medicare’s homebound requirements.

This distinction has enormous consequences. Someone over 65 may have comprehensive coverage for medical treatment but little help with the daily tasks necessary to remain safely at home. And this care is expensive: The national median cost of a home health aide was approximately $6,688 per month, while residing in an assisted living facility averaged $6,141 per month in 2025.

For many older Americans, paying for the care they need is simply out of reach. A 2025 Harvard study found that 76% of households age 75 and older could not afford daily assistance from a home health aide after covering housing and basic living expenses. When paid care is unaffordable, those responsibilities frequently fall to relatives or, more rarely, close friends.

Medicaid, the public health insurance program for people who are low-income or have disabilities, is the country’s primary long-term care payer.

Unlike Medicare, Medicaid can pay for personal assistance at home, including help with bathing, dressing and other daily activities. The program covered nearly two-thirds of U.S. home care spending in 2023. The divide between these programs dates back to 1965, when Medicare was created to cover medical care for older adults, while Medicaid was designed to provide health coverage for people with low incomes. Over time, Medicaid became the country’s main payer for long-term care as the need for these costly services grew.

However, Medicaid eligibility generally requires meeting financial and other criteria that vary by state. Many older adults must exhaust most of their savings before qualifying for assistance.

Even being eligible for the program doesn’t guarantee that all needed services will be readily available. States have considerable discretion over the home-based services they provide, and many eligible people spend more than a year on waitlists to get services.

Having coverage, whether through Medicaid or the dwindling options available through private insurers to pay for long-term care, is only part of the challenge. Finding reliable help can be a struggle.

The nation’s direct care workforce, which includes home health aides and personal care assistants, faces persistent recruitment and retention challenges. These shortages may get worse as immigration enforcement and deportations reduce the workforce – one-third of these workers are foreign-born.

The median hourly wage for direct care work was $17.99 in 2025, only $2-$3 per hour more than what fast-food workers earned.

When paid assistance is unavailable, insufficient or unaffordable, daughters and other relatives often fill the gaps by providing additional hours of care.

Family caregivers may have to work fewer hours or quit their jobs. These decisions not only reduce their income right away, but also whittle down their retirement savings and can depress the Social Security benefits they get in the future.

The federal Family and Medical Leave Act provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of job-protected leave to care for certain family members, but the leave is unpaid. And caring for an older parent with chronic health conditions may continue for years after that leave runs out.

Because women are more likely to provide family care, they also face disproportionate exposure to these employment and financial risks.

Over the past two decades, some states have begun to address these gaps. California, New Jersey and about a dozen other states, for example, have launched paid family leave programs. In New York and some other states Medicaid is compensating family caregivers. Washington state is helping finance long-term care coverage.

In 2024, then-Vice President Kamala Harris proposed expanding Medicare to cover more in-home assistance, an approach that would have addressed one of the main gaps in the current system. The Democratic presidential nominee’s proposal never moved beyond the campaign trail after Harris lost the 2024 election.

“Saturday Night Live’s” “Sister” sketch makes light of an uncomfortable family dynamic, but the issue extends well beyond whether brothers and sisters divide responsibilities fairly. Government policies are behind why so much of that responsibility falls on families in the first place.

When public programs do not cover the care older adults need, the need does not disappear. The work, and its financial and personal costs, simply shift to someone else. More often than not, that someone is a daughter.

Jane Tavares, Senior Research Fellow and Lecturer of Gerontology, UMass Boston and Marc Cohen, Professor of Gerontology, UMass Boston

#5504. AI agents are hunting down forgotten subscriptions — and saving people money

AI agents are canceling all the subscriptions that shoppers forgot to end. Some merchants are taking action and blocking attempts to do so

Nashville resident Scott Burka had been paying for his kids' iPad subscriptions and chess accounts without noticing. Muse, an AI agent Meta $META released in September to handle digital chores, found the charges. Burka told the agent he wasn't using any of them, "and it actually helped me cancel approximately $100 worth of expenses a month that were completely just under the radar," he told NPR. That's about $1,200 a year Burka had been spending without realizing it, or nearly two-thirds of what an average American spent on their entire subscription bill last year, according to Mastercard $MA and FT Strategies.

Burka isn't the only one. Other Muse users have handed the agent their bank and credit card statements and used it to cancel subscriptions they no longer needed. Each of those cancellations cuts off money businesses had long collected from forgetful customers. For subscription sellers, the money adds up. Stanford economists Liran Einav, Ben Klopack, and Neale Mahoney estimated in a 2025 paper in the American Economic Review that sellers take in roughly twice as much money, on average, as they would if customers never put off canceling.

Whether a Muse user can stop those charges depends on the seller. Lawyers at Venable, a firm that advises subscription companies on cancellation rules, wrote last week that no federal or state law says whether a company has to accept a cancellation request an AI agent sends on behalf of a customer. Amazon $AMZN has already barred Muse from buying anything on its site, saying the agent broke Amazon's terms of service. A subscription seller could try to block Muse from canceling the same way, and no law clearly says it can't.

Once an AI agent can read someone's email or bank statements, it can find every subscription the person is paying for, lay them out in one list, and cancel whichever ones the person no longer wants. Jeetu Patel, Cisco $CSCO's president and chief product officer, told Business Insider last month that a personal AI agent, on its first pass through his inbox, found he was paying $9,000 a year in subscriptions. Patel asked it for a table showing what each one cost and how long he'd had it, chose two he didn't need, and told the agent to drop them. It canceled both and forwarded him the confirmations. "I'm like, OK, that was kind of creepy how easy it was to do that," Patel said. "And then it saved me 1,000, 1,200 bucks a year just over there." The agent costs him $20 a month, or $240 a year, so those two cancellations alone cover it four to five times over.

Agents also catch charges their owners meant to cancel and forgot about. A Silicon Valley correspondent for Maeil Business Newspaper, a South Korean daily, wrote in September about paying Otter, an AI service that writes up meeting notes, $99 a year for several years. In 2025, the correspondent decided to cancel before the next renewal date, then forgot, and Otter charged another $99 in June. Muse flagged that charge once the correspondent linked a Bank of America $BAC account. The correspondent asked it once to cancel, and Muse took care of everything else, without the correspondent ever visiting Otter's site or hunting for a cancel button.

Sellers of digital services stand to lose the most once agents start turning up forgotten charges. Mahoney, the Stanford economist, points out that people rarely forget they're paying for pet food, because a new bag shows up on the doorstep every month. A credit-monitoring service sends nothing to the door, and it can keep billing customers long after they've forgotten it. The quiet monthly bill from a digital service is exactly the kind of charge an agent turns up.

The agents, in other words, haven't set off a wave of cancellations, at least not yet. That leaves both sides where they started: Muse users keep what they save, and sellers like the Times can still decide whether to let the agents in at all.

Sellers already have the means to make that choice. Kopit Levien told analysts on the same call that the Times has "the ability to permit, to restrict, or to block specific tools." Sellers that shut agents out could lose new customers, though. Jordan Mackler, co-founder and CEO of ScribeUp, which builds subscription-management tools into banking apps, said, "If consumers trust that they can easily see, manage, and cancel recurring charges, our data shows they are likely to expand their overall recurring spend and are more willing to try new services in the first place." A seller that blocks agents protects the forgotten charges it already collects but gives up some of the sign-ups that easy canceling brings in.

No federal rule settles the question. In 2025, a federal appeals court threw out the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) 2024 rule, which would have required sellers to offer a simple way to cancel and stop every recurring charge right away. In February, the FTC restored its 1973 rule, which covers only merchandise plans that mail members a notice of each upcoming shipment. When the FTC asked the public in March whether to bring back parts of the 2024 rule, lawyers at the firm Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner wrote in Legal 500 that the agency had taken only the first step of a process that takes years. In the meantime, the Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act, a federal law, still makes online sellers give customers a "simple" way to end billing, but it never says what simple means, let alone whether a cancellation sent by an agent counts.

#5503. Battery startup Sila lands potential $1B Panasonic deal, plans Central Wash. expansion adding 500 jobs

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am

Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, announced a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the company plans to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

Sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, said Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

“This is a really important blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he said. “We have to take new technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”

While the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky said. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

Batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

Berdichevsky said Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

In August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The company must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

The startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

The company has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round announced in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

Seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

Group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently announced plans for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky said.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our company’s history,” he said.

The first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

“None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky said. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5501. Grand Theft Auto made crime a game. AI is doing the same for hacking

Asaf Wiener is co-founder and CEO of Mate Security. He previously led core products at Wiz and drove the growth of Microsoft Defender. Mate Security sells AI tools for security operations teams.

Fans have waited 13 years for Grand Theft Auto VI. The wait for GTA V’s sequel dragged on through so many delays that it became a meme. When a game takes that long, you’d expect it to feel dated on arrival. But when GTA VI finally arrived this week, the opposite thing happened. The real world has started to look a lot like the game.

Six days before the launch, the FBI issued a FLASH warning about ARTEX, an open-source tool that lets AI agents carry out an intrusion “at machine speed, from reconnaissance through data exfiltration.” Some attacks reached privileged access in under three hours. The GitHub repository has since been taken down, but copies are still out there, and it has already been used against banks, government agencies, and tech companies. Skill, time, and money used to separate a bored teenager from a professional crew. Now a bored teenager with AI can operate like one.

Rockstar knows what a bored teenager can do. In 2022, a 17-year-old broke into the company and leaked early GTA VI footage from a hotel room, using an Amazon Fire Stick and a phone. That took some serious skills and marked the last time anyone would need them. Rockstar spent 13 years building a game that feels like real life. In the same stretch, real life took on the rules of the game. AI turned the hacking craft into a criminal loop. You pick a target, try, fail, try again, at almost no cost, with the push of a button, from your couch. While developing the latest GTA took more than a decade, reality caught up in a fraction of that.

That shift left defenses behind, because they were built for a slower pace. Attackers now run on three-hour clocks, while most security programs run on fiscal years. The best attacks don’t look like attacks at all. They arrive as job offers, invoices, calendar invites, and logins that look almost normal. Meanwhile, defenders are being asked to move faster and to tell real from fake at the same time.

When the first GTA VI trailer came out, half of the internet asked the same question. Is this gameplay or real footage? Corporate security teams ask that every day now. In September, a Binance engineer went through two rounds of interviews for what looked like a great job and downloaded the take-home assignment. It was malware. The FBI blamed North Korea, and Binance puts the theft that followed at about $6.3 billion. A day after Microsoft 365 went down this month, attackers were already exploiting the confusion, sending fake outage notices that cited the real incident number.

Now look at how slowly most companies change their defenses. Adopting a new approach means a six-month evaluation, a few more months to roll it out, and a pilot that waits for next year’s plan. I understand the caution, because security leaders have been burned by tools that promised a lot and broke things in production. But an attack that moves at machine speed doesn’t wait for procurement. Attackers are playing on easy mode, and the defense is stuck on a loading screen.

The obvious answer is to make defense faster, and speed does matter. But fast and wrong is still wrong. A team that misreads that signal will shut down its own business over a broken router, while the real attack walks in looking like a job offer. Making the right call takes context that even the best AI model doesn’t have on its own, like who owns the server, whether that user really logged in from Lisbon, and what breaks if a system goes offline. That context lives inside your company, and defense only works when your AI agents know it too.

The leaders I see handling this well have changed three things.

Know the business first. Before buying more detection, they make sure their defenses understand which systems matter, who relies on them, and what normal looks like. AI can’t tell an attack from a failure without that context.

Save the caution for what can’t be undone. Ending one session can be reversed in minutes, so it can happen right away, within rules the team sets. Decisions that can’t be taken back get a closer look and a person’s sign-off.

Change in weeks, not quarters. They try agentic defense early, measure how often it gets real cases right, and give it more room as it earns trust.

In GTA, players can reload their last save. Security teams don’t have that luxury. Companies that make the right call at machine speed will still be around for the next GTA installment, however long it takes.

#5500. Comparing Franchises? Make Sure AI is Working For You, Not Against You

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI is a useful tool in the middle phase of franchise research, but NOT at the beginning or end — here’s why.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

As I’m sure you’re aware, AI is the dominant topic of discussion across the business world right now. If you haven’t already become aware of how AI is impacting your business, then you may be living under a rock.

In the small business world, AI has already become instrumental in supporting under-resourced entrepreneurs. As a franchise consultant, I see this every day. Office support tools? Check. Rendering of services during a sales call? Check. Customer follow-up? Check. AI has got you covered.

Similarly, I am seeing more and more prospective franchise buyers using AI in the research phase. It’s become the first stop on the due diligence research journey, understandably so, since these AI tools are highly effective at comparing large volumes of information. However, as a franchise consultant, I’ve also seen where AI is being misused and ultimately causing more indecision and uncertainty than confidently signed franchise agreements.

What I’ve discovered? AI is most useful in the middle phase of your research. Let me explain.

The due diligence process can be loosely broken down into three sections: discovery, brand comparison, and final decisions. That middle, time-intensive comparison section? These are the objective criteria you need to compare across various brands. This is where AI is your best friend. However, those two bookending pieces (discovery and the final decision)? These demand nuance and rely on intangibles that only you can decide. This is where AI is a terrible tool.

So let’s break down these three phases of franchise research and parse out where AI is beneficial and where you need to rely more on your judgment.

Right now, if you go out to three different AI platforms and ask them what franchise you should buy, you’ll get three very different answers.

Why? AI is terrible at franchise identification. Since AI is pulling from the internet, much of the information is promotional. The real information is hidden behind disclosure laws / walls. Furthermore, AI cannot know the actual people behind the brand or concept — it can’t meet them in person or understand the differentiators and support that only come from getting to know a brand’s team.

Most importantly, identifying the brands that you want to explore further requires preliminary work — work that is difficult to shortcut with AI because it’s unique to you. This is where you’ll want to first hone in on your individual requirements and goals.

What role do you want to have in the business? Do you want to work solo or hire employees? Do you want a location-based brick-and-mortar business or a service brand that provides services at varying job sites? What industries are you open to and which ones give you the ick? Answering questions like these (and many more) will help to narrow down your parameters.

Be careful not to put the cart before the horse. Take time to answer these questions before you dive into nuances of different brands. Pro tip? Consider reaching out to a franchise consultant. Working with a professional can be very useful in this phase because they will be able to help you establish and develop your criteria and apply it to a variety of viable brands.

Once you’ve identified a handful of brands you are interested in exploring further based on the criteria you determined in the initial research phase, it’s time to start a deep dive into brand comparisons. In the past, I’ve seen so many candidates toil over these comparisons, entering data into spreadsheets and trying to make sure they’re comparing apples to apples.

Historically, one of the most time-consuming and tedious parts of the due diligence process has been comparing Franchise Disclosure Documents (FDDs). This is a 23-section monster document that provides you with a full breakdown and scope of a potential franchise. This includes everything from financial projections to territory information to complicated legalities.

Often, franchise candidates will seriously compare anywhere from 3-6 brands – that’s a lot of content to review in the FDDs. However, with AI, you can upload the brand FDDs and ask it to create a comparison of how they are similar and how they differ. Since every FDD has the same 23-section structure, it’s a good data set for AI tools to analyze and present to you in easily understandable reports, although there is no exact uniform way franchises are required to disclose information, so getting apples-to-apples comparisons requires very careful review of AI output.

Any other great uses for AI at this stage? Have it create a sensitivity analysis (best case, worst case and expected case) spreadsheet for you. Have it provide common financing options. Have it create projection models. Essentially, use it to synthesize all the information that will help you to make the final decision. Let it do the heavy labor, while you review and analyze the outputs.

At the end of the day, AI can’t make value judgments for you — that’s still more art than science. And more than anything, starting a business requires an emotional commitment and mindset shift–that is nothing AI can help you with.

Have you got that sensitivity analysis spreadsheet? That’s a fantastic tool, but a spreadsheet can’t make assumptions for you. To do this, you need to speak with individual franchisees and confirm the information during the validation stage.

You had AI break down common financing options? Great, but it doesn’t understand your risk tolerance and emotional makeup. You will need to determine whether you have the financial backing and spousal support to make an investment. Additionally, AI may be able to provide a list of financial professionals in your location, but it can’t make a recommendation for that person based on actual experience — you’ll need to network or rely on your franchise consultant for that.

Ultimately, AI is a powerful tool you should absolutely use in the franchise research process. However, it’s not a catch-all replacement for either finding the right business model or the final decision-making.

As I’m sure you’re aware, AI is the dominant topic of discussion across the business world right now. If you haven’t already become aware of how AI is impacting your business, then you may be living under a rock.

In the small business world, AI has already become instrumental in supporting under-resourced entrepreneurs. As a franchise consultant, I see this every day. Office support tools? Check. Rendering of services during a sales call? Check. Customer follow-up? Check. AI has got you covered.

Similarly, I am seeing more and more prospective franchise buyers using AI in the research phase. It’s become the first stop on the due diligence research journey, understandably so, since these AI tools are highly effective at comparing large volumes of information. However, as a franchise consultant, I’ve also seen where AI is being misused and ultimately causing more indecision and uncertainty than confidently signed franchise agreements.
