#5499. From LA to Memphis, 10 big US jails share one strain

WorldAtlas ranks the 10 largest US jails, but court delays, paperwork lags and disputed counts mean their headcounts keep shifting

The officials who run America's big jails and the lawyers who fight them tend to agree that these places have too many people in them. A jail is where people wait for a court date, for a transfer to prison or for release, and in the largest jails thousands of people are waiting on any given day. The complaint about that crowding comes from both coasts and from both sides of the courtroom. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani calls the scale of imprisonment a problem for the whole country, according to The Associated Press. In Houston, defense attorney Andino Reynal says his county locks up far more people than it needs to, according to KPRC Click2Houston. When an elected official in one city and a defense lawyer in another make the same complaint, a big jail's headcount is worth reading as a possible sign of strain rather than only as a measure of what a county can handle.

The number of people in a big jail depends both on how many people come in and on how quickly courts and clerks' offices move them back out. What speeds or slows each of those steps differs from county to county, so two jails of similar size can be full for very different reasons. Because those forces change, a county can see its jail population rise or fall by thousands of people within a few years, and officials in several counties now report counts far from earlier estimates. When a jail holds more people than it was built or staffed for, the people held inside and the county taxpayers who fund it both bear the cost.

WorldAtlas set out to rank the largest jails in the U.S. by the number of people held in them, a group that includes Rikers Island in New York, Harris County's jail in Houston, Maricopa County's jails in Phoenix, and Shelby County's jail in Memphis, Tenn. Each figure reflects one moment in a situation that keeps changing, in counties working to shrink their jails and in counties struggling to find room.

The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department runs the biggest jail operation in the country. It is a network of jails rather than a single building, and Men's Central Jail and the Twin Towers Correctional Facility are its largest pieces. WorldAtlas reports that the system holds about 19,836 people daily, far more than the 13,849 it counts at Rikers Island in New York. A newer local figure puts that lead in doubt. The Los Angeles Daily News reports that the county's jails hold about 12,500 people today. On that count, Los Angeles would hold fewer people than the Rikers figure, so its claim to the biggest jail depends on which count a reader uses and when it was taken. Either way, the people who set that number mostly work outside the jail walls.

The latest change came from California voters, not from the county. Voters passed Proposition 36 in 2024, and the surge in arrests that followed pushed the county's jail population up to a peak of about 13,500, according to the Los Angeles Daily News. Los Angeles County had no separate say in that vote, and voters across the whole state can refill a jail system the county is trying to empty. The added people entered jails that were already struggling with crowded housing, with the care of people who are mentally ill and with the use of force inside.

The county wants to shrink the system enough to close Men's Central Jail. The Los Angeles Daily News reports that the closure would require a population far below today's, which means moving thousands of people out rather than a few hundred. The sheriff runs the buildings, but judges decide who leaves them. "Neither the Court nor the County can predetermine or guarantee that particular individuals will be diverted, released, or otherwise handled in a manner that advances specific population reduction targets," said David Slayton, executive officer of the Los Angeles County Superior Court.

WorldAtlas ranks the Rikers Island complex in New York City second among the country's biggest jails, holding about 13,849 people. That rank rests on a headcount that more recent reporting does not match. By November 2026, the city held about 6,700 people on the island, according to The Associated Press. If the lower count holds, Rikers Island is a much smaller jail than its rank suggests. The gap fits a city that is working to empty the jail, and on Rikers Island the falling population is the main fact to watch.

New York City officials treat the number of people on Rikers Island as the obstacle to closing it, not as capacity to manage. The Associated Press reports that Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plan aims to bring the population down to a little over 4,000. Even the lower current count sits well above that goal. The city has to reach that smaller population before it can replace the island with jails in the boroughs. Every person kept out of Rikers Island brings the closure closer, and the size of the jail measures how far the city still has to go.

New York City has bound itself to a deadline it cannot meet. The city is legally required to close Rikers Island and replace it by 2027, The Associated Press reports, but the mayor's plan sets the closure for 2032, the year the last replacement jail, in Manhattan, is expected to open. The city cannot empty the island until its final replacement exists, and it cannot speed up construction by decision alone. Meanwhile, conditions inside have brought in a federal court. The New York City Department of Correction runs Rikers Island, but a federal judge has appointed an outside manager there. The court's step shows that the trouble lies in how the jail is run, not only in how many people it holds.

Roughly 10,000 people spend each day in the Houston jail run by the Harris County Sheriff's Office, a total that places it third in the nation, according to WorldAtlas. That count still leaves out some of the people the county detains. Harris County holds more people than its own jail can take, and it sends the rest to other places. More than 900 Harris County inmates are held in private facilities, KPRC Click2Houston reports, and some of them are housed as far away as Louisiana. The jail's own headcount therefore understates how many people Harris County detains.

The crowding began in the courts, not in the jail. The sheriff's office, which runs the jail, traces the overcrowding to cases that piled up in the county courts after Hurricane Harvey and then the COVID pandemic, according to a Harris County Sheriff's Office statement reported by KPRC Click2Houston. If the sheriff's office is right, the jail is likely to stay crowded until judges work through those delayed cases.

Sending people away costs the county more than keeping them in its own jail. Holding someone in an outside private facility costs an average of $91 a day, compared with $53 in the county jail, according to KPRC Click2Houston. The county pays for that overflow from its main budget, and a delay in the courtroom has become a standing expense for the county.

The county has tied itself to outside beds for years, not months, under a contract that runs until 2028, according to KPRC Click2Houston. At least one of the officials who oversee the deal is uneasy about it. "This is one of those things that keeps me up at night," Harris County Commissioner Lesley Briones said of the contracts.

WorldAtlas estimates that Maricopa County's jail system near Phoenix, which spans several facilities, holds 9,265 people. That estimate makes it one of the largest jail populations in the country. The deadliest problem in the system is the drugs that reach the people inside. Drug-related causes killed more people in Maricopa County's jails in 2025 than every other cause combined, accounting for 20 of the 39 deaths in custody there that year, according to AZFamily.

People held in Maricopa County's jails die far more often than people held in other big urban jail systems. "In the case of Chicago and New York City, they’re a quarter the rate of deaths that we have here in Phoenix in the Maricopa County system," criminologist Andy Hall told AZFamily. Hall is comparing rates, not totals. Maricopa County's large population cannot account for the gap, and the size of the system does not explain those deaths.

Jail officials have tried to stop drugs at the door, but the deaths have continued. They added body scanners and new drug-detection dogs, according to AZFamily, and four people still died in two weeks at Lower Buckeye Jail, between late June and the July 4 weekend. In Hall's view, the jail's own staff are one of the main ways drugs get inside. If he is right, screening the people who come through the entrance may not be enough to keep drugs out.

Curran-Fromhold Correctional Facility, Philadelphia's main intake jail, holds an estimated 8,811 inmates, enough to place it among the half-dozen largest jails in the country, according to WorldAtlas. As the main intake jail, it is where Philadelphia receives people into its jail system. Most readers would expect a population that size at a sprawling county network, yet this estimate belongs to a single city facility. On paper, a figure that large would make one Philadelphia building as busy as some entire county systems.

The size of the building argues against reading that estimate literally. Curran-Fromhold has room to house about 2,000 people, and the population figure is only an approximation. Nothing on record settles which of those numbers describes the jail on a given day. There is no evidence that thousands of extra people are crowded into its beds, and none that the larger figure counts people held anywhere else. The jail earns its place among the nation's largest on a rough estimate.

Metro West Detention Center in Miami is Miami-Dade County's largest jail, and WorldAtlas reports that it averages about 7,050 inmates, more than Dallas County holds in its jail. A county count puts that figure in doubt. The county's corrections department put the jail's population at 2,332 as of January 2023, according to NBC 6 South Florida. On that count, Metro West would fall well short of Dallas. One figure is an average, and the other is the latest count the department had given in early 2023, so neither settles the jail's size. Even the smaller count was the highest of any Miami-Dade jail at the time.

The jail's size is in dispute, but the rise in force inside it is not. Officers at Metro West used force 380 times in 2022, up from 198 in 2019, according to NBC 6 South Florida. Miami-Dade Public Defender Carlos Martinez, whose office defends people held in the county's jails, traced the trouble inside them to how the county pays and staffs its guards. "We have a serious toxic mix because they are not paying enough to the guards, and therefore, people are not even applying to become guards, and therefore you have a lot of officers spending overtime," Martinez said in 2023. If he is right, the county could ease part of the pressure inside Metro West by changing what it pays officers.

No one at Metro West lost a job as the use of force rose. No staff member there was fired for using force in the three years through early 2023, according to NBC 6 South Florida. The higher count does not show that officers acted wrongly in any single case. It does show that the jail's discipline record stayed the same while officers used force far more often.

Dallas County, Texas, holds its place among the country's biggest jails by a very slim margin, keeping about 6,385 people in its jail, slightly more than Cook County does, according to WorldAtlas. With so little room between the two, neither position should be read as settled. The Dallas count also captures a population that keeps shifting. The county recently kept its jail below 6,775 people a day for a month, which was its longest stretch under that level in more than a year, according to The Dallas Morning News. Dallas's rank reflects the moment the jail was counted more than any fixed size.

Some of the people in Dallas County's cells are waiting on documents, not on a judge. When a case ends, the jail needs paperwork from the clerks before it can release or transfer the person. Those papers reached the jail 20 days after a case ended, on average, in 2025, according to The Dallas Morning News. Part of the jail's headcount therefore depends on how fast the county handles its own paperwork.

The delay also costs taxpayers, and the county is trying to stop it where the paperwork starts. The Commissioners Court has approved at least $450,000 in payouts since 2024 to resolve civil rights claims by people kept in jail beyond their release dates, according to The Dallas Morning News. The county's answer is to get judgments right the first time. "If we don't get the judgment done correctly at first it doesn't matter how efficient we are on the backend because it's going to be kicked back," Steven Autry, Dallas County director of judicial and corrections operations, told The Dallas Morning News.

The change depends on the people behind it as well as on the process. The Dallas Morning News reports that District Attorney John Creuzot, whose office helped push for the new approach, lost his race for another term and will step down in January.

Cook County, Ill., cut the size of its jail through deliberate policy choices. Even after that cut, the county holds about 6,294 people in Cook County Jail in Chicago, according to WorldAtlas, enough to rank eighth among the country's largest jails. In the early 2010s, the county routinely held more than 10,000 people there, so the jail today holds far fewer people than it once did. Releasing more people before trial was one of the policy changes behind the decline. Most people in the jail have not yet had their day in court, and that made pretrial release a policy that could reach a large share of its population.

Releasing people before trial did not end the jail's role as a place that holds people with mental illness. When the jail's daily count stood at 9,000, about a third of those inside were living with a mental health condition, according to the National Library of Medicine. The county has moved many people out before trial, and the ones still held are more and more likely to need serious care. Those people remain in the custody of the Cook County Sheriff's Office, which runs the jail.

In Orange County, Calif., one agency answers for everyone the county locks up. The Orange County Sheriff's Department runs the jail as a network of buildings rather than a single jailhouse. Three of its sites are in Santa Ana: the Intake Release Center and separate central jails for men and for women, while a fourth, the Theo Lacy Facility, is in the city of Orange. On a typical day, the department holds around 6,000 people across those sites, the ninth-largest jail population in the U.S., according to WorldAtlas. That total is better understood as people than as a rank. Each of those people depends on the sheriff's department for medical care and physical safety, and the department's responsibility grows with every person booked in.

In Orange County, the cost of holding that many people shows up in what happens to them inside. The concerns raised about the system center on deaths in custody, the medical care detainees receive, and the force used against them. Keeping people alive, treating them when they are sick and not harming them are the most basic duties the sheriff's department owes everyone it holds. Those three concerns go to the core of that duty, and they are a truer test of a system this large than its place among the country's biggest jails.

The Shelby County Sheriff's Office runs the downtown jail in Memphis, Tenn., and WorldAtlas estimates that it holds 5,765 people. That estimate ranks the jail 10th among the largest in the U.S. Sheriff Anthony Buckner gives a much smaller number. FOX13 Memphis reports that he put the population at more than 2,700 during a Sept. 1, 2026, tour. Neither count settles how many people the county holds there today, and the correct one determines whether Shelby County runs one of the country's very largest jails or a much more modest one. Its place on the list is best read as provisional.

On either count, the jail has little or no room to spare. It was built for about 2,800 people, according to FOX13 Memphis. The sheriff's count comes close to that limit, and the WorldAtlas estimate goes far beyond it. When nearly every bed is in use, staff have few places to move people if part of the building fails. This building has been in service for more than 40 years, and in June its air conditioning broke down in a major outage.

Putting off repairs on an old, full jail doesn't save the county money. Instead, the bill grows when something breaks. "We know that if maintenance goes untouched, then it becomes crisis management and it becomes crisis maintenance. And we know that when we're in those states, it costs way more money than to make repairs when you're in a crisis state," Buckner told FOX13 Memphis. County taxpayers pay that higher bill, and the people held inside live with each breakdown until the repairs are made.

#5498. ‘Absurd ambition’: Pulumi expands into software delivery with AI agents that ship and fix code

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too big to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting new software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

“The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” said Joe Duffy, the company’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how big we’re willing to dream.”

The ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The company has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy said there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

Annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he said. The company isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

Pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the company in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The new products take that approach further:

To decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Duffy said he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

“Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” said Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”

Both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise plans.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy said.

AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy said. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Duffy said many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The new products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

Plenty of company: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He said Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The new products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he said.

“This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy said. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”

Bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

Neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy said.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy said no launch in the company’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

The business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy said. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

Duffy said Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the company, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy said, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

About 40 of the company’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy said Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building new products.

Despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the company, Duffy said Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”

Asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy said Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”

#5497. Gen X’s $2.3 trillion caregiving curse: I’m the sister from John Mulaney’s SNL skit and I did the math

Chandra Bozelko is a journalist who covers criminal justice and an editorial liaison at The OpEd Project.

On Saturday Night Live this weekend, John Mulaney sold America its oldest elder-care product. “Sister,” his pitchman explains, is a live-in, 24/7 caregiver who is “completely free, and also your sister.” Mikey Day’s Dr. Grant, author of Not It! A Son’s Guide to Elder Care, explains how it works: years of internalized sexism have convinced her that caring for Mom and Dad is her job and somehow not yours. The best part, another brother adds, is that the parents drew up the will before she moved in, so you still get half the house she’s deep cleaning. Within a day, the sketch had 2 million views on YouTube, and women all over the country were sending it to their brothers.

The joke lands because it isn’t one, particularly the part about finances. It’s impossible to create or maintain wealth while caregiving.

I have no brothers, but I’m the sister. For the last 14 years (and several years in the past) I have been my parents’ full-time caregiver, without pay. My father passed away in 2022 and somehow the work increased taking care of one parent. I clean up after her at every meal, several times a day. I manage her medications, take her to specialists, deal with her insurers, rub lotion on her feet, run her errands, log in for her on some device several times a day. I’m a columnist, and my work has shrunk to fit around her care: missed meetings, moved deadlines, the same explanation of her health given again to every editor and board I work with. Each year I earn less than I would have, and each of those years goes into my Social Security record as a smaller number, almost a zero in 2024. Whatever I do earn goes to medical supplies and surprise expenses. I don’t invoice for any of this so, technically, nobody owes me anything. But he cost is borne by me.

Earlier this month, AARP released a report, built on the Urban Institute’s long-range income model, estimating that the typical working caregiver will lose $120,500 over her lifetime in wages, workplace retirement income and Social Security. Across a single generation of caregivers, those born in the early 1980s, the losses come to $2.3 trillion. And that study counts only caregivers who kept their jobs. The sister in the sketch, the one who moved in, isn’t in that number. Her losses are larger because the damage doesn’t end when the caregiving does. Social Security calculates benefits from a worker’s 35 highest-earning years, and every year without a paycheck goes into that average as a zero. A woman who leaves work for five years to care for a parent doesn’t just lose five years of income. She locks in a smaller check for the rest of her life, long after the person she cared for has died.

In 2024, America’s 59 million family caregivers provided 49.5 billion hours of care, work the AARP Public Policy Institute values at $1.01 trillion, more than total Medicaid spending that year. Three in five of those caregivers are women. But the trillion-dollar figure measures only what the care is worth. It says nothing about what the care costs the person giving it, or where that money ends up. The will joke does. It is the most precise line of economic analysis anyone has delivered on caregiving this year: she does the work, and the family’s wealth is split as if she hadn’t.

Meanwhile, she is spending down whatever she had. AARP’s 2026 out-of-pocket study, released in October, found that caregivers now spend an average of $11,508 a year on caregiving, nearly 60 percent more than in 2021 and about 31 percent of household income. Caregivers who retired earlier than planned spend more, $18,940 a year. Most of it goes to housing, food and medical bills: the mortgage on the parents’ house, the groceries, the copays. Research cited by the TIAA Institute found that nearly a quarter of caregivers have less than $1,000 saved for retirement. Caregiving doesn’t just stop a woman from building wealth. It eats the wealth she already had.

Her lost wages are a leave policy her employer never had to fund. Her unpaid hours are home-health services the state never had to buy. Her savings pay down the expenses of a household that isn’t legally hers. And her labor keeps her parents out of a nursing home, which keeps their house and savings from being spent on one. That intact estate is then divided, often equally, among children who did not do the work. The brothers in the sketch aren’t only getting their weekends back. They’re getting their raises, their 401(k) matches, their full Social Security records, and half the house.

This is why caregiving is so rarely described as a financial arrangement, and so often described as love. Calling it love settles the accounts in advance. No one owes her anything, because what she gave was a gift. Employers that face no leave costs, governments that avoid paying for home care, and siblings who get back to “my life and the stuff I like to do” all benefit from keeping it that way. The rhetoric of priceless care conveniently treats it as worthless.

Some of the fixes are already written. The Social Security Caregiver Credit Act, reintroduced in April by Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy and New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, would credit caregivers who provide at least 80 hours of care a month with up to five years of deemed earnings, so that those years stop counting as zeros. Congress should pass it, and extend it. Caregiving should earn retirement contributions, not just retirement credits. States can pay family caregivers through Medicaid at real wages, not token stipends. And families can do what the law doesn’t require: put the caregiving into the will. A sibling who gave years of labor to keep the estate intact has contributed to it, and an even split that ignores that contribution isn’t fair. It’s a transfer from her to everyone else who retires on full pensions and she retires on a three-digit Social Security check, in an apartment, while the house she cleaned for years is sold and split down the middle.

#5496. How I Turned Professional Relationships Into a Business Growth Strategy

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Leading a franchise network with more than 1,800 locations has taught me that the strongest business opportunities often begin long before a sales conversation.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I didn’t build that audience to create another sales funnel. I wanted a place to share ideas, recognize the accomplishments of people across our franchise network and connect with professionals who face many of the same challenges I do. What I’ve come to appreciate is that those relationships can create opportunities long before anyone has a reason to discuss doing business together.

Leading my business, Anago Cleaning Systems, a franchise network of over 1,800 small business owners, has reinforced that lesson. Growth requires more than finding the next client or prospective franchise owner. It requires building a reputation that gives people a reason to trust you before the first business conversation.

That thinking has shaped how I approach LinkedIn. My professional network has grown to more than 10,000 connections, but I don’t consider the number itself the achievement. The real value comes from the conversations, introductions and relationships that develop when people know what you stand for.

Here are four lessons I’ve learned about making professional relationships part of a long-term growth strategy.

Too many entrepreneurs treat professional networking as another sales channel. Their content focuses on what they’re selling, why it’s better and how someone can purchase it.

Yet people generally don’t join professional communities hoping to receive more sales pitches. They’re looking for valuable information, new perspectives and connections that help them navigate their own challenges.

My monthly newsletter explores scaling businesses, executive leadership, organizational culture and franchising. Rather than making every edition about franchise opportunities, I focus on sharing lessons that business owners can apply regardless of their industry.

That approach gives people a reason to stay connected. Someone may never become a client or franchise owner, but a useful idea can lead to a conversation, an introduction or an opportunity neither person anticipated.

Some of the most meaningful stories we share through LinkedIn aren’t about corporate leadership. They’re about the independent franchise owners building businesses within our network.

Recognizing their milestones, highlighting their accomplishments and sharing moments from our seminars and events provides a perspective that corporate messaging alone cannot deliver.

Prospective business owners want to understand the people behind an organization. They want to see how individuals are growing, what support looks like and whether the culture aligns with their expectations.

For entrepreneurs, there’s a broader lesson here. Your customers, employees and business partners often provide the most compelling evidence of your company’s value. Giving them visibility creates a more credible picture of the business than repeatedly telling people how successful you are.

One thing I’ve noticed through building my LinkedIn network is how difficult it can be to predict where a professional relationship will lead. Someone might initially connect with me because of an article about leadership, begin following my newsletter and eventually develop an interest in our franchise network. Another connection might work in commercial property management and find value in the facility management trends we share.

That’s why I’ve never viewed LinkedIn as simply a sales tool. I use it to maintain relationships with people who have different interests, professional backgrounds and business goals. Those connections create opportunities for conversations that might not otherwise happen.

As our network has grown, I’ve also come to appreciate how closely sales, marketing and recruiting overlap. A prospective franchise owner, commercial client, or future employee may first encounter our organization through the same piece of content. What happens next depends on the relationship we build.

I recently explored LinkedIn Premium All-in-One with that in mind. Based on the criteria I set, it suggested professionals whose backgrounds aligned with leadership, entrepreneurship and franchise development. I reviewed their experience and looked for shared interests that could make a future conversation worthwhile. Rather than approaching those connections with an agenda, I wanted to understand where a professional relationship might naturally begin.

The exercise reinforced why bringing sales, marketing and hiring capabilities together makes sense for entrepreneurs. A connection that begins around a shared business interest may eventually lead to a customer relationship, a partnership or a conversation about joining the organization. Tools that support those overlapping responsibilities can make it easier to spot opportunities without treating every interaction as a transaction.

Publishing content is only part of the equation. The conversations it creates can be just as valuable.

Sharing articles, discussing leadership challenges and highlighting developments across our franchise network help me stay connected with people whose experiences differ from my own.

That exchange matters. Entrepreneurs can become so focused on explaining their businesses that they overlook the opportunity to listen. A thoughtful comment, an unexpected question or a different perspective can reveal something worth exploring further.

Consistency is more important than volume. You don’t need to post constantly or turn every professional interaction into content. You need to contribute often enough, and with enough substance, that people understand what you stand for.

Leading a large franchise organization has taught me that growth rarely comes from a single strategy. It requires strong operations, capable people, effective marketing and relationships built on trust.

Professional networking is one part of that larger picture, but it’s an increasingly valuable one. Platforms such as LinkedIn give entrepreneurs opportunities to establish credibility and maintain relationships beyond their immediate markets. The challenge is resisting the temptation to measure success only through connections, impressions or immediate leads.

The relationships that eventually create meaningful opportunities often begin with something much simpler: an idea worth sharing, a conversation worth continuing or an accomplishment worth recognizing.

If you’re thinking about how to build those relationships more intentionally, LinkedIn’s new Small Business Playbook offers practical ways to grow your network, build credibility and find customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to see what fits the way you work.

When people already understand your perspective and trust what you bring to the conversation, the next business opportunity doesn’t have to begin with an introduction. It can begin with an existing relationship.

I didn’t build that audience to create another sales funnel. I wanted a place to share ideas, recognize the accomplishments of people across our franchise network and connect with professionals who face many of the same challenges I do. What I’ve come to appreciate is that those relationships can create opportunities long before anyone has a reason to discuss doing business together.

Leading my business, Anago Cleaning Systems, a franchise network of over 1,800 small business owners, has reinforced that lesson. Growth requires more than finding the next client or prospective franchise owner. It requires building a reputation that gives people a reason to trust you before the first business conversation.

#5495. Anthropic’s stock is now just 15 cents above its IPO price, a stunning reversal of its first day pop

Anthropic’s stock has come within a hair of falling below its initial public offering price on Friday, erasing the gains made one day earlier during the AI company’s blockbuster Wall Street debut.

Shares in the buzzy AI lab traded as low as $83.05 on Friday, down more than 14% on their second day of trading, before recovering some ground and climbing to roughly $87 in midday trading. The shares are down more than 25% from the intraday high of $115.10 they achieved on Thursday, the first day the stock traded.At its lowest point on Friday, Anthropic’s stock traded just a nickel above its IPO price of $83, at which Anthropic was valued at approximately $1.5 trillion.The retreat in the stock comes amid broader weakness in technology shares, as investors reassess valuations across the board. Problems at AI giant Nvidia and the results of the midterm elections have also worried the markets in recent weeks.

Anthropic’s decline marks a sharp reversal from Thursday’s opening session, when Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, 34% above the IPO price, and then surged even higher, briefly pushing the company’s market capitalization above $2 trillion. The stock quickly pared back those gains though to close at $97.17, still 17% above its offering price and an impressive first day.

Anthropic’s IPO was one of the largest in history, with the company raising approximately $91 billion through the share sale (including a 147 million-share over-allotment sold by the deal’s underwriters on Friday), plus an additional $26 billion private placement. All told, Anthropic raised more than $115 billion in the offering—capital that will be vital to its efforts to stay ahead in the AI race, regardless of how the stock trades in the coming days and weeks.

#5493. Nvidia employees alleged Jensen Huang threatened and harassed staff, 2007 suit shows

Claims by two staffers, including Nvidia's first in-house lawyer, surfaced as Huang seeks to return as CEO; his representative called them false

Two Nvidia $NVDA employees accused Jensen Huang, then the company's CEO, of threatening staff and making sexually explicit remarks, according to allegations in a 2007 California lawsuit described by Bloomberg.

Stephen Pettigrew, Nvidia's first in-house lawyer, stated in California Superior Court filings that he witnessed Huang berate and menace employees. Pettigrew claimed his dismissal came after he voiced worries about how executives behaved. The company pointed to shortcomings in his job performance as the reason it let him go.

"He would scream at them, threaten them with extreme bodily harm and make sexually oriented comments while thrusting his hips in a demonstration of the sex act," according to a brief filed by Pettigrew's attorneys in the age discrimination and wrongful termination suit.

Court filings in the case also describe an unnamed "senior executive at Nvidia" accused of making sexual comments and of vowing to tear an employee's arm off and hit them with it, according to Bloomberg. Pettigrew demanded upward of $2.6 million in compensation. Nvidia once offered $175,000 to resolve the matter, according to court records.

Nvidia filed counterclaims of its own, demanding that Pettigrew give back company records. The dispute concluded with a private agreement reached in December 2009.

Michael Winston, Nvidia's senior vice president for human resources, lodged a 2005 complaint alleging discrimination. He claimed he was dismissed for protesting "Huang's abusive treatment of employees, including conduct he believed constituted sexual harassment." Details of that complaint appear in documents from Pettigrew's case. Deposition testimony in that case indicated Winston was brought on in September 2004 and remained for only four weeks.

A representative for Huang said: "These false allegations are from over 20 years ago and were made by two fired employees. The thousands of employees who have shown support for Jensen over the last week show they are false." Nvidia representatives did not respond to requests for comment. Pettigrew and Winston have both died, and lawyers who represented them or their relatives did not respond to attempts to reach them.

Huang, 63, stepped down as CEO earlier this month in the wake of revelations about two extramarital affairs, according to Bloomberg. He is now petitioning directors for permission to come back, and both the board and senior management have publicly said no. Huang has acknowledged "torturing" the people closest to him in order to draw out their best efforts, Bloomberg said.

Some Nvidia employees have urged the board to bring Huang back. An internal suggestion-box post asking directors to weigh employee sentiment has drawn more than 1,600 replies, and a number of them call for restoring him to the role. Nvidia named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO, and the board is searching for a permanent chief executive.

#5492. Solana Tokenized Stock Hits $1.2B as Wall Street Moves Equities Onchain

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Solana’s tokenized stock market has reached $1.22 billion in circulating value, nearly doubling in less than a month as demand for blockchain-based equities accelerates.

Growth has been driven by platforms including Ondo Finance, xStocks and Backpack Securities, which are bringing exposure to major US companies onto Solana. Apple, Nvidia, Tesla and other household names are increasingly appearing in crypto wallets and decentralized trading platforms.

The expansion is also attracting traditional financial infrastructure. The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC) plans to connect its tokenization service to Solana in 2027, potentially opening another route for established securities to enter blockchain markets.

JUST IN: Tokenized equities are now a billion dollar asset class on Solana.$1.22B in circulating value, nearly double where October closed. pic.twitter.com/d7T8UgQIfM

Ondo Finance has become one of the biggest contributors to Solana’s tokenized stock market. The platform brought more than 200 tokenized US stocks and ETFs to the network in January, covering companies such as Nvidia, Apple, and Meta.

Its expansion has continued through additional trading and wallet integrations. According to the Solana Foundation’s October ecosystem report, Ondo’s tokenized assets on Solana surpassed $500 million.

Meanwhile, xStocks has accumulated $7.5 billion in trading volume on Solana, while Backpack Securities has processed more than $6 billion in tokenized asset trading volume.

Securitize is also expanding its presence. The company added 13 US equities to its Solana-based offering on November 2, bringing its total catalogue to 25 stocks. Its products include shares in Exxon Mobil, Disney, Salesforce, and GameStop. Unlike purely synthetic products, Securitize says its tokens are backed one-to-one by underlying shares and provide security entitlements with applicable economic and ownership rights.

The biggest institutional development came on November 12, when DTCC announced plans to connect its Tokenization Service to Solana during the second half of 2027. The integration would allow eligible securities held through its Depository Trust Company subsidiary to become available in tokenized form on Solana.

We are advancing our multi-chain strategy with plans to connect the DTCC Tokenization Service with @solana, expanding network choice for market participants.DTC-tokenized assets are expected to be available on Solana in the second half of 2027. ➡️ https://t.co/OdWc9KDeQS pic.twitter.com/vLTK1291A3

DTCC is one of the most important pieces of infrastructure in US financial markets. Its subsidiaries processed $4.7 quadrillion in securities transactions during 2025, while its depository provided custody and asset servicing for $114 trillion in securities.

The initial tokenization service launched on October 28, with support for Canton Network and DTCC’s private Besu network. Solana will become another destination as the company expands its blockchain integrations.

Twenty financial institutions signed agreements to access the service at launch, including JPMorgan, Bank of America, Citi, Morgan Stanley and UBS. DTCC says tokenized securities distributed through its service will retain the ownership rights, investor protections and regulatory safeguards associated with traditionally held securities.

This gives Solana a potential connection to established securities infrastructure rather than relying exclusively on crypto-native issuers and trading platforms. But the integration is still planned for 2027.

As of now, the $1.22 billion milestone reflects a relatively small market compared with traditional equities. But the combination of expanding stock offerings, billions in cumulative trading activity, and growing institutional involvement suggests tokenization is becoming a more serious part of Solana’s financial ecosystem.

Solana is attracting billions in tokenized stock trading, but Bitcoin Hyper is betting that the next opportunity lies in bringing Bitcoin liquidity into a faster, more flexible blockchain environment.

Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER) is developing a Bitcoin Layer 2 powered by the Solana Virtual Machine (SVM). The architecture aims to combine Bitcoin’s enormous liquidity base with the speed and programmability associated with Solana.

Users will be able to bridge BTC into the Layer 2, where they can access faster transactions, decentralized exchanges, staking, and other DeFi applications. Its design also uses zero-knowledge proofs and periodic state commitments to Bitcoin for settlement.

That combination could open an interesting route for tokenized financial markets. Solana has already demonstrated demand for bringing traditional equities onchain. Bitcoin Hyper is targeting a different pool of capital: Bitcoin holders who want access to applications beyond simply holding BTC.

The project has already attracted more than $33 million during its presale, while its testnet infrastructure is taking shape. Its wallet, explorer, faucet, and testnet bridge are among the components being rolled out ahead of the next development phase.

The HYPER token currently costs just $0.0136, with presale staking offering an advertised 35% APY. That yield gives early participants another incentive to hold their tokens while the network develops. For comparison, conventional SOL staking yields are considerably lower than that offered by the presale rate. Bitcoin Hyper is using staking rewards to attract early participation before its wider ecosystem goes live.

The fundraising milestone also puts the project on a defined timeline. Bitcoin Hyper’s presale is scheduled to conclude on November 26, leaving buyers with a shrinking window before the next stage.

#5491. ‘It might be too tough’: Trump second-guessed his immigration crackdown after the midterms. Then his Labor Department doubled down

After a blue wave in the November midterms, President Donald Trump told CBS News’ 60 Minutes on Nov. 8 that his immigration crackdown “might be too tough.”

His administration just doubled down anyway. On Nov. 17, the Labor Department proposed an overhaul of the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, the step most employers have to clear before sponsoring a foreign worker for a green card. Companies would face longer recruitment campaigns and a two-year bar on filing after laying off U.S. workers in similar jobs, and occupations in short supply, including nurses, would lose their exemption from the standard labor market test. For companies that sponsor foreign hires, that means more time, more paperwork and more ways to get turned down. The Labor Department received 117,849 PERM applications in fiscal 2025, down 22.4% from the year before.

“I think I got an A plus for closing up the border. I got very high marks for getting the bad ones out,” Trump said. “But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs that created one violation of breaking the law—and that was that they came into the country illegally.”

“I think it might be too tough, yeah,” Trump continued, regarding his immigration policy. “And a lotta people would say that it’s great. But a lotta people think it’s too tough.”

And Trump has made the case for foreign workers before. In an interview with Fox News in November 2025, Trump conceded that the U.S. needs foreign labor due to domestic workers lacking “certain talents.”

“You also do have to bring in talent,” Trump said. “We don’t have talented people here. You don’t have certain talents, and you have to. People have to learn.”

The White House and Donald Trump did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fortune.

Under the existing system, employers generally have to obtain Labor Department certification demonstrating that there are not enough qualified and available U.S. workers for a particular position—meaning hiring a foreign worker won’t negatively affect wages and working conditions for domestic workers. The employers typically use the process to sponsor foreign laborers for employment-based green cards.

But the proposed changes would require employers to conduct more extensive recruitment campaigns, eliminate administrative exemptions and prohibit employers from filing PERM applications for positions in the same or similar occupations for two years after laying off domestic workers in those same roles. The department is also proposing to extend recruitment advertising periods to at least 90 days and impose additional documentation and reporting requirements on employers.

The consequential part of the proposal lands on the bypass standards—which have allowed certain occupations to be exempt from the standard labor market test if the roles were in need of workers. The standard requirement would be extended to occupations that are in short supply—including professional nurses and scientists of “exceptional ability.”

But Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said these changes would ensure American workers will receive priority for high-skilled, high-paying positions.

“American Workers are the best in the world, and they deserve the first and best job opportunities. Existing regulations have instead allowed companies to sponsor foreign workers without fully considering American workers first,” Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said in a press release. “This proposed rule change will ensure American workers are first in line for high-skilled, high-paying job opportunities over foreign labor.”

And in May, USCIS issued a policy memorandum introducing guidance that would also make it harder for foreign workers already living in the U.S. to obtain green cards without leaving the country. The memorandum emphasizes that adjustment of status is a “discretionary decision” over an automatic entitlement. Essentially, eligible immigrants already in the U.S. that can apply for lawful permanent residency through USCIS are not guaranteed.

“Given the significant privileges granted to lawful permanent residents, USCIS reminds its officers that they must consider and weigh all the relevant evidence in the record,” the memo read, “taking into account the totality of the circumstances to determine whether the alien is suitable for permanent residence and if approval of the alien’s adjustment of status application is in the best interest of the United States.”

The Trump administration also tightened employment-based green card sponsorship in September 2025, with an imposed $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B visa applications.

“The proposed H‑1B fee is intended to recover the costs incurred across the federal government to adjudicate, vet, and support lawful immigration programs that otherwise must be funded by taxpayers,” U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services spokesperson Zach Kahler said in a press release.

Comments on the proposal are due Jan. 19, 2027.

Joshua Hong is a News Fellow at Fortune covering data, AI, cybersecurity, energy, and retail.

#5490. Latest findings point to fuel supply, not Blue Origin’s engines, in loss of Amazon Leo satellites

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

The two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA said.

In its latest update on the investigation, ULA said it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

On Tuesday, ULA said early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

The BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp said Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the company looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

The finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own New Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn launches reserved for Leo.

ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA said.

The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA said it will share more as the investigation continues.

#5489. Anthropic mathematician claims he and Claude solved math's most famous problem

Levent Alpöge posted a proof in the Lean programming language, and the Riemann hypothesis claim awaits outside review

Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said on Friday that he believes he has proven the Riemann hypothesis with help from the company's Claude AI model.

"I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis," Alpöge wrote in a statement on his website. No outside experts have reviewed the proof, according to AFP.

Alpöge posted the proof in Lean, a formal coding language in which a computer can confirm each stage of an argument in sequence. The AI-written version runs more than 250,000 pages, according to The Wall Street Journal. He said his approach also settles the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, a more sweeping formulation of the same question, according to AFP. He plans to write up the full argument.

Bernhard Riemann proposed the hypothesis in 1859. It deals with how prime numbers are spread out. The Clay Mathematics Institute named it one of seven Millennium Prize Problems in 2000, each carrying a $1 million award. By the institute's criteria, a claimed solution needs a peer-reviewed publication and must then hold up for two further years of examination, according to AFP.

"If the proof is correct and understood, this completes a dictionary between different branches of math where the connections were only partial," Hector Pasten, a mathematician at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile, told Scientific American.

Alpöge said the result arrived as Sunday evening rolled over into Monday, a few days ahead of Anthropic's IPO, according to The Wall Street Journal. He called the timing "horrible" and sent CEO Dario Amodei a note requesting approval to make the news public. "The fact is that there was a constraint to respect," Alpöge wrote. Anthropic stock slid during its first full session on the market, and the company did not respond to a request for comment, according to The Wall Street Journal and AFP.

Anthropic disclosed in August that an unreleased Claude model had advanced a long-standing finding tied to the Riemann hypothesis without proving it, according to AFP.

The claim follows OpenAI's September announcement that it had claimed a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, another Millennium Prize Problem. A credit dispute followed. Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University, accused OpenAI of racing ahead after it learned of related work he had posted with Alpöge a day earlier. OpenAI said it never saw their work.

In October, OpenAI posted 722 papers claiming answers to open problems, including advances on the Riemann hypothesis. The company pulled three papers within days after finding errors, and said the results were "at different stages of verification."

#5488. Nearly 15% of Americans expect prices to rise 15% or more next year, a pace the U.S. hasn’t seen in 79 years

Even in 1979, the year of the Iranian revolution, gas lines and Paul Volcker, American inflation never got above 15%. It peaked just below that level in early 1980 before Volcker’s rate hikes broke it, according to the Federal Reserve’s own history. Prices haven’t risen faster than 15% a year since 1947.

A meaningful slice of Americans expects prices to rise faster than that over the next year anyway. “Almost 15% of consumers expect (or claim they expect) inflation of over 15%,” UBS chief economist Paul Donovan wrote in a Nov. 20 note titled “The benign inflation scenario.” In the University of Michigan’s October survey, 16% of consumers said prices would rise 15% or more over the next year, about the same share as a year earlier, according to the survey’s own tables.

The typical household is far calmer, and getting calmer. Median year-ahead inflation expectations “plunged from 4.7% last month to 3.7% this month,” University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers director Joanne Hsu said in the final November reading released Friday. That gap between the most frightened consumers and the data is what anyone setting prices or pay should watch. In the late 1970s, expectations that came loose from the numbers ended up feeding the inflation.

Since the government’s consumer price records begin in 1913, 12-month inflation has cleared it in only two stretches: on and off from 1917 to 1920, peaking at 23.7% in June 1920, and from November 1946 to June 1947, after World War II price controls came off, according to BLS data compiled by the St. Louis Fed and the BLS’s own history of the index.

To hit 15% next year, prices would have to rise about four times as fast as the 3.7% they rose in the 12 months through September.

Consumers “tend to expect future inflation that is higher than official estimates of current inflation,” Fed economists wrote in a 2016 note, in part because they remember price increases more readily than cuts and weight the things they buy most often. They also feel price levels, not rates: grocery prices were up more than 27% from five years earlier as of early 2025, the Minneapolis Fed noted, even as the inflation rate itself had cooled.

Partisanship matters, too, Michigan’s survey team has found. Independents’ inflation expectations “have consistently been closer to the political party not in the White House,” Michigan’s survey team found in 2024, and survey director Joanne Hsu said “the overwhelming size and persistence of the partisan gap has generated substantial economic uncertainty.”

Voters have already said what they think of prices. About 9 in 10 midterm voters called the cost of living a “crucial” or “major” factor in their vote for Congress, and about 6 in 10 of them backed Democratic House candidates, according to the AP Voter Poll of roughly 100,000 voters. Republicans took a blistering set of losses in House, Senate and governor’s races, AP reported. About two-thirds of voters said President Trump’s policies had fueled inflation; in 2022, only about half said the same of President Biden’s, AP reported.

Everyday costs weighed hardest. About 6 in 10 voters said they were “very concerned” about food and grocery costs, according to AP’s analysis of the poll, and about 1 in 5 said inflation had caused their family severe hardship, according to CBS News exit polls. Among voters earning less than $50,000, about 6 in 10 said they were worse off than two years earlier.

Americans have braced for price spikes before. In May 2008, with gas at records, Michigan’s year-ahead expectations jumped to 5.2%, the highest since February 1982, CNBC reported. Inflation did climb, to 5.6% in July 2008. Then the financial crisis hit, and by July 2009 prices were 2.1% lower than a year earlier, per BLS data.

The bigger miss came last year. Tariff announcements pushed Michigan’s year-ahead expectations to 6.5% in April 2025, the highest since 1981, with 60% of respondents volunteering comments about tariffs, the Boston Globe reported; the preliminary May reading hit 7.3%, before the final came in at 6.6%, per the University of Michigan. Actual inflation that April was 2.3%.

This time the median isn’t the outlier. Michigan’s typical household now expects 3.7%, the same rate as September’s actual inflation.

In 1979, the Iranian revolution cut output by 4.8 million barrels a day, about 7% of world production, and oil prices more than doubled between April 1979 and April 1980, per the Fed. This year it’s the Iran war. Brent crude is up more than 60% from before the fighting and briefly topped $117 a barrel in late October, Al Jazeera reported. U.S. diesel hit records in September. Gasoline was up 37.4% in the 12 months through October, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Those are the prices people see every week, and they drive what households expect. Donovan’s argument is that U.S. median inflation “has been falling to near pre-pandemic norms,” while the visible costs, airfares and diesel-driven shipping, come from the Iran war. Airline fares rose again in October, per BLS.

Fed researchers have tracked this pattern for decades. A 2016 Fed note found households hear more news about prices when gas prices swing hard; in 1979, a year when gas rose around 20% or more, more than 10% of households reported hearing bad news about rising prices.

Back then the inflation was everywhere. Consumer prices rose 13.3% in 1979 and 12.5% in 1980. This October, BLS said prices rose 0.4% for the month, with core prices up 0.3%. It couldn’t publish an annual rate, because it collected no prices in October 2025, when the government shut down. Bank of America estimates the rate at about 3.8% headline and 2.7% core.

Michigan’s median household expected 9.7% inflation in both 1979 and 1980, according to the 2016 Fed note. Boston Fed researchers Philippe Andrade and Michael Wicklein found in 2025 that the 1978–80 surge in expectations was “much larger than the increase that rising prices usually would imply.” More than 5 percentage points of it couldn’t be explained by actual prices at all; gasoline accounted for about one point. They call it the de-anchoring of expectations, and it’s what Volcker spent the early 1980s grinding out.

The central bank is the other difference. The fed funds rate went from 10% at the start of 1979 to 19% by the middle of 1981, per the St. Louis Fed, and unemployment topped 10%. This Fed raised rates a quarter point in September, then held them at 3.75% to 4% at its Oct. 28 meeting, with two officials voting for another hike.

In 1979, the typical household’s 9.7% guess was, if anything, too low; inflation came in at 13.3%. Donovan’s slice of consumers is expecting more than the Volcker era ever delivered, while the median household now expects 3.7%. The next read on who’s right is the November consumer price index, due Dec. 10.

Nick Lichtenberg is business editor and was formerly Fortune's executive editor of global news.

Sheriff was previously a vice president at DoorDash and has held leadership roles at Amazon, Starbucks and Parachute Home. His roles focused on customer experience, product growth, strategy and marketing.

Protect AI acquired Huntr, and Palo Alto Networks later acquired Protect AI.

“Huntr was a bet that open source gets safer when vulnerabilities are visible to the people who can fix them, even when that made life uncomfortable for vendors who’d rather keep things quiet,” Nygate said in a post announcing his career change and impending new baby.

Earlier in his career, he spent more than a decade at Microsoft over two stints, most recently leading teams that served the Azure Partner Experience group.

#5486. Canada is giving Ford $324 million to retool its Oakville plant for Super Duty trucks

The C$464.5 million from the Strategic Response Fund also supports a new stamping plant, and the government says it will protect more than 2,000 jobs

Cole Burston / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Canada's federal government announced C$464.5 million in funding on Friday to retool the Oakville Assembly Complex in Ontario, owned by Ford $F Motor Co.'s Canadian unit, for production of the F-Series Super Duty truck. The amount equals $324 million, according to Bloomberg.

The money comes through the Strategic Response Fund and supports Ford Motor Company of Canada's project of nearly C$5 billion, the government said. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand, the member of Parliament for Oakville East, made the announcement in Oakville.

The funding goes toward enlarging and re-equipping the Oakville plant, and toward building a new stamping facility that will let Canada make more big auto components at home. Ford has announced it will introduce multi-energy variants of the Super Duty trucks. Trucks built in Oakville will supply the North American market and be exported to other countries, the government said.

The government said the investment will protect more than 2,000 jobs at the complex and support production of up to 100,000 vehicles a year. The Ontario government is contributing C$294.6 million to the project.

"Canada is an auto nation, now and into the future," Joly said in a statement. "In a more complex global economy, that means protecting well-paying jobs and securing our world-class auto sector."

Bev Goodman, president and CEO of Ford Motor Company of Canada, said in a statement that the investment reflects the company's confidence in Canadian manufacturing. "Oakville gives us the capacity to build more of the trucks our customers count on and makes Ford stronger on both sides of the border," Goodman said.

Ontario Economic Development, Job Creation and Trade Minister Vic Fedeli said in a statement that tariffs and trade complexities continue to pressure the auto industry. He said the retooling and expansion of the Oakville facility shows the strength of Ontario's business environment and workforce.

Ford Motor Company of Canada is a wholly owned subsidiary of Ford Motor Co. and employs more than 7,000 people in Canada, according to the government.

#5485. ‘Half philanthropy and half protest’: Noah Wyle and Figs pair up to erase $200 million in real patients’ medical debt

After decades of playing a doctor on the long-running medical drama ER and today’s The Pitt, Noah Wyle has learned a thing or two about what it’s like to be a health care professional and the challenges patients face.

Now, he is taking that passion off-screen, partnering up with popular scrubs maker Figs with a goal to relieve at least $200 million of medical debt in the U.S.

“In my countless interactions with health care professionals over the decades, one thing that stays with me is how they try to do everything right for a patient while the system makes it harder than it should be,” Wyle said in a statement. “Medical debt follows people home, creates long-term devastation, and changes the whole experience of care.”

Americans owe at least $220 billion in medical debt, according to a 2024 KFF-Peterson analysis of federal survey data, and having insurance offers less protection than many assume. In a new Urban Institute study backed by the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, more than one-quarter of U.S. adults said they or a family member owed medical debt at the end of 2025, including 26% of those with health coverage. Hospitals were the most common creditor.

Separately, a Commonwealth Fund survey released in September found that roughly one in three working-age adults with private insurance are paying off medical bills over time, with some pulling from savings or spending less on food and rent to keep up. The issue has also come up on-screen in Wyle’s shows. In one episode of The Pitt, a construction worker who already owes $100,000 in medical bills lands in the ER with serious diabetes complications after rationing his insulin because he can’t afford it.

“Trust is the bedrock of the relationship between patients and clinicians like nurses, pharmacists, and doctors, and that trust is increasingly undermined by the burden, and even fear, of medical debt,” Allison Sesso, president and CEO of nonprofit Undue Medical Debt, said in a statement.

During the next three years, Wyle and Figs will each donate $1 million to Undue Medical Debt, which wipes out, on average, $100 of qualifying medical debt for every $1 donated. The commitment is projected to relieve at least $200 million of medical debt for over 150,000 Americans. The first round of relief is set to take place in time for the upcoming holidays, according to the release.

Wyle, Figs, and Undue Medical Debt over the same time frame will work to develop and share practical resources for health care professionals to help patients navigate affordability. This builds on Figs’ and Wyle’s broader “Healthcare Is Human” advocacy work, focused on addressing systemic pressures making it challenging for health care workers to care for their patients.

“This is an act of half philanthropy and half protest, to underscore what the need is, and see if we can’t get our arms around some better solutions,” Wyle told CNN.

Wyle also serves as Figs’ global brand ambassador and has joined the company on Capitol Hill to push for policies supporting health care workers. He wore the brand’s first black-tie scrubs to the Emmy Awards last year.

Figs, a publicly traded company cofounded by CEO Trina Spear, reported third-quarter revenue of $190.7 million earlier this month, up nearly 26% from a year earlier.

Sydney Lake is an associate editor at Fortune, where she writes and edits news for the publication's global news desk.

#5484. Cases of ‘GTA Flu’ Are Suddenly Spiking Nationwide. Is It Costing Businesses $1 Billion?

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Gen Z workers appear to be the super-spreaders as time-off requests surge up to 32% thanks to Grand Theft Auto VI.

A highly contagious strain of “GTA flu” is spreading through U.S. workplaces. Symptoms include sudden PTO requests, controller cramps and an urge to visit Vice City. The outbreak began yesterday, when Grand Theft Auto VI launched after a 13-year wait, according to Newsweek.

BambooHR, analyzing data on 3.4 million U.S. workers, saw a 13% spike in pre-approved time-off requests for November 19. Global payroll company Remote reported 32% more time off booked than the same day last year, calling it the biggest non-holiday leave spike of 2026, according to USA Today. Gen Z was the hardest-hit group, booking the day at nearly twice last year’s rate.

Some employers have given up fighting it. Logitech gifted its 7,000 employees a paid gaming day, and CEO Hanneke Faber plans to play GTA VI on launch day. At Fort Stewart in Georgia, at least 43 soldiers reenlisted in exchange for a four-day pass timed to the launch.

Economists disagree on the damage. One widely circulated estimate puts the productivity loss at $1 billion. Victor Matheson, an economist at the College of the Holy Cross, tells Newsweek he takes “no issue” with that figure in the short run. But over time, he says, planned absences mean “zero productivity loss,” since workers are swapping one day off for another.

#5483. U.S. lawmakers are nearing a deal to ban Chinese cars, sparing Mercedes

Lawmakers aim to send a bill to President Donald Trump by year-end, with Mercedes-Benz shielded from an outright ban

CFOTO / Future Publishing via Getty Images

U.S. lawmakers are close to striking an agreement that would prohibit Chinese vehicles from being sold in the American market, according to Bloomberg. Last-minute negotiations are partly meant to protect Mercedes-Benz Group AG, where Chinese entities together own nearly a fifth of the shares.

Republicans and Democrats from states that build cars are aiming to deliver legislation to President Donald Trump before year-end, according to Bloomberg. Backers of the measure are racing to get it passed ahead of the new Congress that convenes in January. Details are still being worked out.

If the measure becomes law, automakers such as BYD Co. and Geely Automobile Holdings would lose access to the U.S. car market, according to Bloomberg. Heavy tariffs, along with Commerce Department curbs on technology in Chinese-made vehicles, already keep those cars from reaching that market.

On Wednesday, Republican Senator Bernie Moreno walked automaker representatives through proposed revisions to prior legislation aimed at Chinese connected vehicles, according to Bloomberg. The changes include language that would exempt Mercedes from being banned outright. Automaker representatives were on board with the plan, but a Mercedes official raised concerns and talks are ongoing.

A bill that cleared a Senate panel earlier this year would have blocked automakers with Chinese ownership above 15% from selling vehicles containing data-transmitting technology, according to Bloomberg. China's state-owned BAIC Motor holds a stake close to 10% in Mercedes, and Geely founder Li Shu Fu holds another close to 10%. Together, those holdings put Mercedes above the 15% threshold.

Among the ideas being discussed is a more lenient standard for companies whose ownership is passive and carries no voting power, as well as how that approach would be set up and verified, according to Bloomberg. Bloomberg cited one person with knowledge of the discussions as saying lawmakers are optimistic a deal could be struck as soon as this week.

"We continue to meet with all stakeholders who have a shared interest in ensuring this important legislation becomes law in this Congress," Mercedes said in a statement, according to Bloomberg.

Republican Senator Katie Britt of Alabama, a key center of Mercedes SUV manufacturing, said she reviewed the bill alongside Moreno and expects Mercedes and her state to be protected, according to Bloomberg. "We understand that there will be some adjustments that have to be made, but feel good about Mercedes continuing to be able to thrive in our state and across the country," Britt said.

The White House did not respond to Bloomberg's requests for comment.
