#5482. GTA VI made an estimated $2.36 billion on day one. Now 1,600 Rockstar workers are voting on a union

Vice City has opened its doors. Rockstar Games released Grand Theft Auto VI on Thursday, and by the end of its first day the game had sold an estimated 24.6 million copies worth about $2.36 billion, including preorders, according to tracking firm Sensor Tower. Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, has not confirmed sales figures.

If the estimate holds, that is nearly triple the roughly $800 million GTA V took on its first day in 2013, and it would make GTA VI the biggest entertainment launch on record. But beyond the sales figures, cultural conversation, and think pieces, the people who built the game are asking for eyes on what lies beyond the pixels.

More than 1,600 Rockstar employees in the U.K. are voting through Nov. 26 on whether the company should formally recognize the Rockstar Game Workers Union, part of the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain (IWGB). The proposed recognition agreement follows four months of negotiations between Rockstar management and staff, and a yes vote would make it the largest recognized union in the U.K. games industry, according to the IWGB.

The outcome will test whether the studio behind the biggest launch in entertainment history will give the workers who made it a formal say, at a moment when the rest of the industry is cutting jobs and betting on AI.

In an op-ed for The Guardian published Wednesday, the day before the game’s release, Rockstar North animation programmer and union representative Nestor Uriarte laid out the stakes.

“Winning union recognition would be a huge step forward in securing a meaningful say over our conditions at Rockstar, but its significance would reach far beyond that,” he wrote.

Games like this take years and hundreds of people to make. GTA VI arrives 13 years after its predecessor. Those long development cycles bring constant reshuffling of teams, which can leave workers exposed to layoffs.

That anxiety is not abstract at Rockstar. In late October 2025, the studio dismissed 31 employees in the U.K. and three in Canada, and the IWGB accused the company of union-busting. Rockstar said it fired the staffers for leaking confidential information and that the dismissals were “in no way related to people’s right to join a union or engage in union activities.” The dispute is before an employment tribunal in Glasgow, where closing submissions were scheduled for this week.

There has also been a long-running debate about working conditions at the studio. In a 2018 Kotaku investigation into the making of Red Dead Redemption 2, employees described a culture of “crunch,” the long hours and intense pushes that come before a deadline.

One former employee recalled the development of the original Red Dead Redemption: “If you left early on a weekday or weekend, you’d get dirty looks. You’d feel the stare down, and sometimes you’d see it as you were leaving. There was this culture of, if you don’t put in the hours, you’re not worth working here.”

In a Fortune profile of Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick, Zelnick said delays are sometimes part of game development and that the company’s focus is first and foremost on making a quality game.

The vote reaches beyond Rockstar. Uriarte argues a union would also give workers a voice on AI, warning that “the skills that workers spend years developing risk being devalued as their creative work is replaced by AI.”

Former Take-Two CEO Ben Feder made a related argument in Fortune this month, calling GTA VI the last pre-AI blockbuster video game of its kind.

The cuts are already visible elsewhere. In July, Microsoft said its Xbox division would eliminate 3,200 jobs, about 20% of its staff, over the following year and divest five studios, even as the company trims costs to fund its AI buildout.

With GTA VI marking a generational feat, Rockstar’s union hopes to lock in job security and fair treatment for the teams behind one of the most successful game developers of the modern era.

In Uriarte’s words: “It’s something we can, and must, embrace for ourselves. The future of the industry shouldn’t be a game played over our heads.”

#5481. ‘Sister isn’t free’: Melinda French Gates fact-checks viral ‘SNL’ sketch on eldercare

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:

Sister will provide. True, French Gates said, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

She’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” New America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers said they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

“Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

She left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In its own analysis, The New York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates said she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”

#5480. I Didn’t Have a TV At Home — So I Built a Computer At Age 13 to Compensate. Now My Startup Is On Track to Unlock $1 Billion in Value.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

From an early age, R.C. Willenbrock was the “tech rebel” of his family.

This as-told-to story is based on a conversation with R.C. Willenbrock, founder of AIVC, an AI firm that rebuilds operational and service-focused businesses with AI. Willenbrock, 35, describes himself as the “tech rebel” of his family because both of his parents and his brother had long careers in finance. He started off in finance but ended up taking a different path deeper into computer science and AI.

In his mid-20s, he co-founded CompIQ, a startup focused on helping employers make compensation decisions. He served as its chief product officer until AI recruitment startup Stella.ai acquired it in 2018. Willenbrock began building AIVC, short for AI Value Creation, in October 2025 and is still working at the startup as a builder. The piece has been edited for length and clarity.

I’ve always been someone who has had high self-agency, a huge amount of self-trust. I grew up in Denver and somehow found myself many years later in New York City.

At an early age, you could call me the tech rebel in the family. The rebel in me came out early. We didn’t have TVs growing up in our household, so when it came time to try and figure out how to get a TV in the bedroom, I just built a computer with TV on it. I was 13 years old.

Early on, I was motivated by achievement and success, and I understood those pretty conventionally. I went to Dartmouth, then Morgan Stanley, then into growth equity. Those were paths I understood and respected.

In growth equity, I was basically a glorified cold-caller, talking to founders about businesses they had built. That opened up my sense of what a career could look like. I was curious about the problems they were solving, and I wanted a more direct hand in the outcome.

Over time, that took me into building companies, product development and work that was harder to explain with one job title.

The connecting thread was wanting to solve problems and have a direct hand in the outcome. It took time to stop measuring my choices against what looked like a prestigious career and start trusting what genuinely motivated me.

My first business was Stickworks (started in middle school), stringing lacrosse sticks for people in the neighborhood and on my brother’s teams. I hadn’t even started playing lacrosse myself; I just loved stringing the sticks. I was much less interested in collecting the money, which turned out to be a fairly important part of running a business.

CompIQ, the compensation benchmarking and pay-equity business I started later, taught me something harder. I put all my savings into it and made a lot of mistakes early on, including hiring mistakes. Eventually, the business was on a strong trajectory, and I had brilliant people on the team.

I never intended to start AIVC. It grew out of a persistent problem that I couldn’t stop working on. Through my work with companies and private equity firms, I kept seeing the same gap. People could identify opportunities for AI, but turning those opportunities into a better business required someone to bring together technology, people, operating decisions and responsibility for the result. That work kept falling between organizations.

My view is that AI is making more of the analytical and financial-engineering work in investing easier to reproduce. The hard part is understanding how much value you can create in a particular business and then actually creating it. That was the work I wanted to pursue.

Our first clients came in 2025 through relationships I had built over years. A few private equity firms gave us access to their portfolio companies, and we also had clients outside that network. They knew me and trusted me to deliver.

That history mattered. We had multiple paying clients before AIVC formally launched in April 2026. From the beginning, I wanted our commercial approach tied to outcomes, because I had seen companies pay a lot for work without getting the result they needed. The proposition was that we would put the right people on the problem and take responsibility for making the business better.

Revenue for AIVC’s first year is in the eight figures.

But the number we run the company on is the value we create for clients, because we only earn when they do. We align our incentives with the client — because ultimately our goal is to create value (it’s in our name: AI Value Creation). We get paid when our clients win, so our revenue trails the value we create, sometimes by a lot.

This year we will have created more than $1 billion in enterprise value across our engagements. Eighty percent of the quantified potential is tied to revenue or capacity-led growth, not cost-cutting. This is extremely important to us because most of the AI story revolves around cost-cutting and human displacement. We want to unlock growth by unlocking human capacity — making humans more human.

Be honest about the support that makes taking a risk possible. I’ve taken some big risks, and I haven’t always judged them correctly.

My parents were the backbone that allowed me to take them. They invested time, effort, money and confidence in me. I knew it was okay if I failed.

They’ve worked together for almost 40 years and built their wealth management business within a larger organization. My career has looked very different, but their backing has been fundamental to it. I also have a close group of friends who have been there through the uncertainty.

That’s part of what I want AIVC to provide for other people. There are brilliant people who want to build something and own a meaningful part of the outcome, but making that move can mean taking on more risk than they can carry alone. I want us to provide capital, teammates, resources and someone who will stand behind them when the first attempt doesn’t work.

Get specific about what you’re good at and what you’re bad at. That affects who you hire, what you delegate and where you spend your own time. If you can’t name your weaknesses, it’s easy to build a team of people like you and leave the same gaps uncovered.

Then be someone those people can rely on. You don’t have to be the smartest person in the room. You do have to do the small things well, including the work you don’t feel like doing, and keep improving when things are going well enough that you could get comfortable.

Before taking a big risk, work through the best outcome, the most likely outcome and the worst outcome — and what you would actually do in each. Taking a risk and understanding it should go together.

Talent gets you noticed, and habits get you where you’re going. Do the small, boring things right every day, the ones nobody claps for, because they compound. Most founders overestimate what one big move can do and underestimate what 1,000 small ones will do.

#5479. Google acquires Seattle startup Howie and its AI scheduling assistant

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the company’s experimental arm, announced the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith said on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

We’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD

Users cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it launched publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of users. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

#5478. Why the Startup Playbook Changes When Your Customer Is a Large Institution

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

In regulated markets like healthcare, a working product isn’t enough — startups must also figure out who pays, how adoption happens, and what to prove before scaling.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.

Healthcare is the clearest example. A company can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.

The same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.

Venture capital has historically gravitated toward software for good reason. Once a product works, serving additional customers often requires relatively little incremental investment. Companies can test features, respond to feedback, and expand without rebuilding their business at every stage.

Institutional markets operate differently. Sales cycles can stretch for months or years. Products require regulatory approval, third-party validation, security reviews, or integration with existing systems before customers can use them. Even when an organization recognizes a problem, the person experiencing it may not control the purchasing decision.

Founders need to ask different questions — What must we prove before customers will trust this product? Who controls the budget? What existing processes will the product need to fit into? And how long will it realistically take to turn interest into revenue?

Companies selling into institutional markets face two challenges, proving their product works and convincing customers to adopt it. Clearing one doesn’t guarantee success at the other.   Healthcare makes this clear. Consider a diagnostic startup that develops a test, secures FDA clearance, and demonstrates that its technology performs as intended. It has cleared an important regulatory hurdle. But it may still spend months trying to secure a billing code, establish reimbursement, and convince health systems to incorporate it into existing workflows. The technology works, but the business hasn’t figured out how to get paid for it or make it accessible to the people who need it.

As an example, Pear Therapeutics showed how regulatory success can collide with commercial barriers. Its flagship product, reSET, a digital therapeutic for substance use disorder, received a historic FDA De Novo clearance in 2017, supported by published randomized controlled trials demonstrating clinical efficacy. Yet Pear struggled to secure consistent insurance coverage. It spent tens of millions educating commercial health plans and state Medicaid programs and pursuing dedicated coding and payment pathways. Despite FDA authorization, adoption remained slow and sales cycles stalled. Pear filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2023, and its assets were auctioned off.   This lesson extends to anyone selling into regulated or institutional markets.

Early customer interest is often mistaken for evidence of scalable demand, particularly when a founder pursues a first customer through a pilot. A hospital pilot illustrates the distinction.   A hospital pilot gives a startup a recognizable customer and demonstrates interest in testing its technology. That may look like traction, but it does not ensure a purchase, wider adoption, or recommendations to other health systems.

Founders and hospitals need a shared definition of success. If results take years to evaluate, can the startup sustain itself until then? Revenue potential is often more compelling than cost savings alone. Founders must also confirm whether the pilot is funded and from which budget. Moving from innovation funding to operating funding often requires approval from another team or committee. A pilot may also remain isolated within the system; broader adoption requires integration with hospital workflows and processes—a frequently overlooked hurdle.

Has the founder or company addressed these issues in the pilot? Without clear answers, the pilot risks becoming a costly experiment rather than a path to revenue. End-user acceptance alone does not establish scalable demand, and investors can be misled.

These challenges make the earliest stages of company formation particularly important. Decisions about product development, partnerships, and commercialization can shape a company’s trajectory for years.

At Treehub, we work with founders at this stage, often when the opportunity is promising but the company is still taking shape. We encourage founders to think beyond the technology and understand the environments in which their products will ultimately be used.

That means involving potential customers early, identifying purchasing decision-makers, and understanding barriers to adoption before investing heavily in development. It also means recognizing the value of firsthand industry experience. More than half of the founders in our latest cohort were physicians, bringing direct insight into the problems they aim to solve and the realities of the healthcare system.

AI and new distribution models are also creating opportunities to enter complex markets more efficiently. AI can streamline administrative work and data analysis, while direct-to-consumer platforms and connected devices can help some companies reach customers and validate demand before pursuing traditional institutional channels. These approaches don’t eliminate regulatory requirements, but they can create alternative paths to market.

The traditional startup playbook still has value. Founders should test assumptions early, build efficiently, and listen to customers. But those principles need to be adapted to the markets they’re entering.

Moving quickly without understanding regulatory requirements can create costly setbacks. Securing pilots without a path to paid adoption can produce misleading traction. Building sophisticated technology without knowing who will pay for it can leave founders with a product that works but no sustainable business.

For investors, the lesson is equally important — don’t confuse early validation with commercial viability. Understand what a company needs to prove before it can grow and whether its business model can support that growth.

The most successful founders in complex markets won’t necessarily be the ones who move fastest. They’ll be the ones who understand the obstacles ahead, build around the realities of their customers, and know what needs to be true before scaling makes sense.

For decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.

Healthcare is the clearest example. A company can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.

The same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.

#5477. Your Business Is Busy. But Is It Actually Growing? Ask These 4 Questions to Find Out.

The last quarter of the year is the best time to find out what’s actually earning its keep in your business.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he said, “but you can’t do both at once.”

I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a company.

We tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

I think about Jack’s line a lot this time of year, because the fourth quarter makes business owners a little crazy. The year is almost over, you’ve got revenue goals to hit, budgets to review, and everyone’s already asking about your plans for next year. For a lot of founders, the natural response is to put their heads down and work harder. I’ve done it plenty of times myself, and I’ve learned that a lot of that extra effort goes into motion that never turns into progress.

I’ve spent most of my career working with entrepreneurs building businesses in smaller markets. They know exactly when payroll hits, and they’re building their companies without millions of dollars in outside investment. For them, time is as tight as cash. A business like that can stay incredibly busy for years while nothing really changes.

So before the year wraps up, it’s worth asking a few uncomfortable questions to make sure your time and effort are actually moving you forward.

Revenue is important. I’m certainly not going to argue otherwise. But revenue alone can hide a lot. You can grow sales while your margins shrink. You can bring in new customers who are a nightmare to serve, or hire a bunch of people and add services only to discover you’ve built a more complicated version of the business you already had. I’ve watched founders post record sales and still end the year with less cash and less freedom than they started with.

Before you set another ambitious revenue target, look at what your growth is actually producing. Are you more profitable? Is your team getting stronger? Are your customers happier? Is the business becoming less dependent on you? Those questions will tell you a lot more about whether you’re building something that lasts.

Entrepreneurs are idea people. We love trying new things, whether it’s a new campaign or some shiny piece of software that promises to change everything (cough, cough, AI). I’m guilty of it, too. At some point, though, we have to be honest about the difference between what we enjoy doing and what moves the business forward.

Take marketing. You might spend hours making social media content because you enjoy it, while most of your best customers come from referrals. Or you might be convinced a particular service is your bread and butter, only to find out a less exciting offering is generating most of your profit. The numbers don’t always tell the story we want to hear.

So figure out where your best customers are coming from and what they’re buying. A spreadsheet and an honest hour will get you most of the way there. And if you identify something that’s working, do more of it.

This might be my favorite question, because it’s where founders find the quickest wins.

Every business picks up habits over the years: Meetings that made sense two years ago, reports nobody reads, software nobody logs into, services that stay on the menu because they’ve always been there. Individually, none of these seem like a big deal. Added up, they eat a surprising amount of time and money, and they eat your attention, which might be the most valuable thing a founder has.

Look at what your team spends time on every week and ask a simple question: If we were starting this business today, would we still do it this way? If the answer is no, why are you doing it now?

I love setting goals. I’m a big believer in having a vision and building a plan to get there. I’ve also learned that a new calendar year has never solved an old problem for me. If your sales process is broken in October, a fresh set of goals in January won’t fix it. If you’re spending money on marketing that doesn’t work, a bigger budget just means you’ll waste more of it. And if you’re the bottleneck in every decision, adding more customers is going to make your life harder.

For the first several years of Bolt, I was in every meeting. That made sense when we were scrappy and fighting for every account. As we grew, I started getting in the way of the systems we’d built to run without me. Now the question I ask my team constantly is, “Do I have to be in this meeting?” Usually the answer is no, and the business runs better because of it.

You don’t have to overhaul the whole company all at once. Pick one or two things that would make a real difference, like improving your margins, simplifying an offer, documenting a process or finally handing off something you’ve held onto for too long. Then make those changes now, while you still have some time left in the year.

There’s nothing wrong with pushing hard to finish the year strong. I hope you hit every goal you’ve set. Just don’t get so locked in on a number that you lose sight of what you’re building. Most of us started our businesses to create opportunity and have some control over our time and our future, and a bigger revenue line doesn’t guarantee either one.

Jack was right that you can’t do both at once. So before you lock in next year’s number, ask yourself which season you’re in. If it’s a season to get bigger, run. If it’s a season to get better, give yourself permission to slow down and fix what’s underneath. Either way, choose it on purpose.

A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he said, “but you can’t do both at once.”

I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a company.

We tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

#5476. Zeno Power makes progress on an underwater power system that will eventually go nuclear

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really big step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

Zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

Nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles said.

Boles said the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles said. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”

Retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “important step toward undersea superiority.”

“Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”

Next year, Zeno Power plans to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

The maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The company is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

Since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The company has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

#5475. Genesis AI Raises $500M At $3.5B Valuation To Bring Its Robots To Factories And Warehouses

Genesis AI, a startup teaching robots to perform physical tasks by learning from human movements, announced Tuesday it has raised $500 million in Series A funding at a $3.5 billion valuation.

Premji Invest, Khosla Ventures and Eclipse co-led the round, which brings the company’s disclosed funding to $605 million since its 2024 inception. Genesis previously raised $105 million in a round announced in July 2025.

The company is developing both robots and the AI software that controls them. Its approach combines recordings of human hand movements with training in simulated environments, where robots can practice skills before attempting them in the physical world.

Genesis is initially targeting manufacturing, logistics and laboratories with its robot, Eno.

“We just want to bring something more elegant, more timeless,” co-founder and CEO Zhou Xian told Crunchbase News in an interview. “In the end, this is a very full-stack company. … We have to build all different pieces across the entire stack to make sure we can tightly integrate our technology stack together, and hopefully build the most well-polished and reliable product.

Other participants in the new financing include T. Rowe Price Associates, Durable Capital Partners, Bpifrance, HSG, Nvidia, AMD Ventures, Zoom, Samsung Next and Ericsson. Individual backers include Eric Schmidt, Eric Yuan, Jerry Yang, Xavier Niel and Zach Kirkhorn.

The company plans to use the capital to expand its computing infrastructure, increase robot production and hire more employees, Xian told Crunchbase News. Presently, Genesis has close to 100 employees. It is headquartered in Paris, with offices in San Carlos, California.

Venture funding to robotics startups has soared in 2026, with most of the investment going to companies based in China and the U.S., Crunchbase data shows. All told, global venture funding to robotics startups totaled $9.9 billion in Q3, more than double the $4.3 billion invested in Q3 2025, per Crunchbase data.

The closely related field of physical AI has also seen a surge in venture investment this year.

Genesis’s approach grew out of a challenge Xian encountered during his robotics research: The difficulty of finding enough examples for robots to learn from.

Language models have vast amounts of text to draw on. But robots need a different kind of data to learn how to move and for example, pick up and handle objects. They also need that data to better understand what they’re touching and what happens when they act.

Genesis works by using cameras and gloves to capture people’s hand and finger movements as they work, along with touch information. The company says its robotic hand closely matches the human hand and recording glove, making it easier for robots to learn those movements. Historically, collecting this kind of training data involves hiring people to remotely control robots, Xian said. Genesis aims to collect it from people doing their regular jobs instead.

Those recordings help train the company’s AI model, GENE. Genesis also uses its simulation software, Genesis World, to train and test robot skills in virtual environments. The company claims this speeds up a process that would take longer with physical machines alone.

Genesis traces its origins to a research collaboration Xian started in 2022, also named Genesis, while he was pursuing a robotics Ph.D. at Carnegie Mellon University. The project brought together researchers from more than a dozen universities to develop robotics simulation tools.

After graduating at the end of 2024, Xian teamed up with Theophile Gervet and decided to start a company. Genesis formally launched in March 2025 and expanded beyond simulation into AI software and robot hardware.

Xian said developing those components together would help Genesis make them work reliably as a finished product.

“That requires the intelligence, hardware and everything that goes into training and testing the robots to work as one system,” he said.

Genesis is exploring a rental model in which customers would pay for the robot and its software as a combined service. It has announced a partnership with LG CNS and has other Fortune 500 companies in its prospective customer pipeline, according to Xian. He declined to disclose revenue and did not provide a paying customer count.

Premji Invest partner Vedant Agrawal said in a release that the firm was drawn to demonstrations of robots completing extended tasks independently.

“Completing full tasks in real time, not just short clips, is what turns a robot into something a business can rely on,” he said.

Genesis says it is ramping up Eno production for industrial customers. Looking ahead, it plans to expand into hospitality and healthcare, then consumer and outdoor uses.

#5474. Amazon’s $18B bet on Anthropic tops $200B, for a moment, in the Claude maker’s historic market debut

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The company started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond company agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

The five-year-old company was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he said.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the company.”

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the company to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

#5473. Uncommon Thinkers: Andrew Redd’s audacious plan to turn ocean volcanoes into power plants

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 19, 2026 at 4:42 pm

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid quickly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he said.

He founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

“I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek said. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”

For Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

“I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he said. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”

After graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk company developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

“I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd said. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”

Redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in new natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

He wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

Redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who said the conditions would be “perfect.”

“You can tell,” he said, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”

In launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd said, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion company Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

While the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The company landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd said he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

Endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd said there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

The company now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

“This was always the end goal,” Redd said. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”

We’ll have one more conversation to announce. In the meantime, we’re very excited to see those of you who are coming.:)

P.S. We’re also headed to Berlin soon, including to interview Klarna’s Sebastian Siemiatkowski, who we last sat down with at a tiny coffee shop in San Francisco (before his company became Europe’s most highly valued private company). Hope to see some of you there, too.

Mark Hurd, who until last month was one of two CEOs leading the database software giant Oracle, passed away this morning at age 62, one month after telling employees in a letter that he was taking a leave of absence owing to health reasons. TechCrunch has more here.

SoftBank Group is assembling a rescue financing plan for WeWork that may value the office-sharing company below $8 billion, according to Bloomberg. The new figure is a fraction of the $47 billion valuation the startup commanded as recently as January, and yet it *still* seems a little high when compared with its bigger, profitable, publicly traded rival IWG, whose valuation is roughy half that amount.

Fun fact: Amazon went public in 1997 with $16 million in revenue and a market cap of $438 million. #ThoseWereTheDays. EquityZen allows accredited investors to access proven pre-IPO tech firms like Impossible Foods, SpaceX, Stripe, Rivian Automotive and Epic Games through its pooled funds. Explore EquityZen’s secondary market today.

WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann didn’t plan for his family’s control of WeWork to end at his death but instead expected to pass that control to future generations of Neumanns, too, says Business Insider.

The outlet reports that in a speech Neumann gave to employees in January of this year, footage of which it says it has viewed, Neumann is seen saying that WeWork isn’t “just controlled — we’re generationally controlled.” He reportedly goes on to say that while the five children he shares with wife Rebekah Neumann “don’t have to run the company,” they “do have to stay the moral compass of the company.”

According to BI, Neumann even invoked his future grandchildren, telling those gathered: “It’s important that one day, maybe in 100 years, maybe in 300 years, a great-great-granddaughter of mine will walk into that room and say, ‘Hey, you don’t know me; I actually control the place. The way you’re acting is not how we built it,’” he said.

These may sound like more outlandish proclamations from Neumann, who has a flair for the dramatic. (Talking to Fast Company earlier this year, he compared WeWork to a rare jewel, asking, “Do you know how long it takes a diamond to be created?”)

But before WeWork began coming apart at the seams, Neumann had every reason to believe that he could pass power down to his heirs.

ArsenalBio, a year-old, South San Francisco-based biotech outfit that hopes to improve the ability of T cell therapies to better fight a broader range of cancers, has raised $85 million in Series A funding. #5471. So you got a Microsoft Voluntary Exit Offer? Here’s what to do next

by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm

Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Big Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide, laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically.

Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a big decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman announced the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The company expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept.

Microsoft says the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.

The offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

All of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in new hires.

The worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the company decide for you.

I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a company right now?

Harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.

There is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

One of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

But it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.

It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one company.

“It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.”

Hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more important than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.

The jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI company today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.

Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual company. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.

The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software company.

It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.

Software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.

This cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the big platforms will copy anything that works.

The true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue quickly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

The bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

One venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

1) Think VERY big, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a company that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.

3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.

The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?

Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

There are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise. Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.

On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.

Other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

Whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Big Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a new role, a company of their own or a year with their family.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

Learn more about the technology making it all work.

#5469. Amazon threatens to leave NYC again, this time over delivery bill, as it rallies customers to fight it

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:02 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:56 am

Amazon and New York City are fighting again.

The Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to New Yorkers’ doors. It’s also asking its customers to help fight the bill.

The legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city. Amazon is the main target, but FedEx and several regional couriers would also be covered.

Companies would need a license from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which would also investigate complaints. The bill was introduced in February.

On Thursday, Amazon began showing New York City customers pop-up messages and a homepage banner that reads, “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The notices link to a form and a pre-written letter customers can send to their council members to oppose the bill, Bloomberg reported. Amazon pointed GeekWire to a study by consulting firm AKRF estimating the bill would raise consumer costs by $409 to $664 a year, but didn’t detail how it arrived at the per-order figure.

In a blog post, Amazon said it relies on a network of small delivery businesses in the city. “If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city,” the company wrote. “That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.”

Amazon launched its Delivery Service Partners program in 2018, letting entrepreneurs start their own companies to deliver Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans and uniforms. The companies hire their own drivers, while Amazon pays them to deliver and offers discounts on vehicles, fuel and insurance. The model lets Amazon expand its delivery network without directly employing drivers.

In a statement to GeekWire, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the bill “as written” would threaten more than 40 small delivery businesses the company works with in the city and the more than 5,000 New Yorkers they employ. More than 2,000 Amazon employees also work at its delivery facilities in the city, the company said.

“We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written,” Nantel said. “But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations.” Amazon said neither Council Member Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, nor Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accepted its offer to visit a delivery facility. The company also said customers sent about 20,000 emails to council members within six hours of the campaign’s launch Thursday morning.

The standoff echoes Amazon’s 2019 reversal on its second headquarters. That February, the company abruptly canceled plans to build a 25,000-person “HQ2” office in Long Island City, Queens, after more than a year of competition among cities to host it. Amazon blamed “a number of state and local politicians” who opposed the project, which drew fierce criticism over roughly $3 billion in government incentives.

Amazon stuck with its plans for Arlington, Va., and Nashville and didn’t reopen its search. Polls at the time showed most New Yorkers supported the deal, but Queens officials, labor leaders and activists fought it. State Sen. Michael Gianaris, who led the opposition, accused Amazon of trying to shake down governments to get its way.

It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections.We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.If… https://t.co/UWXVTJhRL6

City leaders backing the delivery bill see a familiar pattern. “Amazon is once again making spurious attacks against this commonsense legislation that would make workers and our streets safer,” said Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, who called Amazon’s warning a “dishonest scare tactic.”

City Council Speaker Julie Menin questioned Amazon’s cost claims in a post on X.

“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote, adding that the council is “crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.”

Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon’s subcontractor model “leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets,” CNBC reported.

Supporters, including the Teamsters union, which has sought to organize Amazon drivers and warehouse workers, say the bill would make the work safer and make it harder for Amazon to distance itself from driver injuries.

Amazon disputes that the bill would improve safety. The company said it has invested more than $2.5 billion in driver safety since 2019, that the serious crash rate for its drivers in New York City fell 35.7% from 2024 to 2025, and that drivers there have averaged nearly $24 an hour since January 2025, with required health coverage and paid time off.

Meanwhile, business groups have run ads against the bill and warned they may sue the city if it passes, according to CNBC. The measure is awaiting review by Menin.

#5468. October 22, 2019

SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son vowed tonight to “double down” on its investment in WeWork as he confirmed plans for a $9.5 billion rescue package that will provide up to $1.7 billion to WeWork cofounder Adam Neumann in exchange for cutting most ties with the company and will give SoftBank an 80 percent stake in the business. In a statement tonight in New York, SoftBank said it would “accelerate” WeWork’s path to profitability and positive free cash flow. More here in the Financial Times.

Forty-six attorneys general have joined a New York-led antitrust investigation of Facebook, officials announced this morning, raising the stakes in a sweeping bipartisan probe that could result in massive changes to the company’s business practices. The Washington Post has more here.

Limited partners or LPs  — the pension funds, the university endowments, the family offices that largely provide venture firms with their spending money — are receiving a lot of attention from venture capitalists, some of it unwanted. VCs have begun knocking down their doors with requests for fresh capital commitments so they’ll have money to invest if the market cools down.

The problem is, many of these LPs are already over-allocated. LPs traditionally invest in many asset classes, such as public equities, and they allocate a small percentage of their portfolio to venture capital. Suddenly, they’re finding they’ve forked over more than they’d intended to VCs.

There are several reasons for this situation. First, VCs are returning to them ever faster for more capital  — sometimes in less than two years’ time  — because they are in vesting at such a furious pace.

Compounding the problem, not all LPs have received returns from their VC investments that they can recycle into new venture capital allocations. In some cases, this capital is still tied up in startups that are raising much more money than in the past and staying private longer. “We have some large exposures to blue chip names where IPOs have been rumored to be coming for a long time already, and now it’s maybe 2021, maybe 2022,” says one manager who asked not to be named. In other cases where startups have gone public, falling prices have prompted VCs to hang on to their shares instead of distribute them.

The result is that LPs are having to cut back on the number of managers they can fund, and that could mean bad news for venture capitalists and startups alike. These LPs don’t have much choice. As the LP explains it, “We have a pretty structured allocation process, and we’re really trying to be creative,” she says. One venture manager who reappeared too quickly for more money was  “easy to walk away from,” says this person. “Others, we’re having to do financial backflips for them to remain strong partners.” Either way, this LP adds, “We can’t add any new relationships right now,” meaning new venture teams in particular are out of luck. “When [VCs] shorten their fundraising cycle by nine months to a year, you can only squeeze the balloon so much.”

SoftBank’s $100 billion “Vision Fund” is one big reason LPs find themselves in their current predicament. From the moment SoftBank began waving money around several years ago, it launched a vicious cycle. According to Chris Douvos, whose investment firm, Ahoy Capital, owns stakes in such venture funds as True Ventures and First Round Capital, “When Andreessen Horowitz hit the scene a decade ago, they changed the tempo of investing and everyone got more aggressive in their dealmaking as a response. Then SoftBank entered the picture in a big way, and it was like a16z on steroids.”

Blueground, a six-year-old, New York-based startup providing turnkey flexible rental apartments, has raised $50 million in Series B funding, roughly six months after raising $20 million in Series A funding. WestCap Investment Partners and Prime Ventures co-led the round. More here.

Databricks, a six-year-old, San Francisco-based SaaS business that’s built on top of a bunch of open source tools, has raised a massive $400 million in Series F funding at a post-money valuation of $6.2 billion valuation. Today’s funding brings the total raised to almost a $900 million. Andreessen Horowitz led the round with new investors BlackRock,  T. Rowe Price Associates, and Tiger Global Management also participating. TechCrunch has more here.

IonQ, a four-year-old, College Park, Md.-based startup that uses charged particles suspended in a vacuum, as the basis for its hardware, has raised $55 million in funding. Samsung and Mubadala Capital co-led the round, joined by Amazon, GV, and New Enterprise Associates. Fortune has more here.

Aurora Insight, a three-year-old, Washington, D.C.-based startup that provides a “dynamic” global map of wireless connectivity that it built and monitors in real time using AI combined with data from sensors on satellites, vehicles, buildings, aircraft and other objects, has raised $18 million in Series A funding. Alsop Louie Partners and True Ventures co-led the round,  joined by Tippet Venture Partners, Rise of the Rest Seed Fund, Promus Ventures, Alumni Ventures Group, ValueStream Ventures, and Intellectus Partners. TechCrunch has more here.

#5467. GTA 6 Flu Is Here: The Impact on Crypto Markets

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

GTA 6 has finally arrived, and millions of gamers are putting everything else on hold, including crypto portfolios.

After 13 years of waiting, Rockstar’s blockbuster release is already disrupting workplaces, dominating social media, and pulling gamers away from their usual routines. Even our newsroom is feeling the impact.

Tonight, the HEAT trade Miami for Vice City when they host the Milwaukee Bucks on a never-before-seen court, wearing an all-new uniform.Tune in to the NBA on ESPN at 7PM ET for A Night in Vice City.Find out how to watch in your area at https://t.co/sLWQH9hxi7 pic.twitter.com/zeihbzB7th

Could GTA 6 be stealing retail’s attention just as digital asset markets struggle to bring individual investors back?

The scale of the launch is hard to ignore. Reports put GTA 6 pre-orders at well over 10 million copies before its worldwide release. The game also carries expectations of $1.85 billion in revenue during its first three days.

Workers are making room for it, too. BambooHR data showed time-off requests for launch day running 9% to 17% above a typical third Thursday of November. A separate Zety survey found 22% of Gen Z workers planned around the release.

That is a sizeable chunk of the demographic that crypto platforms have spent years trying to attract. Gaming and crypto compete for the same online attention, particularly among younger audiences who spend hours on streaming platforms, social media and digital communities.

For us, checking Bitcoin prices, chasing the latest meme coin and following market-moving posts can easily become part of the daily routine. But GTA 6 offers something considerably more entertaining than watching another sideways trading session.

The launch is also driving enormous engagement across YouTube and Reddit. Sensor Tower estimates point to more than 50 million additional visits to food delivery and restaurant apps in the US over 30 days.

Crypto’s social media ecosystem could find itself competing for a much smaller share of that attention.

There is another reason the timing is interesting. Retail crypto trading has been weakening even as the broader market has attracted fresh capital.

eToro clients placed 62% fewer crypto trades in October than a year earlier. Robinhood’s crypto trading volume also fell 48% year over year in October, while Coinbase consumer spot volume dropped 59%.

The figures show that rising market valuations have not translated into the same level of retail trading activity seen during previous cycles.

This leaves crypto exposed to competition for speculative attention. Institutional investors can continue trading through market cycles, but retail often depends on excitement, momentum, and whatever narrative is dominating the internet.

But GTA 6 has all three. The game could temporarily pull casual traders away from exchanges, particularly those who spend their evenings chasing small-cap tokens and following crypto KOLs. Meme coins could be especially vulnerable if their usual audience spends the next several days exploring Vice City instead.

There is also an ironic possibility that GTA 6 could create fresh opportunities for crypto speculation. Gaming-themed tokens and GTA-related meme coins could attract traders looking to profit from the launch itself.

Bitcoin does not need gamers watching charts every minute to keep trading. But an industry built around speculation, online communities, and retail enthusiasm cannot afford to ignore where that attention goes.
